global temperature.name: Global Temperature
global temperature.description: The average temperature across Earth's surface, including land and oceans. A lasting rise means the whole planet is getting warmer, even though individual places still have cold days. This warming changes rainfall and makes many heat extremes more likely.

photo.alt: Earth seen from space, with Africa and cloud bands above the southern oceans against black space.
photo.caption: The Apollo 17 crew photographed the sunlit Earth on 7 December 1972. This view shows the planet as a whole; global mean temperature is calculated from observations across land and ocean, not from a photograph.
photo.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center / Apollo 17 crew

assessment.explanation: Internal estimate for Global Temperature: 8.6 out of 10. People: Heat illness and impaired access to safe work, food and water. Nature: Present climate-attributable loss of habitat condition across land and sea. The people component is 8.0 and the nature component is 9.2; each receives half the weight. We use assumptions about how many people are harmed, how much their health or daily life is affected, and how much habitat is damaged. These amounts are not measured worldwide totals. No extra points for permanent loss of rare nature are assigned without enough information about what was lost and how much. Assessed on 28 September 2026 using the available study evidence, which may come from earlier years. This describes estimated current impact, not a ten-year forecast.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for heat illness and impaired access to safe work, food and water and present climate-attributable loss of habitat condition across land and sea; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Consolidated current warming consequences; no projected tipping-point collapse, all-cause disaster total or historical-duration multiplier

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

incoming: Carbon dioxide builds up in the atmosphere and makes it harder for heat to escape to space. Continued human releases therefore add to long-term warming. The cited evidence gives estimates and ranges for this relationship.

Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.
With fewer reflective low clouds, more sunlight can reach and warm the ocean. In susceptible regions this reinforces the original warming.
Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.
When plants and soils take up less carbon dioxide overall, more of what people release remains in the air. This adds to warming.
If the ocean absorbs a smaller share of the carbon dioxide people release, more stays in the air. This adds to warming.

Removing forests changes shade, water released by plants and the way the surface absorbs and moves heat. It also releases stored carbon. Local temperature effects and wider climate effects are not identical everywhere.

Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.

Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed.

When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.

Some observed high-altitude smoke events temporarily cooled Earth's surface overall. The result depends on particle type, height, lifetime, clouds and the surface below, so the effect is not always cooling.
outgoing: Warmer air can hold more water vapour. When suitable storms form, that extra moisture can fall as heavier rain or snow. Warming does not make every place wetter.
Warming can increase decay, drought, fire and thawing of frozen soils. These changes can release stored carbon or reduce natural uptake, adding to warming that began from other causes.

Warmer, waterlogged ground can help microbes produce more methane, and thawing can expose stored plant material. Water conditions and the breakdown of the gas affect how much reaches the air. The size of this response remains uncertain.
A warmer climate changes the chances and strength of several hazards, including heat and heavy rain. Some can occur together and worsen one another, with different effects in different regions.

Higher temperatures, when combined with enough moisture, make it harder for sweat to cool the body. The change varies by region. The cited projection concerns tropical conditions rather than every place on Earth.

Warming changes the temperature contrast between land and sea and the moisture available in the air. This can change a rainy season's timing or intensity, with effects that differ by region and season.
Warmer conditions allow more heat into ground that has remained frozen for years. More of it can thaw. The projected amount depends strongly on future emissions and the region studied.
Warming can turn some winter snowfall into rain and increase melting. Where rain falls on stored snow, the combined water can raise flood risk, depending on the snow, soil and drainage.
At first, faster melting can send more glacier water into rivers. Continued ice loss eventually leaves less ice to melt, so the long-term water contribution declines in affected river basins.
Warmer weather can cause more rain instead of snow and melt existing snow sooner. Less water then remains stored as snow for later in the year.
Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.
Heat and drought can weaken or kill city trees. Losses are more likely where other pressures combine and trees receive insufficient water or care.
Warmer air melts ice at the surface, while warmer seawater can thin floating ice around the edges. Reduced support can also let ice on land flow into the sea faster.
Warmer air can hold more water vapour. Where moisture is available, this can increase humid conditions and add to the strain of hot weather.
Warmer conditions can increase how quickly water is drawn from soil and plants. Land can begin drying faster even before rainfall becomes unusually low.
Lightning Ignition under Fire Weather Conditions
Hotter conditions can dry vegetation and make a lightning-started fire easier to sustain. Whether lightning strikes and a fire spreads still depends on other weather and local conditions.
Warming can lengthen or intensify fire seasons in some regions. People's smoke exposure increases where those fires produce pollution that reaches inhabited areas.
Hot, sunny weather can speed reactions that form harmful ozone near the ground. Still air can let pollution build up, but suitable starting gases must also be present.
Human-caused warming raises the starting point for daytime and nighttime temperatures. This can make very hot days followed by unusually hot nights more likely, with regional differences.
Warming can raise nighttime temperatures and increase exposure to hot, humid conditions. The loss of cool hours can reduce the relief available after a hot day.
Warming can change moisture, air layering and circulation above subtropical oceans. In some settings this reduces the low clouds that reflect sunlight.

Warmer seawater holds less oxygen, and stronger layering can reduce the supply reaching deeper water. Together these processes can lower ocean oxygen. Projections depend on the future climate scenario.
Warming and added freshwater from melting land ice can make surface water lighter than the water below. Stronger separation can reduce mixing, depending on local circulation.
Warming and added freshwater around Antarctica can make it harder for very dense water to form and sink. The response varies by region and also depends on winds and other conditions.
Warming makes surface seawater lighter than deeper water. The stronger separation can reduce mixing and the movement of oxygen between layers.
Warming changes the energy in storms and the height at which ice melts. These competing effects can shift hail damage toward some places or seasons while reducing it in others.
Warmer ocean and air conditions can provide more energy and moisture to an organized tropical storm. This can favour rapid strengthening, but it does not determine what any individual storm will do.
Warming changes evaporation, precipitation and the timing of snowmelt. These can alter how much water rivers carry and when it arrives.
Higher temperatures and more intense hot periods increase the risk of heat-related deaths. Actual harm depends on health, housing, exposure and access to protection and care.
Warmer conditions can make jobs in hot environments more strenuous and dangerous. Humidity and physical effort affect how much work can be done safely.
Warming can create hotter, drier conditions and longer periods suitable for burning. Actual fires still depend on fuel, ignition and local management.
Hotter conditions put more strain on port workers, equipment and paved surfaces. This can make loading and moving goods less reliable.
Heat makes steel rails expand. Rails can bend out of shape if the heat exceeds what the track's design, installation and maintenance can safely handle.
Higher temperatures make damaging heat more likely during the growing season. Crops can struggle when conditions exceed the temperatures they can tolerate.
Warmer conditions can stress farm animals and change where some germs and disease-carrying insects survive. The effect depends on the disease, location and animal care.
Extreme heat and changes to habitats can put insects under pressure. Some populations may shrink, although the effects differ between species and places.

More global warming makes an Arctic September with almost no sea ice more likely. The assessment puts the yearly chance by the end of the century at about 1% with 1.5°C of warming, compared with 10–35% with 2°C.
Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity
Warmer conditions melt more of the partly compacted snow above glacier ice. Over time, this layer can lose space that would otherwise hold and refreeze meltwater.

Temperature changes can affect where disease-carrying insects survive and how quickly germs develop inside them. Some places may become more suitable for transmission, while excessive heat can make others less suitable.
Heat, drought and fire can damage plants and increase the release of carbon from living things and soils. This can reduce how much carbon dioxide land ecosystems remove from the air overall.
Warmer seawater holds less dissolved carbon dioxide. Warming can also make surface water mix less with deeper water, reducing the ocean's ability to store additional carbon.
Warmer air can support heavier short bursts of rain. Where water builds up faster than the ground and drains can handle it, sudden flooding can become more likely.

Warming increases the amount of water the air can draw from plants and soil. Where rain does not make up the loss, dry conditions can become more severe or last longer. The effect varies by region and season.
Heat and drying can strain forests in river catchments. Greater water loss and fire risk can damage trees and change how water moves through the area.
Warming expands seawater and melts ice on land, raising sea levels. A higher starting water level makes it easier for seawater to flood nearby land.
Warmer conditions can speed the breakdown of dead plant material in soil. Where losses exceed new inputs, soil can hold less water and support plants less well.
Melting snow and sea ice expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This adds heat and can encourage further melting, with the strength of the effect varying by place and season.
Warmer mountain weather can turn snowfall into rain and bring earlier melting. The effect is especially strong where winter temperatures are already close to freezing.
Loss of reflective snow and ice, along with changes in clouds and heat movement, can speed Arctic warming. These interacting changes help explain why the region warms faster than the global average.

In western North American pine forests, warming can help some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter. During severe drought, weakened trees may be less able to resist the increased beetle pressure.
Warmer seawater holds less oxygen and can mix less with deeper water. This can worsen oxygen shortages near some coasts, although nutrient pollution and local currents may have a larger influence.

Warming makes seawater expand, contributing to the rise in average sea level. Melting land ice and changes in water storage add separate contributions, while local land movement affects what a coastline experiences.
Hotter air makes it harder for the body to release heat and can strain the heart and other organs. Health effects depend on humidity, age, housing, existing illness and access to cooling.
Warming and related changes in moisture and salt exposure can speed damage to concrete and steel. Some structures may need earlier repair or have a shorter useful life.

Heat can change crop development, water needs and success in producing seeds or fruit. Harvests may become more variable, but outcomes differ where warmer weather eases cold limits or irrigation protects crops.

In the European models assessed, soil drought covered more land at 3°C of global warming than at 1.5°C. The estimated increase was 40%, with a spread of plus or minus 24%, so this is a model result for that region rather than a universal prediction.
A shorter sea-ice season can make some Arctic routes open to ships for longer. Actual use still depends on safety, facilities and whether the journey is economically worthwhile.

A study of 2,339 mainly undisturbed Northern Hemisphere river catchments linked each 1°C of local annual warming with an average snowmelt-flood peak 4.7 days earlier. Results varied widely between catchments, with a standard deviation of 5.0 days. The average is not a forecast for every river.
Warming melts ice within frozen ground. The land can sink unevenly, creating hollows, ponds and unstable surfaces.
Retreating glaciers can leave larger lakes of meltwater. Sudden flood risk increases where the barriers holding that water are weak and exposed places lie downstream.
Warmer air and ground can lengthen the thaw season and speed decay in northern soils. Wet areas with little oxygen may release more methane.
Warming changes how mountain snow builds up and how often rain or meltwater enters it. These changes can alter snow stability and the timing of avalanches near mountain routes.
Warmer air and ocean water can thin Antarctic glaciers near the coast. The point where ice lifts off the ground and starts floating may move inland.
Warming makes Arctic sea ice thinner and more broken up. This can change how readily winds and currents move it.
Dark sediment on glacier surfaces absorbs sunlight and encourages local melting. Warmer conditions can enlarge the small melt holes around these patches.
Warming changes meltwater, salty water pockets and light inside snow and sea ice. This can change when ice-dwelling algae grow and how much coloured material they produce.
Warming can increase meltwater stored in or beside glaciers. If that stored water drains suddenly, a large flood can follow downstream.
Sustained warming can raise the height at which snow lasts through summer above an ice cap's summit. The cap then loses its remaining area where snow can build up over the long term.
Warming may expose more bare mountain ground while reducing the cold, snowy conditions some species need. Suitable habitat can shrink even where the total ice-free area grows.
Warming coastal water can make more places or longer seasons suitable for temperature-sensitive germs such as Vibrio bacteria. This can affect seafood safety and exposure through contact with water.
Warmer air and sea water thaw ice-rich coastal ground and make it easier for waves to wear away. The effect is strongest along exposed, vulnerable shorelines.
Warming can destabilise Antarctic ice shelves through warmer surrounding seas. In some places, surface meltwater can also widen cracks and contribute to break-up.
Repeated changes around freezing can make water in existing rock cracks freeze and thaw. The resulting pressure can gradually loosen or move pieces of rock.
Hot, sunny weather with little air movement can help ground-level ozone build up. The gases that form it, clouds and air mixing also matter, so temperature alone does not determine pollution.
Warmer air creates more meltwater on ice surfaces. Water entering cracks can deepen them and destabilise ice that is already vulnerable.
Hot air makes it harder for an electrical transformer to release the heat it produces. Its hottest parts can become hotter still, ageing insulation faster and increasing failure risk.
Warming can make new places suitable for some introduced species or help them survive longer seasons. It can also make conditions worse for other invaders, so effects differ by species and region.

Heat increases plants' demand for water and can add to stress from drought, fire and land use. It may favour a more open tropical landscape, but temperature alone does not determine the outcome and the thresholds remain uncertain.

Warmer seasons and later autumn frost can let some plants release pollen for longer. The cited monitoring covers a limited network and measures season length, not every person's exposure or the total pollen produced.

Warming can increase drying and erosion pressures on dryland soil and plants. It does not prove lasting land damage on its own. Rain, management and several measures of land condition need to be considered.

Warmer air can carry more water vapour, allowing long bands of moist air to transport more water. This does not guarantee more events or stronger winds in every place, and historical trends depend on the available record.
Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly
Warm, moist air near the ground can rise more strongly if the air above allows it. Warming higher up, dryness or a layer that blocks rising air can prevent this potential from becoming a storm.
Lightning Flash Density and Seasonality Anomaly

Warming changes moisture, rising air and the ice processes involved in lightning. Models disagree on how these effects combine, so the direction of future lightning change remains uncertain in many regions.
Migratory Bird Timing, Route, and Stopover Disruption
Warmer seasons can change when food becomes available along bird migration routes. Some birds adjust successfully while others do not. An early arrival in one year does not prove a lasting mismatch.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction

Warming can dry lower forest margins and prevent young trees from establishing, while allowing trees to grow higher where cold once limited them. Both boundaries and local moisture need to be checked before claiming the forest is shrinking overall.
Amphibian Chytrid Infection Prevalence and Mortality

Temperature affects both amphibians and the fungus that infects their skin. Infection can be greatest at intermediate temperatures, so warming may increase suitability in cold places but reduce it in already hot places.
North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre Circulation Strength

Warmer or less strongly cooled surface water may sink less and change northern Atlantic flow. Temperature alone cannot determine the response because salt content and transported heat also affect density and circulation.
Warmer seasons can let some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter in greater numbers. Excessive heat or a lack of suitable trees can instead limit outbreaks.
Warmer water holds less oxygen and may mix less. Severe oxygen loss is more likely where extra nutrients and weak circulation already create pressure. Temperature alone does not establish it.
Warming can add heat and drying stress to forests. Large-scale tree loss depends on other pressures and uncertain local limits, so it cannot be inferred from temperature alone.
A longer Arctic growing season can help some shrubs spread. The response depends on the species, moisture, snow, grazing animals and disturbance.
Heat and changing seasonal timing can stress some pollinating insects. Population or colony losses usually involve several pressures, including food, habitat, chemicals and disease.
Warming can increase evaporation and change when snowmelt and river water arrive. This can alter how much surface water remains stored through the year.
Sustained ground warming can enlarge areas that stay unfrozen within otherwise frozen terrain. Snow, water, soil and plants determine where these areas develop.
Warming can make the warm edge of a species' habitat unsuitable. Its overall range shrinks if it cannot establish enough new habitat in cooler places to make up the loss.

human.summary: A warmer climate can make heat, floods and drought more damaging to daily life. People may need more protection at work and more energy to keep homes safe.
consequences: Long hot periods can increase heat illness and strain the body, especially where people cannot cool down.
Heat combined with drought can reduce crops and livestock production.
Keeping buildings cool can increase electricity use and household bills in exposed cities.
human.hiddenCost: More warming increases damage to health, food supplies, water, buildings and nature. Those costs are often missing from the price of the activities releasing heat-trapping gases.
human.whoPays: People with little money or protection often have the hardest time recovering. This includes places that released little of the pollution causing the warming.

planet.summary: A warmer climate changes conditions across land, oceans and ice. Many species and habitats face several pressures at once.
consequences: Some species lose places cool enough for them to survive.
Less snow and ice changes how much sunlight is reflected and when fresh water reaches rivers.
Repeated or stronger heat can exceed the conditions that ecosystems can recover from.
planet.physicalLimit: There is no single temperature at which the whole economy fails. To stop adding warming from carbon dioxide, human releases must fall to the amount removed and stored.

response.defaultDriver: Burning coal, oil and gas, clearing land and continuing to use high-emissions equipment add heat-trapping gases to the air.
levers: Cut emissions across power, transport, buildings, farming and industry.
Fund protection for exposed communities, while cutting carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases.

measurement.metric: Global mean surface temperature anomaly above 1850-1900
measurement.unit: degrees Celsius
measurement.geography: global with land-ocean coverage diagnostics
measurement.cadence: monthly with annual synthesis
measurement.method: Use the published change in average temperature across Earth's land and ocean surface. Keep the comparison period, area covered and status of recent estimates. A satellite measurement of one layer of air is a different measure.
measurement.uncertainty: Different datasets cover different places and adjust observations in different ways. Sea-temperature methods and the chosen comparison period also affect results. Recent values may be revised.
measurement.boundary: If the source stops updating, show the last reviewed yearly value and say how old it is. Missing months cannot be worked out from a TULIP score.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Warmer, waterlogged ground can help microbes produce more methane, and thawing can expose stored plant material. Water conditions and the breakdown of the gas affect how much reaches the air. The size of this response remains uncertain.
Thawed plant material can decay in wet ground with little oxygen. Microbes can produce methane during this process, and some of that gas can escape into the air.
Food in landfill can decay with little oxygen and produce methane. The amount released depends on waste handling and whether the gas is captured.

Plant material breaking down in flooded fields can produce methane, which escapes through plants, bubbles and the water surface. The amount varies with water management, soil, added organic material and the growing season.
When frozen ground thaws and sinks, water can collect in the new hollows. The breakdown of previously frozen material in this wet ground can release methane.
Finding gas leaks can reduce methane releases when operators repair them and check that the repair worked. Measuring a leak by itself does not stop it.
Methane made in thawing northern soils and lakes can escape into the air if it is not broken down first. The amount varies greatly with temperature, wetness and the route the gas takes.

Livestock, manure and flooded rice fields can release methane, with amounts depending on farming methods. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports global farm-gate methane emissions of 142 million tonnes per year, plus or minus 42 million, during 2007–2016. This excludes later food-processing and delivery stages.
Permanently unfrozen ground can provide places for methane to form or routes for it to escape. Organic material and low-oxygen conditions are needed for this pathway.
Liquid manure breaking down without oxygen produces methane. Capturing and using or destroying the gas can reduce how much escapes.
More cattle generally means more total methane from digestion within the herd. Diet and productivity change emissions per animal and per amount of food produced.
outgoing: Methane traps heat and has contributed to the warming already observed. The cited assessment estimates its contribution over a particular historical period, with an uncertainty range rather than one exact value.
Methane is a powerful heat-trapping gas, especially over the near term. Its added warming can intensify some heat, rainfall and other climate extremes.
Methane adds to near-term warming. This can increase exposure to dangerous combinations of high temperature and humid air.
Warming caused by methane can change moisture and air circulation. These changes can affect the timing and variability of seasonal rains.

Removing methane from air uses highly reactive chemicals called hydroxyl radicals. More methane can use some of that capacity and stay longer, but other chemical and weather changes can increase removal instead.

More methane across the atmosphere traps additional heat and also affects ozone and water vapour high above Earth. A local leak or brief concentration spike is not equivalent to a change in the global annual heat balance.

human.summary: This gas adds strongly to warming over the near term. It also helps form ground-level ozone, which can affect breathing and crops.
consequences: Added warming can make dangerous hot periods more severe within the lifetimes of today's buildings and services.
Ozone can damage plants and worsen breathing problems in exposed populations.
Food prices can become less dependable when heat and ozone reduce harvests together.
human.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

planet.summary: Rapid warming from this gas can put ecosystems under pressure before they have time to adjust. Its contribution to ground-level ozone can also damage plants.
consequences: Faster change can push some ecosystems beyond their capacity to recover.
Ozone can harm plant tissue and reduce the way crops and wild plants use sunlight.
Added warming increases pressure on ice and frozen soils, which can reinforce further change.
planet.physicalLimit: A rise in methane concentration is not the same as the amount people emitted. Natural releases and the methane removed from the air must also be accounted for.

response.defaultDriver: Warmer, waterlogged ground can help microbes produce more methane, and thawing can expose stored plant material. Water conditions and the breakdown of the gas affect how much reaches the air. The size of this response remains uncertain.
levers: Finding gas leaks can reduce methane releases when operators repair them and check that the repair worked. Measuring a leak by itself does not stop it.

incoming: Replacing an existing forest with an oil-palm plantation is one form of permanent forest clearance. Evidence must establish that sequence. Nearby plantations alone do not prove why a forest was lost.
High demand for leather and plant-based clothing fibres can add pressure to clear forests. This link depends on where materials come from and whether supply chains avoid newly cleared land.

Demand for meat, animal feed and other farm products can encourage expansion onto forest land. This is less likely when existing farmland, higher yields or effective protection meet the demand without new clearing.
Outward growth of homes, roads and other city facilities can replace forest with built land. This is one part of overall forest loss, not an explanation for all of it.
Expanding crop fields and livestock pasture can permanently replace forests. Agricultural expansion is a major direct cause of global forest loss.
Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection.
outgoing: Clearing sections of a forest can split continuous habitat into smaller pieces. More exposed edges and larger gaps can make those pieces harder for wildlife to use.
Cutting forests removes living trees that absorb carbon dioxide and disturbs stored carbon. It can also reduce how much carbon the area takes up in future.
Clearing forests removes food, shelter and stable local conditions for insects. Populations can decline where the remaining habitat cannot support them.
Removing trees reduces fallen leaves and roots that replenish soil. Exposed ground can then lose organic material through erosion, heat and faster decay.
Clearing and splitting forests can make the remaining trees less able to withstand heat, drought, pests and fire. Trees may die where several of these pressures occur together.

Clearing and splitting tropical forests can reduce moisture recycling and increase fire exposure. Combined with climate change, this may favour a more open landscape, but the scale of change is uncertain and some damaged areas can regrow.

Removing forests changes shade, water released by plants and the way the surface absorbs and moves heat. It also releases stored carbon. Local temperature effects and wider climate effects are not identical everywhere.
Removing large areas of forest changes how land stores heat and returns water to the air. These changes can affect winds and seasonal rains, with results depending on where clearing occurs.

Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.
Clearing trees within a river catchment removes canopy and roots. This can increase erosion and allow rainwater to reach streams more quickly.
Clearing plants from peatland often comes with drainage or conversion to another use. This can expose stored peat and remove plants that help build and protect it.

Removing forests changes roots, soil and water use. It can reduce groundwater replenishment where runoff increases, but can increase it where trees previously used much of the water. Local evidence is needed.

Forest clearing changes contact between wildlife, domestic animals and people. This can create opportunities for germs to cross species, but most clearing does not cause an outbreak and the transmission route needs evidence.

Clearing forests can release stored carbon and reduce later uptake by trees. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change land assessment reports a broad literature range of 0.5–3.5 billion tonnes of carbon per year from tropical forest loss and damage (reported as the weight of carbon alone).

Losing forests changes how water enters soil, returns to the air and reaches rivers. This can worsen shortages where those forest functions help maintain dependable supplies, but the response is local.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Forest loss can increase sediment and rapid runoff reaching rivers. Flood risk depends on how the water moves downstream and whether people or buildings are exposed.
Clearing and splitting forests removes habitats used by native species. Some plants and animals may become less common or disappear from the affected landscape.
Damaged or cleared forests can interact with drying and human ignitions to change fire patterns. The result also depends on available vegetation and land management.
Removing trees leaves soil with less protection from rain and fewer roots holding it. Erosion can increase on vulnerable slopes during heavy rain.
Forest loss can change river flows, water quality and stream habitats. Freshwater wildlife may be harmed where these catchment changes reach the water.
Losing forest-based jobs, food or other benefits can add pressure for people to move. Economic, political and climate conditions also shape that decision.

Losing forests and other natural habitat removes flowers, nesting sites and shelter used by pollinating insects. This can add to pressures from chemicals, disease and climate rather than acting as the only cause of colony loss.

human.summary: Losing forests can disrupt the water, food and income that nearby communities depend on. The consequences vary with how the cleared land and remaining forest are managed.
consequences: Dry-season fires and smoke can damage homes and harm breathing.
Changes in the water trees return to the air can make local or regional rainfall less dependable.
People may lose forest products, jobs and some natural protection from floods.
human.hiddenCost: Clearing trees can remove wildlife habitat, stored carbon and benefits such as cleaner water. Income from timber or farming does not necessarily cover those losses.
human.whoPays: People who depend on forests, including Indigenous communities, can lose food, income and cultural places. Water users farther downstream can also be affected.

planet.summary: Removing forests takes away habitat, stored carbon and the role trees play in moving water. Remaining patches may become less able to withstand further damage.
consequences: Isolated habitats leave some species with fewer places to move or breed.
Less moisture returned by trees can contribute to drying and fire exposure in affected regions.
Cleared or damaged land may take up less carbon than the forest it replaces.
planet.physicalLimit: There is no universal amount of clearing that makes every forest collapse. Recovery depends on remaining trees, soil, fire, rainfall and connections between habitats.

response.defaultDriver: Expanding farmland is the main direct cause globally. Roads, mining, demand for products and weak protection of land rights also contribute.
levers: Track where products come from and enforce rules against clearing natural forests.
Protect community land rights and existing forests. Restore damaged land with suitable native species.

components.label: Human impact
components.explanation: Pollution and water-related harm to health and daily life around intensive production.

components.label: Nature impact
components.explanation: Soil, freshwater and habitat damage from intensive agriculture.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Rising demand for food and animal feed can encourage farms to produce more from each area of land. This is one response alongside imports, expanding farmland or reducing demand.
Livestock production based on purchased feed needs large, steady supplies of crops such as maize and soy. This can support more concentrated and intensive farming systems.
Manufactured plant nutrients can support higher crop yields where soil nutrients limit growth. This makes repeated high-output cropping possible, alongside its other resource needs.
outgoing: Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.
Pumping water for crops can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds the water that seeps back in. The shortage can build up over years, making wells less reliable.
Adding crop nutrients faster than plants can use them leaves material that rain or irrigation can wash away. It can then reach rivers and other waterways.
Large farming systems can waste water when delivery equipment leaks or watering does not match crop needs. The problem depends on how the system is designed and managed.
Intensive soil disturbance and too little return of organic material can reduce the soil's stored plant matter. The outcome depends on the farming practices used.
Frequent ploughing, removing crop remains and leaving fields bare can expose soil. Wind and heavy rain can then carry away the fertile upper layer more easily.
Removing varied habitats and exposing insects to farm chemicals can reduce their numbers. The effect depends on farming practices and the species involved.
Farms that depend heavily on manufactured plant nutrients are exposed to energy prices and supply disruptions. Sudden cost increases can affect planting decisions and farm income.
Large livestock operations need steady supplies of crops such as maize and soy for feed. This ties animal production to the land, water, nutrients and trade used to grow those crops.
Too many grazing animals, or repeated trampling on wet ground, can press soil tightly together. Water and roots may then find it harder to move through the soil.
Persistent Pesticide Residues in Sediment and Biota

Some farm chemicals remain in soil and sediment long after use and can enter living things. Current farming alone does not prove where an older chemical came from, and not all pesticides persist or enter food chains.

Farm chemicals can reach streams through runoff, drains or water moving through soil. Whether they arrive depends on the chemical, weather and farm practices. Use on a field does not by itself prove water contamination.

Spraying farm chemicals can send droplets or dust beyond the intended field, and some chemicals can move through the air later. Suitable weather, equipment and buffer areas can greatly reduce this movement.
Expanding crop fields and livestock pasture can permanently replace forests. Agricultural expansion is a major direct cause of global forest loss.

Manure, crop remains and other nitrogen inputs can release nitrous oxide through soil processes. Emissions depend on the practices and conditions. The basic Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimate for qualifying managed-soil inputs is 1% of added nitrogen, with a default range of 0.2–1.8%.
Flooded rice fields create soil conditions with little oxygen. Decaying organic material can then produce methane.
Establishing an oil-palm plantation can remove forest if it expands onto forested land. A plantation's presence alone does not prove recent clearing. Earlier land cover and timing need to be checked.

Poorly suited farming can remove protective plants, erode soil, drain water reserves or leave salts behind. Well-managed crops, irrigation and restoration can instead maintain or improve dryland condition.
Disturbing dry soil and removing cover can make farmland more vulnerable to wind erosion. Keeping plants, windbreaks and suitable grazing or ploughing practices can instead reduce dust losses.
Clearing land for crops or heavy livestock pressure can reduce trees in savannas. The link applies where those activities overlap the vegetation being measured.

Crowded animals, frequent movement and poor disease controls can help germs persist or reach workers and food. Effective controls can reduce some risks, and outcomes differ by germ and farming system.

Livestock, manure and flooded rice fields can release methane, with amounts depending on farming methods. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports global farm-gate methane emissions of 142 million tonnes per year, plus or minus 42 million, during 2007–2016. This excludes later food-processing and delivery stages.

Farming can release carbon dioxide through land conversion, energy use and the production of inputs. The amount depends on which activities, gases and stages the source includes. Methane and nitrous oxide need separate accounting.
Simpler habitats, pesticide exposure, nutrient losses and land clearing can harm plants and animals around farms. The effect depends on local practices and documented exposure.
Nutrients lost from farms can reach coastal water and encourage growth that later uses up oxygen. The connection depends on transport downstream and the actual oxygen response.
Farm nutrients can contribute to coastal areas with very little oxygen after extra algae decay. Evidence is needed that the nutrients reached the water and helped cause the oxygen loss.
Large areas of one crop, fewer habitats and pesticide exposure can reduce food and safety for pollinating insects. Farm management and the surrounding landscape affect the outcome.
Farms dependent on costly inputs or facing damaged soil and limited water can become less reliable. Food access is affected when these pressures change harvests, prices or household income.
Frequent soil disturbance, few crop types and chemical pressures can change the communities living in farm soil. Local measurements are needed to show which organisms and functions are affected.
Agricultural burning, ammonia and other farm emissions can contribute to air pollution. Health impacts depend on the pollutants released and people's actual exposure.

Pesticides and a lack of varied flowers or habitat can contribute to losses of pollinating insects or colonies. Parasites, disease, nutrition and weather also matter, so the affected species and exposure need to be identified.
Farms seeking high crop output may apply more nitrogen nutrients. Actual use depends on the crop, existing soil fertility and how precisely nutrients are managed.

Some concentrated livestock farms store liquid manure in lagoons. Whether they use this system depends on farm design and local rules, so livestock concentration alone does not prove a lagoon is present.
More concentrated livestock production can place more cattle in a managed area. Actual density depends on available land and how animals are kept and moved.

human.summary: Large-scale crop and livestock production supplies food but can also concentrate pollution, health and worker risks. Farmers, workers and consumers can be affected when water, animal health or feed become unreliable.
consequences: Nutrients leaving fields can pollute rivers and make drinking water harder to treat.
Heat can make farm work unsafe and harm livestock health and production.
Rising fertiliser or feed prices and animal disease can raise food costs.
human.hiddenCost: Food prices may leave out damage from water overuse, pollution, lost habitat and heat-trapping gases. Health and working conditions also affect the wider cost of food production.
human.whoPays: Farm workers, small producers, low-income consumers and people using water downstream may bear costs they did not choose.

planet.summary: Large-scale crop and livestock production can put nearby water and habitats under pressure through fertilizer, manure, feed production and land use. Effects depend on farming methods and the surrounding landscape.
consequences: Nutrients washed downstream can feed algae and reduce oxygen as they decay.
Large areas of one crop can support fewer kinds of pollinating insects and wildlife.
Loss of soil organic material can make land less able to retain water and recover from stress.
planet.physicalLimit: Farms depend on usable soil, water, nutrients and tolerable heat. Limits differ by crop, production method and place.

response.defaultDriver: Subsidies, buying rules and demand can reward producing more even when soil, water or health are harmed.
levers: Reduce avoidable fertilizer losses, livestock emissions and damage to soils using locally tested methods.
Support farming that protects water, health and habitat, and reduce food waste without harming nutrition or incomes.

incoming: Rainfall changes linked to this Indian Ocean pattern can affect crop harvests. Their effects on food availability also depend on where crops are grown and how farms and supplies are managed.
Animal illness can reduce milk, meat and egg production or kill livestock. Restrictions on moving animals can also interrupt food supplies.
More expensive plant nutrients raise farming costs. If farmers cannot afford enough, food production may also fall.
When heat reduces the hours people can safely work on farms, less food may be produced or collected. The effect depends on the timing of the heat and the protection workers have.
A shortage of crops used as animal feed can reduce livestock production. This can affect the availability and price of meat, milk and eggs.
Food can spoil or become unsafe when it is not kept cold enough during storage and transport. This reduces the amount available to eat.
Changes in Pacific ocean temperatures can bring heat, drought or flooding to farming regions. These conditions can damage harvests and interrupt food supplies.
Changes linked to unusually cool Pacific waters can bring destructive rain to some regions and drought to others. Harvests and fisheries may be affected in different ways across regions.
Hot, humid conditions make it harder for farm workers to cool down safely. They can also strain crops and animals, reducing food production in exposed regions.
Unreliable seasonal rains can disrupt planting, watering and harvesting. Farms that depend heavily on these rains may produce less food.
outgoing: Food can be lost at each step from farming to storage, shops and homes. How much is wasted depends on facilities and behaviour, rather than a fixed share of food demand.

Demand for meat, animal feed and other farm products can encourage expansion onto forest land. This is less likely when existing farmland, higher yields or effective protection meet the demand without new clearing.
Producing and delivering food uses machinery, plant nutrients, refrigeration and transport. Fossil fuels and fossil-generated electricity used in these steps release carbon dioxide.
Growing more crops increases demand for nutrients to replace those removed at harvest. This can increase the production of manufactured fertilisers.
Rising demand for food and animal feed can encourage farms to produce more from each area of land. This is one response alongside imports, expanding farmland or reducing demand.
Demand for rice can increase the area or intensity of flooded cultivation. The response also depends on yields, trade, diets and available water.

Demand for palm-containing products can encourage more production. Forest loss occurs only when the extra supply comes from clearing forest, rather than higher yields or land that was already cleared. This differs greatly between regions.

human.summary: Demand for farm products can put pressure on land and water when supply expands faster than those resources can support. Households feel the effects through food costs and reliability.
consequences: Prices can rise when demand grows faster than available food supply.
More crop and grazing land can mean more clearing and water use.
Places relying on imported food are exposed when harvest failures disrupt their suppliers.
human.hiddenCost: Producing what people eat can bring costs from land clearing, water use and pollution. Diet-related illness can add further costs, depending on the foods and people involved.
human.whoPays: Farm workers, nearby communities, consumers and health services can share different parts of the burden.

planet.summary: Demand for meat, animal feed and other farm products can encourage expansion onto forest land. This is less likely when existing farmland, higher yields or effective protection meet the demand without new clearing.
consequences: Producing and delivering food uses machinery, plant nutrients, refrigeration and transport. Fossil fuels and fossil-generated electricity used in these steps release carbon dioxide.
planet.physicalLimit: Food production depends on suitable land, water and healthy soil. Expanding production by clearing natural habitat can weaken these supports. The outcome varies by place.

response.defaultDriver: Prices, farm support and the products available in shops shape demand. They do not always reflect the full effects of producing food.
levers: Support varied, nutritious foods with lower land and emissions demands where appropriate.
Protect natural habitats in food supply chains and reduce food lost between farms, shops and homes.

incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Growing cities may spread outward into more land when housing, roads and planning favour low-density development. City growth does not always take this form.

Growing cities may use water faster than supplies and pipes can expand. Restrictions become more likely during shortages, but growth need not lead to rationing when efficiency, reuse and services keep pace.
City growth changes housing, transport, industry and energy use at the same time. Emissions can rise or fall depending on these choices, and some activity may shift into neighbouring regions.
Outward growth of homes, roads and other city facilities can replace forest with built land. This is one part of overall forest loss, not an explanation for all of it.
City growth can increase water demand and pollution both inside and outside city boundaries. Better services, more efficient use and changes in industry can moderate or reverse the increase.
Growing urban populations, incomes and business activity can increase demand for flights. Ticket prices, airport capacity and other travel options may limit that increase.
Growing cities concentrate food shops, restaurants and households, creating more opportunities for waste. Storage, transport and collection practices determine how much is actually discarded.
City growth adds buildings needing cooling and surfaces that store heat. This can increase both air-conditioning use and the amount of cooling gas in equipment.
Rapid city growth without adequate drains, waste services or water supplies can create breeding places for some disease-carrying insects. Dense populations and travel can increase contact and spread.
Hard urban surfaces can send rainwater quickly into combined rainwater and sewage pipes. Overflow risk rises where storage and pipe capacity cannot handle the flow.
Paved surfaces and drains can send rainwater to rivers before it soaks underground. Local leaks, storage basins and designs that let water soak in can offset or reverse that effect.
Development can remove habitat and add roads, noise or light that interfere with wildlife movement. Parks, gardens and safe crossings can preserve useful links for some species.

Dense urban activity creates opportunities for small plastic particles to enter or re-enter the air from wear, handling and dust. Cities also receive particles from elsewhere, so location alone does not identify the source.
Piers, seawalls and other underwater structures can provide places for the attached life stage of some jellyfish. More suitable surfaces can support later releases of free-swimming animals.
Urban growth can change contact with animals through habitat expansion, waste and food systems. It does not identify an outbreak's source by itself, and better services can reduce risk.
More buildings and infrastructure can increase demand for cement and concrete. Reuse, material-saving design and construction standards can reduce the amount of new material needed.
More people and buildings can increase water use at the same time of day. Efficiency, prices, climate and network design affect how large those peaks become.

human.summary: Growing cities need housing, water, drains, trees and transport to keep pace. When those services lag, more people can end up exposed to heat or flooding.
consequences: Paving without enough shade and drainage can leave neighbourhoods hotter and more flood-prone.
Water, sanitation and transport services can become strained.
Rapid growth can increase housing costs and pressure on residents to move.
human.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

planet.summary: City growth changes housing, transport, industry and energy use at the same time. Emissions can rise or fall depending on these choices, and some activity may shift into neighbouring regions.
consequences: Outward growth of homes, roads and other city facilities can replace forest with built land. This is one part of overall forest loss, not an explanation for all of it.
City growth can increase water demand and pollution both inside and outside city boundaries. Better services, more efficient use and changes in industry can moderate or reverse the increase.
planet.physicalLimit: Expanding an administrative boundary does not mean new land was built on. Different map versions must be made comparable before measuring change.

response.defaultDriver: The growth of towns and cities as more people live and work in them. Replacing plants and soil with buildings and roads can trap heat and leave rainwater with fewer places to soak into the ground. Planning and public services affect how these changes are managed.
levers: Include affected communities in decisions about protection, services and recovery.
Fund practical support and monitor who can actually access it, especially where people have few alternatives.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

High demand for leather and plant-based clothing fibres can add pressure to clear forests. This link depends on where materials come from and whether supply chains avoid newly cleared land.

Large volumes of discarded clothing can overwhelm waste services and add to unsafe burning or dumping.
human.hiddenCost: Frequent replacement of cheap clothing creates waste and pollution costs beyond its shop price. Small fibres can escape during production, washing and disposal.
human.whoPays: Communities near factories and waste sites, workers and water-treatment services can face burdens that clothing prices do not cover.

incoming: Repeated periods of heat and humidity can make work and daily life unsafe. They can contribute to pressure to move, alongside jobs, housing, family ties and other factors.
Drought or flooding linked to unusually warm Pacific waters can damage harvests, water supplies and livelihoods. Some households may move when they have few ways to recover locally.
Repeated failures of seasonal rains, or destructive downpours, can damage crops, homes and incomes. Some people may move when local recovery becomes too difficult.
Thawing frozen ground can damage buildings, roads and essential services. People may need to move when repairs or continued protection become too difficult.
Moving before repeated disasters destroy homes can reduce emergency displacement. The benefit depends on providing a safe, supported destination and involving the people who move.
Long-lasting difficulty obtaining enough food can push people to leave their homes. Jobs, conflict and other economic conditions also influence whether people move.
Climate hazards can repeatedly damage homes, water supplies and livelihoods. Some people may move temporarily or permanently when they cannot recover safely where they live.
Losing forest-based jobs, food or other benefits can add pressure for people to move. Economic, political and climate conditions also shape that decision.
Climate hazards can contribute to people leaving unsafe homes or damaged livelihoods. Social, economic and political conditions also determine who moves and who can recover locally.
outgoing: People forced to move have unequal access to savings, housing, documents and aid. These differences can widen the gap between households able to recover and those left behind.
Large or repeated movements of people can overwhelm housing and public services. Authorities need enough capacity to coordinate land access, legal arrangements and community participation.
Rapid displacement increases demand for shelter, food, water and health care along routes and at destinations. Local services may struggle to expand as quickly as needs grow.

human.summary: People forced to move may lose their homes, income and support networks. Receiving communities need enough housing and services to help newcomers settle safely.
consequences: Children's schooling and families' access to regular care can be interrupted.
Water supplies, clinics and affordable housing may face extra demand.
Competition for land, jobs or aid can add tension, though conflict is not inevitable.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to housing and repeated disruption can create repair, temporary accommodation and moving costs. The burden depends on insurance, public support and safe alternatives.
human.whoPays: Residents, landlords, insurers and public services may share the bill. People with little savings or secure housing can have fewer recovery options.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Mining and processing draw on materials, land, water and energy. The amount needed depends on technology, recycled inputs and what activities are counted.
Growing battery production can concentrate extraction, water use and waste in mining regions. This can add to local pressure on land and water supplies.
Frequently replacing clothing increases demand for fibres, water, energy and processing chemicals. Resources are used to make replacements while existing clothes may still be usable.
Removing carbon dioxide can require land, water, energy and materials. The demands differ greatly between methods and can create pressure on other resources.
Designing buildings to use less concrete can reduce demand for newly extracted materials. Changing the cement recipe alone does not guarantee lower material use.
Factories that cannot yet replace fossil-fuel heating continue to use fuel and other resources. Cooling water and materials remain part of the demand from these high-temperature processes.

More mining, especially of poorer-quality deposits, can require more rock, water and energy for each useful amount of mineral. Recycling and production methods affect the resulting demand for new resources.
Making new plastics uses fossil raw materials, energy, water and other resources. Reuse and recycled inputs can reduce some of the demand for new material.
Conventional steelmaking uses large amounts of ore, fuel and other materials. More efficient production and recycled steel can reduce demand for newly extracted resources.
outgoing: Producing plant nutrients requires energy and raw materials. Shortages of these inputs can raise production costs and prices paid by farmers.
Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.
Pumping more groundwater than rain and other sources replace gradually reduces underground reserves. This can continue over years or decades.

human.summary: Shrinking local water, soil and material reserves can make essential supplies harder or more expensive to obtain. Households and farms with few alternatives are more exposed.
consequences: Falling groundwater can raise pumping costs and make wells less dependable.
Losing fertile soil can reduce harvests and increase spending on farming inputs.
Cities, farms and ecosystems may compete for the same limited resources.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

planet.summary: Using water, soil and other reserves faster than they recover can weaken ecosystems that depend on them.
consequences: Falling groundwater can reduce flow to rivers and wetlands.
Damaged soil may support less life and cope less well with drought.
Already depleted systems can take longer to recover after a climate shock.

incoming: Warming can increase decay, drought, fire and thawing of frozen soils. These changes can release stored carbon or reduce natural uptake, adding to warming that began from other causes.
More flying generally means more jet fuel burned unless efficiency or fuel changes offset it. Burning fossil jet fuel releases carbon dioxide into the air.
Making plastics and related chemicals uses fossil raw materials and energy. Production and some disposal methods can release carbon dioxide.
Power plants that burn fossil fuels release carbon dioxide whenever they run. Continued reliance on them for busy hours keeps those releases going.
Burning natural gas to make electricity releases carbon dioxide. The amount per unit of power varies with the technology and efficiency. The cited assessment reports a range.
Factories continue releasing carbon dioxide while boilers and high-temperature equipment burn fossil fuels. Slow replacement with suitable cleaner systems prolongs those releases.
Chemically changing limestone to make cement releases carbon dioxide. Fuel used to heat the process adds a separate contribution. Both are included when assessing total production emissions.
Keeping coal- and gas-intensive metal-making methods in use continues to release carbon dioxide. Reductions depend on replacing or changing those processes effectively.

Chip manufacturing can release heat-trapping gases through energy use and specialized process gases. These are not all carbon dioxide, so any combined climate total must retain the source's gas accounting.
Backup engines burning diesel or gas release carbon dioxide while running. More frequent or longer use increases that contribution unless efficiency or fuel changes offset it.
If available clean power cannot reach users or be stored, fuel-burning generation may still be needed. The emissions effect depends on which power sources actually run instead.
Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases.
Draining carbon-rich wetland soil exposes stored plant material to air. Its decay can continue releasing carbon dioxide. The rate depends on soil, climate and land use.
When electric freight options and their supporting systems are unavailable, diesel vehicles remain in use. Their continued fuel burning releases carbon dioxide.
Additional ship journeys burn fuel and release carbon dioxide. The total depends on the number of journeys, their length and the fuels used.
Continuing to use diesel trucks keeps releasing carbon dioxide from fuel burning. Long-lived vehicles and the services built around them can delay a switch to cleaner transport.
When dried peat breaks down in air, it releases carbon dioxide. Fires can release this long-stored carbon much more quickly.
Damaging or removing coastal wetlands can release some of the carbon stored in their plants and soils. The amount depends on how the land is disturbed and what happens to the material.
Making and transporting large volumes of short-lived clothing uses energy. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, it releases carbon dioxide.
Thawing ground exposes long-frozen plant and animal remains to decay. This can release carbon dioxide and, where the ground is waterlogged, methane.
Electricity with lower emissions can replace power made by burning fossil fuels. It can also reduce emissions when it replaces fuel burning in transport, heating and industry.
Closing coal-fired power stations stops their fuel-burning emissions. The overall reduction depends on what replaces their electricity.
Wind, solar and other renewable sources can reduce carbon dioxide emissions when their electricity replaces fossil-fuel generation. Adding capacity alone does not guarantee that replacement.
Taking carbon dioxide out of the air can balance a limited share of ongoing releases. The removal must be extra, measured and stored for long enough to count as a lasting benefit.
Using less energy for heating, cooling and other building services can reduce fuel-burning emissions. The reduction depends on the energy source and actual use after the upgrade.
Efficient electric heating can replace boilers and furnaces that burn fossil fuels. The climate benefit depends on the equipment's performance and how its electricity is made.
Shared transport can reduce emissions when it replaces more polluting car journeys. The result depends on how vehicles are powered and how many people use them.
Walking and cycling avoid fuel-burning emissions when they replace motorised journeys. Safe routes help more people make that switch.
Electric vehicles replace oil use with electricity. Their climate benefit generally grows as the electricity supply becomes cleaner, while vehicle and battery production still matter.
Changes to cement ingredients, fuel use and production can reduce carbon dioxide releases. The reduction depends on which methods are used and how well they perform.
Making steel with very low emissions can reduce carbon dioxide releases when it replaces coal-based production. The full benefit depends on the energy and materials used.
Advanced water treatment needs energy. It can add carbon dioxide emissions when that energy comes from fossil fuels.
Draining peat exposes partly decayed plant material to air, allowing it to release carbon dioxide as it breaks down. Fires and the loss of plants can add to these carbon losses.
Moving flexible electricity use to cleaner hours can reduce emissions if it actually changes which generators run. Extra use later must not cancel the avoided emissions.
City growth changes housing, transport, industry and energy use at the same time. Emissions can rise or fall depending on these choices, and some activity may shift into neighbouring regions.

Petrol and diesel vehicles release carbon dioxide as they burn fuel. Electric vehicles shift much of the emissions from use to electricity production, while making vehicles and roads adds separate emissions.
More artificial intelligence computing can increase data-centre electricity use. The associated carbon dioxide depends on how much of the electricity supplied is generated from fossil fuels.
Mobile networks use electricity for radio equipment and supporting systems. Fossil-fuel electricity and diesel backup generators release carbon dioxide while supplying that power.
The equipment carrying internet traffic over long distances needs electricity. Its indirect carbon dioxide emissions depend on the fossil-fuel share of that power supply.
Producing and delivering food uses machinery, plant nutrients, refrigeration and transport. Fossil fuels and fossil-generated electricity used in these steps release carbon dioxide.
