scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Irrigated farms draw water from supplies also needed by households, businesses and rivers. Heavy use can leave less available during dry periods.
City growth can increase water demand and pollution both inside and outside city boundaries. Better services, more efficient use and changes in industry can moderate or reverse the increase.
Long dry periods reduce river supplies and the water replenishing underground reserves. Shortages become more likely if demand stays high.
Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
Less water replenishing underground stores can reduce dependable supplies and increase saltwater intrusion near coasts. Large reserves or lower pumping can protect users from short-term shortages.

Losing forests changes how water enters soil, returns to the air and reaches rivers. This can worsen shortages where those forest functions help maintain dependable supplies, but the response is local.
Poorly managed oil and gas wastewater can contaminate fresh supplies, while extraction also uses water. These pressures matter especially where usable freshwater is already limited.
Irrigation pumping can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds replacement from rain, rivers or managed replenishment. Other users then have less dependable water available.
Large industrial withdrawals can compete with households, farms and wildlife for slowly replaced groundwater. Persistent use above replenishment reduces available reserves.
Public water supplies can strain groundwater when pumping repeatedly exceeds replenishment. Alternative sources and lower demand can reduce the shortfall.
Pumping coastal groundwater faster than it is replaced lowers freshwater reserves and pressure. Less usable water may remain available to local users.
Evaporation removes water from lakes and reservoirs before people or ecosystems can use it. This can worsen shortages in hot or dry river basins.
Persistently low river or reservoir inflow leaves less renewable water for people and ecosystems. Demand can then become harder to meet.
Taking a large share of available river or lake water increases competition among users. Less remains for other households, farms and the environment.
Leaks mean utilities must take more water to deliver the same usable amount. This adds pressure where supplies are limited.
A continuing gap between dependable city water supplies and demand directly indicates a strained system. The size of the gap depends on local sources and operating rules.
A short burst of high demand can exceed water treatment, pumping or storage capacity. This can happen even when total yearly supply appears sufficient.
outgoing: When demand approaches available water supply, safely treating and using water again becomes more valuable. It helps most when it replaces water taken from an already stressed source.

When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.
Limited water can bring animals together around fewer drinking places and make cleaning harder. Poorer water quality and closer contact can increase the spread of disease.
When reliable water supply cannot meet normal demand, utilities may ask or require people to use less. The restrictions depend on local operating decisions.

human.summary: Limited water can bring animals together around fewer drinking places and make cleaning harder. Poorer water quality and closer contact can increase the spread of disease.

human.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.

incoming: Pumping water for crops can reduce underground reserves when use exceeds the water that seeps back in. The shortage can build up over years, making wells less reliable.
Long dry periods can reduce the water replenishing underground stores while increasing demand for pumping. Reserves fall faster where withdrawals already approach or exceed replacement.
Irrigation that needs more pumping for the same harvest can drain underground reserves. The effect depends on how much of the extra water returns as usable groundwater.
Pumping groundwater for irrigation lowers reserves when withdrawals keep exceeding replacement. A record of water use alone does not show that an underground store is shrinking.
Pumping groundwater for public supplies can lower water levels if use stays above replacement. Other sources or reduced demand can change that balance.
Factories, mines and power facilities can reduce groundwater reserves when sustained pumping exceeds replacement. The actual balance must be assessed for the underground water body concerned.

Changes in pressure between rivers, lakes and groundwater can move water into depleted underground stores or reduce flow back to the surface. This redistributes water and must be assessed across the connected system.
Utilities using groundwater may pump extra water to replace what leaks from pipes. Reserves decline faster if replenishment cannot keep up.
outgoing: Falling groundwater levels reduce the reserves people can reach and make pumping more costly. Users who depend on wells may then face tighter supplies.
Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Power disconnection can remove cooling or interrupt essential home medical equipment during extreme heat. This can increase the risk of death, especially for people with limited alternatives or existing illness.
Higher temperatures and more intense hot periods increase the risk of heat-related deaths. Actual harm depends on health, housing, exposure and access to protection and care.
Failures in transport, water or health services can prevent people from getting protection during extreme heat. Several failures together can increase the risk of death.
Heat warnings can help prevent deaths when they trigger contact with vulnerable people, access to cooling and health-service preparation. An alert alone is not enough.
City plans can help prevent heat-related deaths when forecasts trigger funded action. This includes reaching vulnerable people, opening cooling spaces and protecting outdoor workers.
Making safe indoor temperatures available to people at greatest risk can help prevent heat-related deaths. Cooling must remain affordable and available when needed.
Insulation, shade and ventilation can reduce dangerous indoor heat when upgrades suit the local climate and allow heat to escape. Lower exposure can reduce estimated heat-related death risks.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming and more dangerous heat. Greater exposure can increase heat-related death risks, especially where people lack cooling and health care.
Heat combined with other hazards can increase death risks where people lack protection or health support. Age, illness, housing and opportunities to recover all affect the outcome.

incoming: Traffic releases particles and gases that people breathe. Exposure to this pollution can contribute to lung and heart disease, depending on the level and duration.
Very small airborne particles can reach deep into the lungs. Studies following people over time link greater long-term exposure with a higher risk of death from natural causes.
Larger or longer fire seasons can expose people to more smoke and fine particles. Breathing this pollution can harm the lungs and heart and increase illness and death risks.

Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

Breathing ground-level ozone irritates and damages airways, especially in exposed or vulnerable people. Studies reviewed for World Health Organization guidelines also link short-term outdoor increases with a small rise in daily deaths from all causes.
Pollen can irritate the nose and eyes or worsen asthma in people who are sensitive to it. Outdoor counts do not measure each person's exposure, and many exposed people have no symptoms.
Drifting farm chemicals can reach workers, homes and schools through air or direct contact. Harm depends on the chemical and dose. Detecting drift alone does not establish a health effect.

Windblown mineral particles can worsen air quality near their source and far downwind. Health effects depend on the particles and actual exposure. A visible dust plume alone does not establish illness.
Agricultural burning, ammonia and other farm emissions can contribute to air pollution. Health impacts depend on the pollutants released and people's actual exposure.
Conditions that favour ground-level ozone can increase harmful exposure where the necessary gases and people are present. Actual health burden depends on how much pollution people breathe.
Hospital admissions attributed to wildfire smoke are one measured part of the health effects of polluted air. They do not include every symptom, illness or effect outside hospital care.
Diesel freight releases fine particles and other harmful gases. People near busy freight routes can face greater exposure and related heart or lung risks.
Sulfur dioxide from coal burning can form fine particles downwind. Exposure to these pollutants can harm the lungs and heart, with controls affecting how much is released.
Fine particles breathed during a smoke event can worsen heart and lung health. The assessment applies to the exposed population and time period measured.
Longer exposure can increase the amount of smoke breathed and the chance of harm. People with existing health problems may be especially affected.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Breathing polluted air can increase heart and lung illness and shorten lives. Families may face treatment costs and time away from work or school.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

planet.summary: The main measure here concerns harm to people from polluted air. Effects on plants, water and climate depend on the pollutants and require separate measurements.

levers: Connect useful warnings with accessible health services and practical protection for exposed people.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for pollution and local water-function losses attributable to chip fabrication and current water and habitat condition deficit around production and supply routes; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Pollutant and water outcomes, not semiconductor output or nominal electricity consumption alone

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

components.label: Human impact
components.explanation: Pollution and local water-function losses linked to chip fabrication.

components.label: Nature impact
components.explanation: Water and habitat damage around production and supply routes.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: More artificial intelligence computing increases demand for advanced chips and memory. Manufacturers may respond by running existing factories more heavily or building additional production and packaging capacity.
outgoing: Chip factories need very clean water for production and cooling. In places with limited supplies, that use can compete with households, other businesses and nature.
Chip factories use electricity, water, chemicals and process gases and create waste. Together these flows describe the resources used and pollution associated with the factories covered.
Chip factories use large amounts of electricity and some heat-trapping process gases. Carbon dioxide from energy use must be distinguished from other greenhouse gases released during manufacture.

human.summary: Chip factories need reliable electricity, very clean water and careful chemical handling. A disruption at a few concentrated sites can affect many industries.
consequences: Large factories may compete with other users for dependable power and water.
Air emissions, wastewater and workplace chemicals need effective controls.
Companies depending on the same factories can experience supply problems together.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

planet.summary: Making chips uses electricity, very clean water and specialised chemicals. Some process gases add a warming effect beyond the emissions from power use.
consequences: Factories can place large water and energy demands in the same industrial region.
Heat-trapping process gases and local pollutants need separate controls.
Concentrated production makes the effects of a few facilities significant for the wider supply chain.
planet.physicalLimit: A national average does not show how one factory performs. Total production, total environmental impact and impact per unit are different measures and must remain separate.

response.defaultDriver: More artificial intelligence computing increases demand for advanced chips and memory. Manufacturers may respond by running existing factories more heavily or building additional production and packaging capacity.
levers: As online services grow, plan how to keep their equipment powered and cool. Check that local water supplies can meet its needs.
Use independent routes and tested backups where shared failures could interrupt essential communication.

measurement.metric: Semiconductor fabrication water, electricity, and wafer output
measurement.unit: cubic metres, megawatt-hours, and wafer starts per year, reported separately
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting
measurement.method: Keep clear which products, processes, materials, energy, emissions, water and waste are included. A value per unit of output is valid only when both amounts cover the same facility, place and period.
measurement.uncertainty: Some facilities do not report publicly, and production methods differ. Trade accounting, assumed emission rates and revised records can also change the estimate.
measurement.boundary: A national average does not show how one factory performs. Total production, total environmental impact and impact per unit are different measures and must remain separate.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Undersea fibre cables carry information between coastal landing stations and land-based networks. They provide important international connections for calls, data and online services.
outgoing: The equipment carrying internet traffic over long distances needs electricity. Its indirect carbon dioxide emissions depend on the fossil-fuel share of that power supply.
Long-distance data routes connect network operators to facilities where they exchange traffic. Those facilities depend on the routes remaining available.
Mobile networks need wider cable and core networks to carry information beyond a local radio mast. A working mast alone does not provide an end-to-end connection.
Failure of major data routes or switching equipment can interrupt communications used by power, water, transport and emergency services. Alternative paths determine how much service continues.

human.summary: The main routes carrying digital traffic support everyday communication and services. Concentrated failures can disrupt much more than the equipment at one site.
consequences: Broken routes or switching systems can interrupt communication across a wide area.
Operating and expanding networks uses electricity.
A lost connection can disrupt shops, deliveries and the way emergency teams work together.
human.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
human.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.

planet.summary: Major digital networks need physical equipment, electricity and maintenance. Their wider documented risks also concern disruption to connected human services.
consequences: Moving and switching data uses energy across a distributed network.
Growing traffic requires equipment and supporting facilities.
A network failure is not by itself evidence of damage to a natural ecosystem.
planet.physicalLimit: Exposure to a hazard does not prove a service failed. Different services cannot be combined into one score without explaining how they are weighted.

levers: As online services grow, plan how to keep their equipment powered and cool. Check that local water supplies can meet its needs.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. response.defaultDriver: Damage can arise from anchors, fishing activity and natural hazards. Concentrating routes without independent backups increases disruption risk.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current pollution, noise and climate-related health and function losses from aviation and current climate and habitat condition deficit attributable to aviation; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current manufacturing pollution and climate-related health and function loss and current plant, supply-chain and climate habitat condition deficits; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

human.summary: Extracting minerals directly creates demands for land, water, energy and waste management. Greater activity can increase these pressures in the places where extraction occurs. Making more batteries requires reliable supplies of mined and processed materials. Constraints and environmental pressures at those stages carry through to battery production.
domains: housing, support after moving and public services
consequences: Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection. Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.

More mining, especially of poorer-quality deposits, can require more rock, water and energy for each useful amount of mineral. Recycling and production methods affect the resulting demand for new resources. Shortages of important resources can worsen existing tensions. Conflict risk depends strongly on how resources are shared and whether institutions can resolve disputes fairly.
human.hiddenCost: Mineral extraction can affect water, land and nearby communities. The size of those impacts differs greatly between mines and extraction methods.
human.whoPays: Local and Indigenous communities, workers and water users can bear costs, while manufacturers face supply interruptions.

planet.summary: Mines can directly remove forest, while their roads and settlements open nearby areas to further clearing. The wider loss depends on local development and forest protection.

incoming: Growing cities may spread outward into more land when housing, roads and planning favour low-density development. City growth does not always take this form.
Good public transport can support homes and services closer together. Housing and planning policies need to support that pattern for outward spread to slow.
outgoing: Outward housing growth often adds roads and other paved areas. Dark pavement absorbs sunlight and stores heat that is later released into the surroundings.
Building outward can remove trees and cover soil with roads and buildings. Tree cover can shrink if development does not protect existing trees or provide suitable space for replacements.
Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.

human.summary: Homes spread far from jobs and services can increase travel time, fuel costs and the cost of providing roads and utilities. Effects depend on transport choices and how neighbourhoods are planned.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

planet.summary: Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.
consequences: Outward housing growth often adds roads and other paved areas. Dark pavement absorbs sunlight and stores heat that is later released into the surroundings. Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.

incoming: Adding wind, solar and other renewable power can increase electricity made with low emissions. The benefit depends on connecting the supply and keeping the power system reliable.
Storing electricity allows power generated at one time to be used later. This can help the system use more wind and solar power when demand and supply do not match.
Moving flexible electricity use to times when cleaner power is available can make it easier to use that supply. The benefit depends on which demand can safely change time.
Closing coal-fired power stations can make room for electricity with lower emissions. Replacement power and reliable service need to be planned together.
Delays in building power lines can keep new low-emissions electricity from reaching users. Generation alone is not enough if the network cannot carry it.
outgoing: Electricity with lower emissions can replace power made by burning fossil fuels. It can also reduce emissions when it replaces fuel burning in transport, heating and industry.
Replacing local fuel-burning power stations with cleaner electricity can reduce nearby air pollution. The improvement depends on which plants reduce output or close.
Heat pumps use electricity to move heat. Their climate benefit grows as the electricity they use is produced with fewer emissions.
Charging vehicles with electricity made using fewer fossil fuels reduces the emissions from driving them. Electric vehicles still require materials, roads and space.
Low-emissions electricity can power electric steel furnaces and the production of hydrogen used in some steelmaking methods. The benefit depends on the whole production process.
Cleaner electricity can reduce emissions from parts of cement production, including some heating and carbon-capture equipment. Other emissions from the raw materials still need to be addressed.
Some methods that take carbon dioxide out of the air need large amounts of energy. Using low-emissions electricity helps avoid creating new emissions that cancel part of the removal.

human.summary: Replacing fuel-burning power with lower-emissions electricity can improve air quality and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Benefits depend on which generation is actually replaced.
consequences: Nearby communities can breathe less pollution when fossil-fuel plants reduce output or close.
Less fuel use can reduce exposure to sudden fossil-fuel price rises.
Cleaner power can support lower-emissions heating, travel and industry.
human.hiddenCost: Cleaner generation still needs investment in power lines, storage and suitable sites. Land and mineral impacts need careful management.
human.whoPays: Bills, public funding and private investment determine who pays and who benefits.

planet.summary: Low-emissions electricity can reduce the climate impact of power and the activities that switch to using it. The benefit depends on replacing higher-emissions supply.
consequences: Fewer long-lived greenhouse gases are released when fossil generation is displaced.
Less fossil fuel may need to be extracted and burned.
Cleaner power enables lower-emissions heating, transport and industry.
planet.physicalLimit: Projects depend on equipment, skilled workers, land and dependable connections to the grid.

response.defaultDriver: Projects depend on equipment, skilled workers, land and dependable connections to the grid.
levers: Build generation and networks together, with enough dependable supply to replace high-emitting plants.
Protect communities and habitats when choosing sites and sharing benefits.

human.whoPays: Operators, electricity users and public funding may share costs. Market rules determine how benefits reach customers.

incoming: When electricity demand approaches available supply, moving some use to another time becomes more valuable. Only demand that can safely change should be shifted.
outgoing: Moving flexible electricity use to times when cleaner power is available can make it easier to use that supply. The benefit depends on which demand can safely change time.

Fair payments for changing electricity use can help participating households afford their bills. The benefit depends on programme design and whether households can participate safely.

human.summary: Shifting flexible electricity use can help the power system cope with busy hours. People need fair payment and protection against unsafe or unaffordable participation.

human.whoPays: People with flexible equipment may benefit more than households unable to shift essential use.

planet.summary: Moving flexible electricity use can make better use of existing low-emissions supply. Benefits depend on what generation and equipment are actually avoided.
consequences: Fossil plants used mainly at busy hours may run less.

incoming: Building rules can encourage safer cooling gases when they count emissions from gas leaks as well as energy use. Rules that ignore leaks may miss this opportunity.
outgoing: Replacing powerful heat-trapping cooling gases, preventing leaks and recovering old gases can reduce emissions from cooling equipment. Safe installation and servicing are part of making this work.

Cooling can be provided with less climate damage when equipment uses less harmful gases and is efficient. Affordable equipment and trained technicians are needed to make this benefit widely available.

Controls on old ozone-damaging gases reduce new supply, while recovery and destruction prevent releases from existing equipment. Improvement is slow because stored gases can still leak and some remain in the air for many decades.
Stratospheric Ozone Column Depletion and Recovery

Reducing ozone-damaging cooling gases lowers the future supply of reactive chlorine and bromine high in the atmosphere. Recovery is slow and uneven because old equipment, long gas lifetimes and weather still matter.

Using less powerful heat-trapping cooling gases and preventing leaks reduces their contribution to warming. The benefit is measured against what would happen if those releases continued without controls.

consequences: People can retain access to cooling with fewer heat-trapping releases.

Preventing leaks can reduce equipment problems and household losses.

human.whoPays: Households and businesses face upgrade costs. Targeted support can help people unable to afford them.

planet.summary: Changing cooling gases and managing leaks can reduce powerful heat-trapping releases. Old equipment and discarded gas also need careful handling.
consequences: Lower-impact gases can reduce emissions from each leak.

A limited amount can balance emissions that remain difficult to eliminate.

incoming: Projects that use habitats to protect people can fund their recovery and care. Lasting benefits depend on maintaining those habitats after construction or planting.
outgoing: Recovering plants and soils can take carbon dioxide out of the air and store the carbon. The benefit lasts only as long as that additional carbon remains stored.
Repairing damaged habitats can help native plants and animals recover. Recovery depends on removing the original pressures and maintaining a diverse, connected habitat.
Recovering vegetation and healthier soils can increase the carbon taken up and stored on land. The benefit depends on lasting recovery and protection from renewed damage.
Plant cover and roots help hold soil in place. Restoring them can reduce the amount of fertile ground carried away by wind and water.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Restored wetlands, forests and river floodplains can hold or slow water. This can reduce some flood exposure, depending on their location, size and the flood itself.
Healthy habitats provide the living systems needed for natural protection. Wetlands can store floodwater, while trees can provide shade and help cool their surroundings.

human.summary: Repairing damaged habitats can support people who depend on healthy land and water. Benefits depend on lasting recovery and care.
consequences: Farming, fishing and other local livelihoods may gain from healthier ecosystems.
Some projects reduce flooding, heat, erosion or water-quality risks.
Restored places can regain cultural, recreational and community value.
human.hiddenCost: Poor projects can displace people, plant unsuitable species or claim carbon benefits that do not last.
human.whoPays: Landholders, communities and public or private funders share costs. Rights and access need protection.

planet.summary: Repairing damaged ecosystems can rebuild habitat and the processes that support it. Lasting benefits require the original pressures to be reduced.
consequences: Plants and animals can regain connected places to live.
Healthier soils and vegetation can store carbon and help regulate water.
More resilient habitats can recover better from some climate stresses.
planet.physicalLimit: Recovery depends on removing the original pressure and maintaining suitable habitat under a changing climate.

response.defaultDriver: Recovery depends on removing the original pressure and maintaining suitable habitat under a changing climate.
levers: Protect remaining healthy ecosystems and restore suitable native variety on damaged land.
Respect Indigenous and community rights and fund long-term care and monitoring.

incoming: Missing observations or alerts leave people with less time to prepare. These gaps show where better monitoring, communication and response plans are needed.
outgoing: Better monitoring and accessible alerts can reach people who previously lacked useful warnings. People also need to trust the warning and have practical ways to act.
Earlier warnings give services time to prepare and help people move before danger arrives. This can reduce the number of urgent rescues needed at once.
Heat warnings can help prevent deaths when they trigger contact with vulnerable people, access to cooling and health-service preparation. An alert alone is not enough.
Warnings can reduce unequal disaster losses when they reach vulnerable groups and come with real options for protection. Access to transport, shelter and support matters.
Reliable heat forecasts help cities decide when to activate protective measures. Clear communication helps services and residents act together.

human.summary: Useful warnings give people time to prepare before danger arrives. They protect people only when alerts reach them and practical action is possible.
consequences: Timely preparation can reduce injuries and deaths.
Households and services can protect people and important supplies earlier.
Shared plans help weather, health and emergency teams work with communities.
human.hiddenCost: Forecasting equipment and messages need continuing funding. An accurate alert has limited value without practical help to act.
human.whoPays: Public agencies and communities need resources for communication, safe transport and shelter.

planet.summary: Early warnings can give people time to prevent additional environmental damage during emergencies. They do not remove the underlying hazard.
consequences: Preparation can reduce avoidable spills or damage from an unmanaged emergency.
Earlier action may protect sensitive habitats and essential facilities.
Monitoring can reveal when several hazards are developing together.

response.defaultDriver: Warnings can fail to reach people or arrive without enough time, trust or means to respond.
levers: Design messages with exposed communities, in accessible formats and local languages.
Connect alerts to funded evacuation, shelter, health and essential-service plans.

incoming: Growing illness during hot weather shows where cities need stronger preparation. Plans can connect forecasts with cooling, health services and support for people at greatest risk.
Reliable heat forecasts help cities decide when to activate protective measures. Clear communication helps services and residents act together.
outgoing: City plans can help prevent heat-related deaths when forecasts trigger funded action. This includes reaching vulnerable people, opening cooling spaces and protecting outdoor workers.
Coordinating cooling spaces, health services and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. The plan needs staff, funding and follow-through.
City heat plans can protect workers when they include enforceable rules and practical support for safer work. A plan without workplace measures may leave this exposure unchanged.
City plans can coordinate cooling spaces, transport and support for people at greatest risk. Protection against electricity shutoffs can help keep home cooling available.

human.summary: A funded city plan can turn heat forecasts into practical protection. It needs to reach people whose homes, work or health leave them most exposed.
consequences: Early action can reduce preventable heat illness and deaths.
Workers, older people, children and people without safe cooling may receive targeted support.
Health services, utilities, employers and housing teams can coordinate their response.
human.hiddenCost: A plan needs staff, outreach, transport and safe places to cool down. Writing the plan alone does not protect people.
human.whoPays: Local agencies, employers and service providers share responsibilities. Support should reach people facing the greatest exposure.

planet.summary: Heat plans can support long-term changes that keep cities cooler. Environmental benefits depend on including measures beyond emergency air conditioning.
consequences: Shade and suitable building design can reduce sudden peaks in cooling demand.
Greener public spaces can provide cooler surroundings.
Local observations can help direct future heat-reduction work.
planet.physicalLimit: Protection depends on timely action, accessible services and conditions inside homes and workplaces.

response.defaultDriver: Protection depends on timely action, accessible services and conditions inside homes and workplaces.
levers: Set local alert triggers and clear responsibilities, backed by budgets.
Protect workers and invest in shade, cooler buildings and accessible cooling during emergencies.

incoming: Cooling can be provided with less climate damage when equipment uses less harmful gases and is efficient. Affordable equipment and trained technicians are needed to make this benefit widely available.
A building that stays comfortable with less energy is cheaper to cool. This can help more people maintain safe indoor temperatures.
Shade and other ways of keeping buildings cool can reduce the need for continuously powered air conditioning. This can help people who cannot afford high electricity bills.
City plans can coordinate cooling spaces, transport and support for people at greatest risk. Protection against electricity shutoffs can help keep home cooling available.
Losing electricity can stop fans and air conditioning during dangerous heat. Households unable to afford continued service may lose access to safe temperatures.
outgoing: Making safe indoor temperatures available to people at greatest risk can help prevent heat-related deaths. Cooling must remain affordable and available when needed.
Efficient cooling, affordable energy and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. These measures work best together.
Expanding powered cooling can increase electricity use during the hottest hours. Efficient equipment, cooler buildings and careful demand management help limit that increase.

human.summary: Affordable, reliable ways to stay cool can protect people during dangerous heat. Access must include those unable to buy or operate cooling on their own.
consequences: Safe indoor temperatures can reduce heat illness and deaths.
People with health conditions can receive protection when heat is especially risky.
Households may avoid choosing between a manageable bill and a safe temperature.
human.hiddenCost: More cooling can raise electricity demand, bills and gas leakage if equipment and supply are poorly planned.
human.whoPays: Households need affordable running costs as well as affordable equipment. Public support can target those with the fewest alternatives.

planet.summary: Safe cooling can be provided with less environmental pressure when efficient equipment and better buildings are part of the programme.
consequences: Efficient systems reduce electricity demand and the need for cooling gases.
Insulation and shade limit unnecessary energy use.
Ways of cooling without powered equipment reduce dependence on air conditioning.
planet.physicalLimit: Cooling protection depends on reliable power, efficient equipment and access during the hottest periods.

response.defaultDriver: Cooling protection depends on reliable power, efficient equipment and access during the hottest periods.
levers: Combine efficient cooling with shade and suitable home improvements.
Provide targeted bill support and plans for outages and residents with medical needs.

incoming: Repeated flooding by seawater increases the need to protect essential buildings and services. Better siting, drainage and access can reduce damage within their design limits.
outgoing: Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Safer locations, drainage, water storage and protective works can reduce exposure to flooding. Maintenance and the size of future floods determine how well protection holds up.
More storage, treatment capacity and protection from floodwater can reduce sewage overflows. Separating rainwater from sewage flows can also ease pressure on the system.
Designing essential services for future floods can make failures less likely. Backup routes, spare capacity and maintenance help services continue when one part is damaged.
Keeping roads and essential services working during floods can reduce urgent rescue needs. It also helps emergency teams reach people who still need assistance.

human.summary: Services designed and maintained for flooding are more likely to keep working during an event. Protection has limits and needs to match future conditions.
consequences: Water, power, transport and health services can suffer fewer interruptions.
Households may face fewer repeated losses and outages.
Avoided damage can reduce some recovery costs.
human.hiddenCost: Flood walls and drainage can move water problems elsewhere or encourage building behind defenses that can still fail.
human.whoPays: Public budgets, owners and nearby communities share costs, including people downstream.

planet.summary: Well-designed flood protection can reduce pollution released when essential services fail. Designs that work with natural habitats can provide additional benefits.
consequences: Restoring wetlands or floodplains can create space for water and wildlife.
Protected sewage and chemical facilities are less likely to release pollution during floods.
Fewer infrastructure failures can limit damage to nearby waters.
planet.physicalLimit: Every defense has a design limit and needs maintenance. Future floods may exceed past experience.

response.defaultDriver: Every defense has a design limit and needs maintenance. Future floods may exceed past experience.
levers: Use future conditions in design and protect natural flood-storage areas where suitable.
Combine engineered protection with land-use limits and avoid adding unsafe development.

measurement.metric: Critical assets meeting a declared flood-resilience standard
measurement.unit: assets and percent of assessed assets
measurement.geography: named asset, operator service area, network, city, or infrastructure portfolio
measurement.cadence: event-based or operational with monthly and annual rollups
measurement.method: Record the equipment and service affected, capacity, number of users, interruption start and restoration time. Keep planned work and backup options separate from failures. Where appropriate, account for how long the disruption lasts.
measurement.uncertainty: Some incidents go unreported, and one failure can trigger others. Causes, equipment lists, user counts and overlapping outages can make totals uncertain.
measurement.boundary: Exposure to a hazard does not prove a service failed. Different services cannot be combined into one score without explaining how they are weighted.

incoming: When demand approaches available water supply, safely treating and using water again becomes more valuable. It helps most when it replaces water taken from an already stressed source.
outgoing: Treated water can replace some water pumped from underground. This reduces pressure only if total pumping actually falls.
Using treated local water again can reduce the need to remove salt from seawater. The choice depends on water quality requirements and the amount available.
Investment in collecting and treating used water can reduce releases of untreated sewage. Reuse helps when it improves the treatment system as well as finding a new use for the water.
Advanced water treatment needs energy. It can add carbon dioxide emissions when that energy comes from fossil fuels.

human.summary: Treating water so it can be used again can strengthen local supplies. Safety and benefit depend on suitable treatment and replacing demand on other sources.
consequences: A dependable local supply can become available for suitable uses.
Communities may be less exposed to drought or imported-water disruption.
Investment can improve wastewater treatment and reduce pollution.
human.hiddenCost: Treatment needs energy and maintenance and can produce concentrated waste. Poor pricing can put useful water beyond some people's reach.
human.whoPays: Utilities, customers and public funding share costs and benefits.

planet.summary: Using treated water again can reduce pressure on rivers and groundwater when it replaces new withdrawals.
consequences: Less fresh water may need to be taken from natural sources.
Effective treatment can reduce polluted discharges.
Reduced withdrawals can leave more water for ecosystems.
planet.physicalLimit: Required treatment depends on whether the water will be drunk, used on crops or used for another purpose.

response.defaultDriver: Required treatment depends on whether the water will be drunk, used on crops or used for another purpose.
levers: Match treatment to the intended use and monitor relevant contaminants.
Use efficient cleaner energy and protect affordability and water needed by rivers and habitats.

measurement.metric: Treated municipal and industrial wastewater reused
measurement.unit: million cubic metres per year and percent of treated flow
measurement.geography: declared basin, aquifer, utility, catchment, floodplain, or administrative reporting area
measurement.cadence: event-based to monthly with annual accounting
measurement.method: Keep the water sources, uses, area and time period clear, along with what each percentage is divided by. Keep event definitions and model versions consistent. Measured, modelled, legally permitted and estimated amounts are different.
measurement.uncertainty: Missing gauges or wells, withdrawals, returned water and exchanges between rivers and groundwater affect estimates. Reporting quality and the detail of models also matter.
measurement.boundary: Missing data do not mean no flow, no water use or no impact. A result for an entire river basin cannot be applied directly to one building or household.

incoming: Unreliable harvests increase the need for farming methods that handle heat, water shortages and other shocks. The most useful changes depend on local crops and conditions.
outgoing: A mix of crops, healthier soils, better water management and useful forecasts can make harvests more dependable. These measures reduce some risks but cannot prevent every loss.
Keeping soil covered, maintaining roots and disturbing it less can reduce erosion. Better water management can also slow the washing away of fertile ground.

More efficient farming can reduce groundwater use when limits also control total withdrawals. Saving water on each field does not help overall if irrigated production expands enough to cancel the saving.
More dependable local harvests can reduce the need to replace losses with imported food. The effect depends on which foods are grown and the shocks the farms face.

human.summary: Farming adapted to local climate risks can make food and farm incomes more dependable. Measures need to suit the crop, soil and water available.
consequences: A mix of crops and better planning can reduce some harvest shocks.
Healthier soil can hold water better and reduce dependence on costly inputs.
Worker protection and more reliable production can support rural livelihoods.
human.hiddenCost: Changing practices can require equipment, training or temporary income support. Labels alone do not guarantee better results.
human.whoPays: Farmers, workers, consumers and public programs may share the costs and benefits.

planet.summary: Farming methods suited to local risks can protect soil and water while supporting production. Benefits depend on management and limits on total resource use.
consequences: Keeping soil covered can reduce erosion and nutrient losses.
Healthier soil and varied habitats can support stored carbon and wildlife.
More efficient water use reduces total pressure only when extra demand does not cancel the saving.
planet.physicalLimit: No single practice works in every soil and climate. Water use, yields, emissions and working conditions must be considered together.

response.defaultDriver: No single practice works in every soil and climate. Water use, yields, emissions and working conditions must be considered together.
levers: Fund locally tested practices and practical advice for farmers.
Reward measured improvements in soil, water and income, with emissions cuts and worker protection.

measurement.unit: hectares and percent of managed area
measurement.geography: declared country, production region, market, fishery, farm system, or food-supply-chain segment
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to harvest, market, or inventory reporting
measurement.method: Keep the food or animal product, amount, price and stage of any loss clear. Identify the population or workforce behind percentages. Food supply, people's access, safe use and reliability over time are different measures.
measurement.uncertainty: Informal production, trade accounting, market coverage and estimates of losses can affect the result. Fish-stock assessments and population counts may also be revised.
measurement.boundary: Missing reports do not mean no production, waste, disease or exposure. Different products need an explained weighting before being combined.

incoming: Repeated flooding or other danger can make rebuilding in the same place unsafe. This increases the need to plan a move with the affected community.
outgoing: A planned move can reduce unequal disaster losses when people receive suitable housing, services, compensation and ways to earn a living. These protections need to be delivered, not just promised.
Moving a community requires organisations that can coordinate land, housing, money and public services. Experience can strengthen that ability when communities retain a voice and funding lasts.
Moving before repeated disasters destroy homes can reduce emergency displacement. The benefit depends on providing a safe, supported destination and involving the people who move.

human.summary: A planned, supported move can reduce repeated exposure to dangerous or unaffordable hazards. Residents need a real role in decisions and a viable place to live.
consequences: Moving before a disaster can reduce repeated losses.
Planning creates time to arrange housing, land, schools and income.
Keeping communities together may be easier than after emergency displacement.
human.hiddenCost: Moving can disrupt jobs, culture and community ties as well as cost money. A poorly run move can deepen existing hardship.
human.whoPays: Residents, receiving communities and public programs need fair arrangements for land, housing and ongoing services.

planet.summary: Moving development away from repeatedly hazardous areas can create room for natural recovery. The result depends on what happens to both the old site and the new one.
consequences: Floodplains or shorelines may regain space and habitat.
Less repeated rebuilding can reduce disturbance in exposed ecosystems.
Some vacated areas can support wetlands and other natural protection.
planet.physicalLimit: A safer site is not enough without secure rights, income opportunities and community consent.

response.defaultDriver: A safer site is not enough without secure rights, income opportunities and community consent.
levers: Plan voluntary moves with affected communities before an emergency forces decisions.
Guarantee fair support, services and continued cultural ties, including funding for receiving communities.

measurement.uncertainty: Missing reports, changing eligibility, informal activity, financial valuations and survey error affect estimates. Assigning an outcome to a cause adds further uncertainty.

photo.alt: People arriving in small boats plant young mangroves in mud beside a tidal channel.

incoming: Healthy habitats provide the living systems needed for natural protection. Wetlands can store floodwater, while trees can provide shade and help cool their surroundings.
outgoing: Projects that use habitats to protect people can fund their recovery and care. Lasting benefits depend on maintaining those habitats after construction or planting.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Wetlands and connected river floodplains can store water and slow its movement. This can reduce flood exposure within the limits of the land and the event.
Mangroves, marshes, dunes and reefs can reduce some coastal wave and flood impacts. They have physical limits and cannot prevent every flood.
Trees and other vegetation shade surfaces and cool the air as water evaporates. Less heat stored during the day can mean less released into nearby air at night.
Projects can help wildlife when they restore native habitats and connect them to other suitable areas. A project designed only for protection may not provide the same benefit.

human.summary: Healthy habitats can help protect people from heat, waves, floods and erosion. Their protection depends on location, condition and continued care.
consequences: Trees, wetlands and coastal habitats can reduce some harmful exposure.
Projects can provide accessible green space and local work.
Suitable designs may improve water quality and neighbourhood comfort.
human.hiddenCost: Restored wetlands, trees or reefs need space and care. They may fail if pressure continues or future conditions become unsuitable.
human.whoPays: Land users, local communities and public or private funders share costs and benefits.

planet.summary: Using healthy habitats to reduce hazards can also support wildlife and natural processes. Native species, connected space and long-term care help these benefits last.
consequences: Damaged habitats can recover their functions.
Plants and soils may store more carbon.
Projects can reconnect separated landscapes and waterways.
planet.physicalLimit: Natural protection has limits and may take time to recover. It cannot make every exposed site safe.

response.defaultDriver: Natural protection has limits and may take time to recover. It cannot make every exposed site safe.
levers: Protect existing healthy ecosystems and monitor whether restoration is working.
Combine suitable natural protection with land-use limits and engineered measures where needed.

measurement.method: Keep the habitat, species or group, survey method and survey effort clear. State the reference condition and area used for percentages. Habitat area, habitat health, numbers of organisms and benefits they provide are separate measures.
measurement.uncertainty: Some species are harder to detect and some places are surveyed more often. Map detail, season, reference condition and how causes are identified affect estimates.
measurement.boundary: An unsurveyed habitat is unknown, not empty or healthy. Finding a species, counting its numbers, assessing habitat condition and establishing extinction require different evidence.

aquifer overdraft.name: Aquifer Overdraft
aquifer overdraft.description: Pumping water from an underground store faster than it is replaced. Water levels can fall, making wells less reliable. In some places, continued pumping can also pull salty water into supplies used for drinking or farming.

photo.alt: An old irrigation well and wooden lifting structure stand beside green fields at sunset.
photo.caption: A traditional well supplies surrounding farmland. Aquifer overdraft occurs when sustained groundwater withdrawal exceeds replenishment; a single photograph cannot establish that balance.

incoming: Water lost before it benefits crops may be replaced by extra pumping. Underground reserves decline if withdrawals keep exceeding refill and usable return flows.
Treated water can replace some water pumped from underground. This reduces pressure only if total pumping actually falls.

More efficient farming can reduce groundwater use when limits also control total withdrawals. Saving water on each field does not help overall if irrigated production expands enough to cancel the saving.
Pumping more groundwater than rain and other sources replace gradually reduces underground reserves. This can continue over years or decades.
outgoing: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.

Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts.

human.summary: Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve. A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply. Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.

Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts. Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.
human.hiddenCost: Pumping water faster than it is replaced can lower well levels and, in some sediments, cause lasting ground sinking.
human.whoPays: People with shallow wells may lose access first. Farmers, households and water utilities can face deeper pumping or replacement-supply costs.

planet.summary: Excess pumping lowers the freshwater level beneath an island. Saltier water can move closer to the wells, reducing the usable reserve.
consequences: Pumping faster than water is replaced lowers underground reserves. Wells can then reach less water or stop working at their existing depth.
Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.
planet.physicalLimit: Some fine-grained underground layers compact when pressure falls and cannot regain all their storage space. Not every underground water store behaves this way.

response.defaultDriver: Cheap pumping and weak limits on total withdrawals can encourage taking more water than the system can replace.
levers: Set withdrawals using evidence about recharge, connected rivers and essential needs.
Protect suitable recharge areas and reduce incentives for excessive pumping.

measurement.method: Keep the water sources, uses, area and time period clear, along with what each percentage is divided by. Keep event definitions and model versions consistent. Measured, modelled, legally permitted and estimated amounts are different.
measurement.uncertainty: Missing gauges or wells, withdrawals, returned water and exchanges between rivers and groundwater affect estimates. Reporting quality and the detail of models also matter.
measurement.boundary: Missing data do not mean no flow, no water use or no impact. A result for an entire river basin cannot be applied directly to one building or household.

incoming: Warming changes evaporation, precipitation and the timing of snowmelt. These can alter how much water rivers carry and when it arrives.
Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference.
Less stored snow means less water released during the usual melting season. Rivers may receive water earlier in the year and less when it is most needed.
Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.
Storing or diverting river water changes when and how much water reaches places downstream. Operating rules can reduce seasonal peaks or create new daily fluctuations.
Narrow or poorly placed stream crossings can change water speed, depth and sediment movement nearby. These are local effects that need comparison with an unobstructed stretch of stream.
Straightening or confining rivers can move water downstream faster and separate it from floodplain storage. This changes local depths, speeds and flooding patterns.

Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment.
outgoing: Weaker or differently timed river flows provide less fresh water to resist the sea. Saltier water can then move farther upstream.
A dam may receive water at different times or in different amounts than expected. Stored supplies can then become less predictable under existing operating rules.
Changes in river flow can make older water-sharing rules difficult to follow. Agreements based on historical supplies may no longer match the water available.
Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
Changes in when and how much river water arrives can make electricity from dams less dependable. Reservoirs and turbines may no longer receive the flow they were designed around.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.
