incoming: Darkened snow absorbs more sunlight than clean snow. This can make melting begin sooner or proceed faster in the affected area.

A study of 2,339 mainly undisturbed Northern Hemisphere river catchments linked each 1°C of local annual warming with an average snowmelt-flood peak 4.7 days earlier. Results varied widely between catchments, with a standard deviation of 5.0 days. The average is not a forecast for every river.
A smaller or warmer winter snowpack often melts sooner. Rivers may receive an earlier and weaker pulse of meltwater.
Warming can turn more winter precipitation into rain and bring earlier snowmelt. The timing change depends on the river basin, elevation and season.
Dark dust on snow absorbs sunlight and can bring earlier melting and runoff. Fresh snow can bury it and clouds reduce its effect, so the size of the timing change must be assessed locally.
outgoing: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily.
Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference.
Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength.
Earlier snowmelt can send water into a glacier before its drainage channels are ready to carry it. Blockages or sudden changes in those channels can release stored water as a flood.

Earlier snowmelt changes the seasonal mix of snow and glacier water reaching rivers. It can make the loss of late-season glacier support more noticeable, without alone proving that a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
Earlier snow loss reduces the time that cool, moist patches remain on exposed mountain peaks. Specialised plants and animals may face a longer period of heat and drying.

human.summary: Snow melting earlier or faster can send a stronger pulse of water into streams. The effect is greater where the landscape has little capacity to hold the water temporarily. domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
consequences: Earlier melting moves snow-fed river flows toward an earlier part of the year. Less may remain for the warm season unless storage or rainfall makes up the difference. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.

Earlier or faster melting adds water inside mountain snow. Slopes may become unstable when wet layers lose their strength. Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

incoming: Little rain over a long period leaves soil water unreplenished while plants and evaporation continue using it. Soil can become exceptionally dry.

In the European models assessed, soil drought covered more land at 3°C of global warming than at 1.5°C. The estimated increase was 40%, with a spread of plus or minus 24%, so this is a model result for that region rather than a universal prediction.
Dry air draws water from soil and plants more strongly. The ground around roots dries faster when rain cannot replace the loss.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: A long-lasting high-pressure pattern can divert storms and keep rain away from the same region. Dry conditions can then continue for longer.
A persistent pressure pattern can keep some North Atlantic regions short of rain. Whether it prolongs drought depends on the season and location.
Some phases of this pressure pattern can keep rain away from particular North American regions. The drought effect depends on season and location.
Slow-moving bends in high-altitude winds can keep rain away from a region. How much they contribute to a particular drought varies from event to event.

Warming increases the amount of water the air can draw from plants and soil. Where rain does not make up the loss, dry conditions can become more severe or last longer. The effect varies by region and season.

Changing air-pressure patterns around the Arctic can shift storms and temperatures farther south. In some regions and seasons, less rain and earlier snowmelt can leave dry conditions that last into the next season.
Unusually warm tropical Pacific waters can change winds and reduce rain in some regions. Dry soil, low rivers and depleted reservoirs can keep the effects going after the initial weather change.
Warming increases the air's demand for moisture. Where rain stays low, soil and plants can dry faster and drought conditions may last longer.
Long-lasting drought can be one part of a sequence or combination of climate hazards. Its causes and effects still need to be assessed for the drying region.
outgoing: A long drought reduces river flow and the flushing of river mouths. Saltier water can move farther inland and remain there longer.
A long dry period can keep incoming river water low. Reservoirs may fail to refill enough to meet later needs.
Little rain over a long period leaves soil water unreplenished while plants and evaporation continue using it. Soil can become exceptionally dry.
Repeated water shortages can make countries or regions unable to meet agreed allocations. Cooperation may come under strain as the dry period continues.
Lower water volumes during drought can leave salts and pollutants more concentrated. Utilities may need more treatment to provide safe drinking water.
A long drought reduces water reaching dams and may lower stored water levels. Less dependable flow means less dependable electricity generation.
Long dry periods can lower water levels in ground made of partly decayed plants. Exposure to air allows this stored material to break down and release carbon dioxide.
Long dry periods reduce moisture in the soil and the cooling provided by evaporation. Crops, animals and workers can then face hotter local conditions.
Long dry periods can dry vegetation across seasons. This increases the amount that can burn and can extend the time of year with high fire danger.
Long dry periods can reduce the water replenishing underground stores while increasing demand for pumping. Reserves fall faster where withdrawals already approach or exceed replacement.
Long dry periods reduce river supplies and the water replenishing underground reserves. Shortages become more likely if demand stays high.
Long dry periods leave less water in soil and less available for plants to release. More surface energy then heats the air, increasing its demand for water.

Long dry periods leave less water to move through soil and replenish underground stores. The response can be delayed, and falling groundwater may also reflect extra pumping rather than reduced replenishment alone.
Repeated drought can kill trees, increase fire risk and favour plants adapted to drier conditions. A single drought does not prove a permanent change from forest to open vegetation.
Repeated drought can reduce plant cover and leave soil exposed to erosion. Healthy or restored land may recover when rain returns, so a dry period is not automatically permanent degradation.
Drought can dry the surface and reduce plant cover, leaving more material available for wind to lift. Strong winds and loose sediment are still needed, and protective soil crusts can limit dust.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction
Long dry periods can weaken mountain trees and prevent regrowth after damage. Some forests recover when moisture returns, so a short decline in greenness is not proof of permanent loss.
Repeated dry periods can make it harder for savanna trees to establish and survive. Effects are greater where rain and soil already limit growth.
Long water shortages can disrupt a tree's water transport and weaken its defences. The air's demand for moisture also matters, so temperature alone is not enough to describe the exposure.
Long periods of low water can expose mussel beds, increase heat and concentrate pollution. Fish needed for the mussels' life cycle may also lose access.
Severe drought can weaken a tree's protective sap and other defences against beetles. The response varies: moderate dryness can hinder some beetles, and drought links are weak for some species.
Long water shortages can stop trees moving enough water to survive. Heat, pests, fire injury and the condition of the forest can add to the stress.
Long periods of dry soil can damage plants and reduce soil fertility. Microbes and the functions they perform may come under pressure.
Long periods of little rain reduce water entering lakes and reservoirs. Storage can fall or become less dependable if withdrawals continue.
A long drought can reduce a city's source-water supply and lead to restrictions. Storage, transfers, leaks and conservation affect how much use must be limited.
Long periods of low rain and runoff reduce water entering rivers and reservoirs. Snow and groundwater can delay or soften the effect where enough reserves remain.
A long drought can reduce reservoir inflow, river supply and groundwater replenishment available to a city. The resulting shortfall depends on demand and remaining reserves.

incoming: Releasing used water without normal treatment can add pollutants and suspended dirt to a river. Water plants downstream may need extra work and expense to make supplies safe.

incoming: Heat and drying can strain forests in river catchments. Greater water loss and fire risk can damage trees and change how water moves through the area.
Clearing trees within a river catchment removes canopy and roots. This can increase erosion and allow rainwater to reach streams more quickly.
Repeated severe fires can kill trees faster than forests regrow. A river catchment may then be left with less tree cover or a different type of vegetation.
outgoing: Losing trees around rivers can increase erosion and change water flow and habitat. Severe or repeated damage can reduce the ability of freshwater communities to survive and recover.
Without forest cover, more soil can wash into streams supplying drinking water. Dirtier and less predictable source water can make treatment harder and more costly.
Forest damage can change when water reaches a dam and how much sediment it carries. These changes can make electricity generation less reliable.
Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.
Losing trees can increase runoff and sediment reaching rivers. Where bank vegetation is also lost, fewer roots hold the bank in place.

human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Limited stored water or restrictions on releases can leave less water available to turn turbines. Electricity from the dam then becomes less dependable.

incoming: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands

If an island's shallow freshwater reserve cannot provide enough reliable drinking water, the community may need more salt-removal treatment or imported water. Available alternatives determine the choice.
As coastal wells become saltier, ordinary supplies may be less usable. Utilities or households may turn increasingly to equipment that removes salt from water.
Persistent salt problems can exceed ordinary water-treatment capabilities. A utility may then adopt salt-removal equipment where other suitable sources are limited.
Using treated local water again can reduce the need to remove salt from seawater. The choice depends on water quality requirements and the amount available.
outgoing: Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases.

human.summary: Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
consequences: Salt-removal plants need energy to provide water. Where that energy comes from fossil fuels, operating the plants adds carbon dioxide releases. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for present coastal service and displacement-function loss attributable to ice-sheet contributions and current coastal and ice-associated habitat condition deficit attributable to ice-sheet loss; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

incoming: Warmer air melts ice at the surface, while warmer seawater can thin floating ice around the edges. Reduced support can also let ice on land flow into the sea faster.
Carbon dioxide released into the air adds to warming. Warmer air and ocean water increase pressure on the large ice masses covering Greenland and Antarctica.
Warm ocean water can melt floating ice shelves from below. Weaker shelves hold back inland ice less effectively, allowing it to move toward the sea faster.
Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity
The partly compacted snow above glacier ice can store and refreeze meltwater. When it loses empty space or forms impermeable layers, more water runs off and contributes to ice loss.
outgoing: Meltwater from Antarctic ice makes nearby seawater fresher and less dense. This can reduce the formation of water that sinks to the deepest ocean.

Faster ice movement and ice loss can be signs that floating ice is providing less support to ice inland. These observations need local evidence to identify the cause. Ice loss alone does not explain every change.
Losing ice can change where meltwater collects and how it drains. Flood hazards depend on whether water becomes trapped, how it escapes and what lies downstream.
Fresh meltwater from Greenland makes nearby surface seawater less salty and lighter. This can make it harder for water to sink and may weaken Atlantic circulation.
Fresh water from melting ice sheets forms a lighter layer near the ocean surface. This can strengthen the separation from saltier, denser water below.
Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.

Ice lost from land adds water to the ocean and raises average sea level. Greenland's measured loss during 1992–2020 was equivalent to 13.5 millimetres globally, with an assessed range of 11.4–15.6 millimetres.
Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed.
Rising sea levels let waves and storm-driven water reach farther inland. Erosion can increase along coasts made of material that is easily worn away.
Sea-level rise from land-ice loss can push saltwater toward coastal underground freshwater. Pumping, rainwater replenishment and local geology affect how far it moves.
Higher sea levels raise the starting point for coastal floods. Damage can be greater when storms, high tides, heavy rain or river floods occur together.
Losing reflective land ice can expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This can reinforce local warming, depending on what surface is left behind.
Ice loss and related changes to coasts and frozen ground can threaten polar buildings and transport. The risk is greatest where facilities depend on stable ice or land.

human.summary: Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed. Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.

Losing ice can change where meltwater collects and how it drains. Flood hazards depend on whether water becomes trapped, how it escapes and what lies downstream. Sudden releases of stored glacier water can produce river flows far above seasonal levels. Repeated releases change the timing, size and sediment carried by downstream floods.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. incoming: More global warming makes an Arctic September with almost no sea ice more likely. The assessment puts the yearly chance by the end of the century at about 1% with 1.5°C of warming, compared with 10–35% with 2°C.
Warm ocean water can melt sea ice from below and delay freezing in autumn. This shortens the time that sea ice covers the water.
Faster warming in the Arctic can bring earlier spring melting and later autumn freezing. Sea ice then remains for less of the year.

The cited study found that Arctic September sea-ice area fell roughly in step with accumulated human carbon dioxide emissions. Over its assessed record, each extra metric tonne was associated with about 3 square metres less ice, with an uncertainty of plus or minus 0.3 square metres.
outgoing: A longer ice-free season can allow vessels to use northern routes for more of the year. Moving ice, storms, ports, insurance and rules still determine whether traffic actually increases.
Less time covered by bright sea ice leaves darker water exposed to sunlight for longer. More absorbed energy contributes to faster warming in the Arctic.
A shorter season of sea ice leaves Arctic coasts more exposed to waves and erosion. It can also shorten periods when people can safely use ice-based access routes.
A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships.
A shorter ice season reduces stable growing space for algae living in sea ice. Earlier melting can change bloom timing and wash away some of this material.
A longer open-water season gives waves more time and space to attack Arctic coasts. Shores made of thawing, ice-rich ground can erode especially quickly.
Losing sea ice during the sunlit season exposes darker ocean water. The water absorbs more sunlight, adding heat that can encourage further melting.

human.summary: A longer ice-free season can allow vessels to use northern routes for more of the year. Moving ice, storms, ports, insurance and rules still determine whether traffic actually increases. More ships using Arctic routes means more journeys exposed to changing ice conditions. Remote locations and limited rescue or repair services can make disruptions harder to manage.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
consequences: A shorter season of sea ice leaves Arctic coasts more exposed to waves and erosion. It can also shorten periods when people can safely use ice-based access routes. Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.

A shorter ice season can leave thinner and less connected Arctic sea ice. Winds and currents can move this ice more readily through areas used by ships. Moving sea ice can enter planned ship routes and narrow safe passages. Ships may need to wait, change course or seek icebreaker support even when total ice cover is low.
human.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
human.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.

incoming: Mangroves, marshes, dunes and reefs can reduce some coastal wave and flood impacts. They have physical limits and cannot prevent every flood.
Warming expands seawater and melts ice on land, raising sea levels. A higher starting water level makes it easier for seawater to flood nearby land.
Carbon dioxide adds to warming and the resulting rise in sea level. This increases the background pressure behind coastal flooding and erosion.
Changes in Atlantic ocean circulation can raise or lower sea levels along parts of the North Atlantic coast. Flooding there also depends on tides, storms, waves and the longer-term rise in sea level.

A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.
Water from melting ice sheets raises the sea's starting level. Coastal flooding then depends on local tides, storms, land movement and the people or buildings exposed.

Higher sea levels make previously rare coastal water levels easier to reach. Across the assessed tide-gauge locations, relative sea-level rise is projected to make recent extreme still-water levels occur roughly 20–30 times as often by 2050. Local tides, storms and land movement affect the result.
outgoing: When the sea rises, it can become harder for drains to carry used water away. During storms or high tides, pipes can back up and wastewater can spill into surrounding areas.
Higher seawater levels can push salty water farther inland through river mouths and connected underground stores. This is especially important when river flow is too weak to push it back.
Repeated flooding by the sea can add salt to connected underground freshwater stores. Shallow or exposed stores may become less suitable for drinking or farming.
Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.
Seawater can reach low-lying airports near the coast. Flooded runways, access roads or equipment can interrupt flights and damage the airport.
Repeated flooding by seawater can increase expected insurance losses. Insurers may raise prices, limit coverage or stop offering policies in exposed areas.
Rising water can damage coastal wetlands if they cannot build up soil or move inland fast enough. Losing plants and soils can put their stored carbon at risk of release.
Repeated flooding by seawater increases the need to protect essential buildings and services. Better siting, drainage and access can reduce damage within their design limits.
Storms, tides and rising sea levels can bring seawater onto low-lying buildings and services. Whether they fail depends on flood depth, protection, equipment design and available backups.
Repeated coastal floods can increase expected insurance claims and the cost of covering them. Insurers may raise prices, limit policies or leave exposed markets.
Coastal floods can close ports, damage access roads and stop cargo handling. Sea routes can be disrupted even when the open water remains navigable.
Rising seawater can change salt levels in estuaries. This may make particular places more or less suitable for disease-causing organisms, depending on the salt range they tolerate.
Seawater entering fields or freshwater supplies brings dissolved salts with it. Salt left around crop roots can make farming more difficult on low-lying land.
Repeated or expected coastal floods can make continued protection and rebuilding impractical. Communities may need to consider a planned move that protects residents' rights and livelihoods.

incoming: Warmer weather can cause more rain instead of snow and melt existing snow sooner. Less water then remains stored as snow for later in the year.
Warming can shift snowfall toward rain and speed melting. Mountain areas may then store much less water in winter snow than expected.
outgoing: Less stored snow means less water released during the usual melting season. Rivers may receive water earlier in the year and less when it is most needed.
A small winter snowpack stores less water for later in the year. This can make reservoir supplies harder to predict and manage.
A smaller or warmer winter snowpack often melts sooner. Rivers may receive an earlier and weaker pulse of meltwater.
Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed.
A season with little snowfall or unusually early melting leaves less water stored in mountain snow. The change differs with elevation, season and river basin.
Repeated winters with too little snow leave small ice caps with less new ice to replace melting. Their summits and connecting ice can thin until a once-continuous cap breaks apart.

human.summary: Less stored snow means less water released during the usual melting season. Rivers may receive water earlier in the year and less when it is most needed. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
consequences: A small winter snowpack stores less water for later in the year. This can make reservoir supplies harder to predict and manage. Unpredictable stored water makes it harder for dam operators to deliver the expected supply at the right time. Drinking water, flood control or electricity commitments may then be missed.

Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed. After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current food and fishery-livelihood function loss from oxygen-limited marine systems and present integrated marine condition deficit from oxygen loss; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

incoming: Warmer seawater holds less oxygen, and stronger layering can reduce the supply reaching deeper water. Together these processes can lower ocean oxygen. Projections depend on the future climate scenario.
Strongly separated water layers can slow mixing from the surface. Less oxygen then reaches deeper water to replace what living things use.

Less sinking and renewal of deep water can reduce oxygen delivery far below the surface. The cited observations describe this connection in a particular Antarctic ocean basin, not an identical change everywhere.
Warming makes seawater hold less oxygen and can reduce mixing between surface and deep water. These processes contribute to declining oxygen in parts of the ocean.
outgoing: As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available.
Reduced oxygen can shrink suitable fish habitat, move stocks or cause deaths. These changes add to fishery risks, alongside fishing pressure and other local conditions.
Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life.

Less oxygen can reduce the depths and temperatures fish can tolerate and change where their food lives. Responses differ between species, and local oxygen loss may come from nutrient pollution as well as climate change.

human.summary: As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available. domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Reduced oxygen can shrink suitable fish habitat, move stocks or cause deaths. These changes add to fishery risks, alongside fishing pressure and other local conditions. Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.

Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life. Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.
human.hiddenCost: Less oxygen can reduce suitable habitat, growth and reproduction even before large numbers of dead fish are seen.
human.whoPays: Fishing communities, seafood businesses and coastal consumers can face reduced or less reliable catches.

planet.summary: Less oxygen leaves fewer suitable places for many marine animals. Species may need to move or compete within a narrower band of water.
consequences: Fish and other animals can lose usable habitat.
Warmer, more separated water layers can limit the mixing that replaces oxygen.
Sensitive species may become crowded into the remaining oxygen-rich areas.
planet.physicalLimit: Species need different amounts of oxygen. A commonly used low-oxygen threshold is not a universal point at which all marine life dies.

response.defaultDriver: Warming reduces how much oxygen water holds and can weaken mixing. Excess nutrients add pressure in some coastal waters.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions and excess nutrients reaching vulnerable waters.
Monitor oxygen at relevant depths and adjust habitat and fishing management to the observed changes.

outgoing: Changing seawater chemistry can make the materials for shells and coral skeletons less available. Some organisms then have more difficulty building or maintaining them, with large differences between species and conditions.
Changes in seawater chemistry affect species differently. If some organisms grow or survive less well, animals that depend on them can also be affected, changing feeding relationships.
Changing seawater chemistry can slow the building and repair of coral skeletons. If losses outpace replacement, the reef framework can weaken.

Changes in seawater chemistry can harm the growth or survival of some young fish and shell-forming animals. Effects differ between species. Evidence of exposure alone does not show that an entire estuary has lost its nursery role.
Changing seawater chemistry can reduce coral growth and recovery. It can make heat stress harder to withstand, but it is not itself a measure of heat-related bleaching.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Changing seawater chemistry can interfere with early coral growth and the signals young corals use to find a place to settle. Sensitive species may have lower survival.
Changes in seawater chemistry can slow reef building and increase erosion. Weaker structures can become more vulnerable when waves or other disturbances strike.

Changing seawater chemistry can affect growth, reproduction, prey and habitat. It may contribute to changes in where fish live, but direct evidence is generally weaker than for warming and numbers can change without movement.

human.summary: Changes in seawater chemistry can make it harder for some marine animals to build shells or reefs. People depending on seafood and coastal habitats may feel the effects.
consequences: Shellfish hatcheries and reef communities can become less productive.
Fishing households may face lower income or less dependable food supplies.
Damaged reefs can lose tourism value and some of the structure that protects coasts.
human.hiddenCost: Changing seawater chemistry can make it harder for some animals to build and maintain shells or skeletons, affecting seafood and habitats.
human.whoPays: Shellfish growers, fishing communities and coastal businesses may face losses or treatment costs.

planet.summary: Changing seawater chemistry makes shell and reef building harder for some organisms. Effects can spread to the animals and habitats that depend on them.
consequences: Sensitive shell-building species may use more energy or grow and survive less well.
Reefs can weaken when chemical changes add to heat stress.
Losing important shell-forming organisms can change marine feeding relationships.
planet.physicalLimit: Sensitivity depends on species, life stage and local chemistry. There is no single point at which every shell-building animal dissolves.

response.defaultDriver: The ocean takes up some carbon dioxide released to the air. Local runoff and water conditions can add stress.
levers: Reduce carbon dioxide emissions and control damaging local pollution.
Monitor seawater chemistry and adapt shellfish production where practical. Assess experimental treatments carefully.

pacific decadal oscillation.name: Pacific Decadal Oscillation
pacific decadal oscillation.description: A broad pattern of warmer and cooler surface waters in the North Pacific that varies over years and decades. It is linked to changes in regional rainfall and marine conditions. It describes natural climate variability rather than a simple rise in temperature everywhere.

incoming: Unusually warm tropical Pacific conditions can leave a lasting effect on North Pacific temperatures and currents. These effects contribute to longer-lived patterns alongside the ocean's own changes.
Unusually cool tropical Pacific conditions can reinforce some cool patterns farther north. The longer-lived North Pacific pattern also has other causes.
outgoing: Longer-term North Pacific temperature patterns can change where unusually warm ocean episodes are more likely or intense. Individual events still depend on additional conditions.
This recurring North Pacific pattern changes the background distribution of ocean warmth and regional weather. It can influence unusual conditions without determining every event.
North Pacific temperature and habitat changes can make open-water species more available in some places and less in others. Responses differ by species and region.

Longer-lived North Pacific temperature patterns can affect how changes in air pressure travel through the atmosphere. This can alter the chance of particular weather patterns over the Pacific and North America.

Long-lasting North Pacific sea-temperature patterns can influence winds high in the atmosphere. This can affect the jet stream over the Pacific and North America, alongside its own natural variability.

human.summary: This recurring North Pacific pattern changes the background distribution of ocean warmth and regional weather. It can influence unusual conditions without determining every event. Repeated heavy rain and flooding can threaten people and buildings on flood-prone land. Exposure depends on what occupies the affected area.

consequences: North Pacific temperature and habitat changes can make open-water species more available in some places and less in others. Responses differ by species and region. Fish moving away from familiar grounds or seasons can become harder for local fleets to reach. Local catches may fluctuate even if the overall population has not collapsed.

Longer-term North Pacific temperature patterns can change where unusually warm ocean episodes are more likely or intense. Individual events still depend on additional conditions. Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for food and water-function losses during adverse tropical atlantic episodes and current coastal and catchment condition deficits associated with adverse episodes; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.

incoming: Losing sheltered habitat for young fish can mean fewer survive to adulthood. Where this stage limits population recovery, the chance of a serious decline in catches increases.
Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species.
Reduced oxygen can shrink suitable fish habitat, move stocks or cause deaths. These changes add to fishery risks, alongside fishing pressure and other local conditions.
Losing feeding links or suitable prey can reduce the survival of young fish and the ability of stocks to recover. Catch outcomes also depend on fishing and management.
Repeated oxygen shortages can kill fish, reduce living space and harm young animals. Where sensitive stocks are exposed, fisheries face a greater risk of decline.
Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.

Under the high-emissions pathway RCP8.5, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects global maximum fish catch potential to fall by 20.5–24.1% in 2081–2100 compared with 1986–2005. This is a scenario-based estimate of potential catch, not a prediction that every fishery will change by the same amount.
Large oil spills can harm fish and shellfish or force fishing closures. Longer-term population effects depend on exposure, life stage and recovery.
outgoing: Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.
Falling catches create greater food and income risks where communities already depend heavily on fish. The consequences depend on affordable alternatives and trade.

Fewer accessible fish can increase competition over catches and income where access is contested. Scarcity does not inevitably cause conflict. Good agreements and recovery plans can reduce the pressure.
Losing large numbers of harvested predators or other consumers can change the species they eat and those below them. A chain reaction needs evidence at several levels, not just one declining species.

human.summary: Large losses of fish stocks can remove food and income from coastal communities. Replacing those supplies and jobs may take time.
consequences: Fishing families can lose income when fish become scarce or move beyond reach.
Seafood may become more expensive where alternatives are limited.
Processing, transport and trade businesses can also lose activity.
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

planet.summary: Losing large numbers of harvested predators or other consumers can change the species they eat and those below them. A chain reaction needs evidence at several levels, not just one declining species.
planet.physicalLimit: Missing reports do not mean no production, waste, disease or exposure. Different products need an explained weighting before being combined.

response.defaultDriver: Losing sheltered habitat for young fish can mean fewer survive to adulthood. Where this stage limits population recovery, the chance of a serious decline in catches increases.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

incoming: Salt content changes how dense seawater is and how strongly it forms separate layers. These differences help influence the movement and mixing of ocean water.
North Atlantic temperature patterns and circulation vary together. This connection describes that association rather than a single, proven direction of cause.
The Atlantic overturning system is a major part of ocean circulation. A change in its strength changes how water and heat move within that system.
Changes in winds around Antarctica can alter Southern Ocean currents. Their effects differ by place, phase and the time period considered.
Warming changes the heat and freshwater entering the ocean. These changes can alter currents, with different responses in different ocean regions.
Changes in east-to-west tropical Pacific winds affect how surface water moves and how cold water rises from below. The direction of the wind change determines the response.

Changes in Atlantic currents move heat between regions. They can help shape sea-surface temperature patterns that vary over several decades.
Changing Arctic surface currents can carry sea ice in different directions or at different speeds. Ice may move into coastal areas or routes that ships planned to use.
Changing ocean currents can bring more warm water beneath floating ice shelves. Extra melting can reduce support and encourage inland retreat where the shape of the seabed makes the ice vulnerable.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Extra nitrogen carried to the coast can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they use oxygen and can leave too little for other marine life.
More strongly separated water layers slow the replacement of oxygen below the surface. Low-oxygen conditions are more likely where excess organic material is also using up oxygen as it decays.
Untreated water can add nutrients and decaying material near the coast. Breaking down that material uses oxygen and can contribute to shortages for marine animals.
Large growths of algae can use up oxygen as they live and decay. In some coastal waters, this leaves too little oxygen for other living things.
Warmer seawater holds less oxygen and can mix less with deeper water. This can worsen oxygen shortages near some coasts, although nutrient pollution and local currents may have a larger influence.
Warming can reduce oxygen in coastal water and limit mixing with deeper layers. In nutrient-rich areas, faster decay and weaker mixing can worsen oxygen shortages.
Nutrients lost from farms can reach coastal water and encourage growth that later uses up oxygen. The connection depends on transport downstream and the actual oxygen response.
outgoing: If low oxygen near the coast becomes severe and persistent, some areas may lose nearly all usable oxygen. Many animals cannot remain in those conditions.
Too little oxygen makes sheltered coastal water less suitable for young fish and shellfish. Fewer may survive to join the adult populations caught nearby.
Repeated oxygen shortages can kill fish, reduce living space and harm young animals. Where sensitive stocks are exposed, fisheries face a greater risk of decline.
Low oxygen can kill target species or push them away from fishing grounds. Local catches then become less reliable.
Some jellyfish tolerate low oxygen better than fish and other competitors. Oxygen-poor conditions may therefore shift the balance in their favour.

consequences: Too little oxygen makes sheltered coastal water less suitable for young fish and shellfish. Fewer may survive to join the adult populations caught nearby. incoming: When open-water species move, predators and prey may no longer meet in the same places. These changes can reorganize who eats whom in the sea.
More strongly separated saltwater layers can change how nutrients reach the surface. This affects the organisms that grow there and the animals that depend on them.
Changes in the tiny organisms that grow using sunlight alter the food available to other sea life. Different species and feeding relationships may then become dominant.
As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available.
Changes in seawater chemistry affect species differently. If some organisms grow or survive less well, animals that depend on them can also be affected, changing feeding relationships.
Changes in currents move heat and nutrients differently. This can change which organisms grow in an area and the animals that feed on them.
Long periods of unusually warm seawater affect marine species differently. Changes in survival, feeding and energy transfer can disrupt food chains, and larger predators may recover more slowly.

When warm surface water mixes less with deeper water, fewer nutrients may reach sunlit waters. At a Gulf of Lions study site, the less productive season also showed a narrower range of food resources used by bottom-living animals.

Changes in algae growing in sea ice affect when and how much food becomes available to small marine animals. Too little food, or food arriving at the wrong time, can affect animals farther up the food chain.
When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role.

Carbon dioxide changes ocean temperature and chemistry, with further effects on oxygen and currents. Some species lose suitable conditions or food, and repeated losses can leave a less varied food web.
Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.
Losing kelp removes food and complex shelter used by many marine animals. The food web may change, but temporary loss can recover before lasting changes occur.
Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles.
Plastic entering the sea can expose animals to particles and associated chemicals. Effects on feeding relationships depend on particle type, dose and other environmental stresses.
A large offshore oil release can harm young animals, contaminate food and damage habitats. Feeding relationships can change within the area reached by the spill.
outgoing: Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.
Losing feeding links or suitable prey can reduce the survival of young fish and the ability of stocks to recover. Catch outcomes also depend on fishing and management.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.

methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. incoming: Warming and added freshwater from melting land ice can make surface water lighter than the water below. Stronger separation can reduce mixing, depending on local circulation.
Fresh water from melting ice sheets forms a lighter layer near the ocean surface. This can strengthen the separation from saltier, denser water below.
Heavy rain and runoff can make local surface seawater fresher and lighter. This can briefly reduce mixing with deeper water when winds and currents are weak.
Warming changes rain, evaporation and ice melt. In some ocean regions, the resulting differences in salt content and temperature strengthen the separation between surface and deeper water.
outgoing: Salt content changes how dense seawater is and how strongly it forms separate layers. These differences help influence the movement and mixing of ocean water.
More strongly separated saltwater layers can change how nutrients reach the surface. This affects the organisms that grow there and the animals that depend on them.
Strongly separated water layers can slow mixing from the surface. Less oxygen then reaches deeper water to replace what living things use.
A layer of lighter, fresher water at the surface can limit mixing with deeper seawater. This makes it harder to move absorbed carbon away from the surface and into the ocean's interior.
Layers caused by differences in seawater salt content can change surface temperature in the tropical Atlantic. This can influence its warm and cool phases, alongside other ocean and wind processes.
A lighter, fresher surface layer in the North Atlantic can limit mixing and sinking. This weakens a process that helps drive the ocean's large circulation.
North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre Circulation Strength

Changes in salt content alter seawater density and can change northern Atlantic circulation. Fresher water does not automatically mean weaker flow because temperature, winds and the water carried by currents also matter.

human.summary: More strongly separated saltwater layers can change how nutrients reach the surface. This affects the organisms that grow there and the animals that depend on them. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Salt content changes how dense seawater is and how strongly it forms separate layers. These differences help influence the movement and mixing of ocean water. Changing currents move heat, nutrients and drifting organisms to different places. Open-water animals may shift their location or season as food and suitable conditions move.

Strongly separated water layers can slow mixing from the surface. Less oxygen then reaches deeper water to replace what living things use. As oxygen falls, sensitive animals may leave or die while more tolerant ones remain. This changes local feeding relationships and the habitat available.
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

incoming: Unusually warm seawater can favour some harmful algae when nutrients and other suitable conditions are present. Warmth alone does not guarantee a harmful outbreak.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current annual-equivalent coastal storm-surge health and essential-function loss and residual coastal habitat damage from realized surges; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Losing trees removes shade and some natural cooling. Neighbourhoods can store more daytime heat and remain warmer at night, leaving less relief for residents.

outgoing: Hot nights can prevent the body and the home from cooling down. Health risks can therefore be greater than an average daily temperature alone would suggest.

incoming: Human-caused warming raises the starting point for daytime and nighttime temperatures. This can make very hot days followed by unusually hot nights more likely, with regional differences.
A stalled high-pressure pattern can keep heat over an area for several days. Limited air movement and continuing warmth can also reduce nighttime relief.
Persistent wind patterns can keep hot conditions in place through both day and night. This is one possible contributor, not the cause of every heat event.
Warming raises both daytime highs and nighttime lows. Long runs of weather that limit cooling can then produce consecutive hot days and nights.
outgoing: When nights remain hot after very hot days, people have less time to cool down and recover. Observed studies find that this continuous exposure can create greater health burdens than heat limited to the day.

A study of Chinese communities linked sustained hot days and nights with a larger increase in deaths than hot nights alone. The size of the effect is specific to the studied places and methods, with uncertainty in the estimates.

human.summary: Hot days followed by hot nights leave little time for the body to cool and recover. People without safe indoor temperatures face continuous exposure.
consequences: Hospitals and emergency services may face increased demand during prolonged heat.
Homes can remain dangerously warm without suitable cooling, shade or insulation.
Longer cooling demand can coincide with greater pressure on electricity supplies.
human.hiddenCost: Heat continuing through day and night can increase illness and keep electricity demand high. Equipment has less chance to cool between peaks.
human.whoPays: Residents, health services and electricity users may face added costs, especially where cooling or dependable power is limited.

response.defaultDriver: Warming, persistent weather patterns and heat stored in cities can combine to remove the usual overnight relief.
levers: Plan warnings and accessible cooling for the full day and night.

incoming: Wind patterns high above the equator are linked with changes in a travelling pattern of tropical clouds and rain. Researchers are still studying how the two interact.

outgoing: A travelling pattern of tropical clouds and winds can influence active and dry spells within a rainy season. The effect depends on its location and the region involved.
