A band of tropical storm activity moving eastward changes winds and the supply of moisture. During some phases, it changes the chance and intensity of heavy rain in distant regions.
Some eastward-moving tropical storm systems produce bursts of west-to-east wind. These can push warm Pacific water eastward and help a warm phase develop.

consequences: This moving tropical weather pattern influences winds and rainfall over several weeks. It can contribute to unusual conditions but does not uniquely determine them. methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. incoming: Changes in tropical Pacific storms can send a chain of air-pressure changes toward North America. This can favour particular regional wind and weather patterns.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for health and essential-function loss from fires ignited during adverse lightning conditions and current fire-attributable habitat condition deficit; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

incoming: Drying weather removes moisture from vegetation and dead plant material. A lightning strike is then more likely to start a spreading fire. Drying does not itself create lightning.
Hotter conditions can dry vegetation and make a lightning-started fire easier to sustain. Whether lightning strikes and a fire spreads still depends on other weather and local conditions.
Warming can dry vegetation and create hotter fire-prone conditions. Lightning can start fires when thunderstorms bring too little rain to wet that dry material.
Lightning Flash Density and Seasonality Anomaly

Lightning reaching the ground can ignite vegetation when it is dry enough and rain does not put the fire out. Most flashes do not start a recorded fire, and later spread depends on weather and response.
outgoing: Lightning can start a fire when vegetation is dry enough to burn. Smoke exposure then depends on fire growth, wind, the people in its path and efforts to control the fire.

human.summary: Lightning can start fires where vegetation and weather allow them to spread. Communities may then face smoke, damaged property or disrupted travel. Many strikes do not start large fires.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

incoming: Warmer conditions can increase how quickly water is drawn from soil and plants. Land can begin drying faster even before rainfall becomes unusually low.
Long dry periods leave less water in soil and less available for plants to release. More surface energy then heats the air, increasing its demand for water.
Very dry soil provides little cooling through evaporation. More energy heats the land and air, reinforcing hot, dry conditions above the ground.
outgoing: Strong drying conditions increase plants' water demand. Plants may close tiny leaf openings to conserve water, which can reduce growth and make harvests less reliable.
Lightning Ignition under Fire Weather Conditions
Drying weather removes moisture from vegetation and dead plant material. A lightning strike is then more likely to start a spreading fire. Drying does not itself create lightning.
Dry air draws water from soil and plants more strongly. The ground around roots dries faster when rain cannot replace the loss.
Dry air removes moisture from living plants and dead vegetation. Fires can start and spread more easily when dry material, wind and a source of ignition come together.

human.summary: Strong drying conditions increase plants' water demand. Plants may close tiny leaf openings to conserve water, which can reduce growth and make harvests less reliable.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Dry air draws water from soil and plants more strongly. The ground around roots dries faster when rain cannot replace the loss. Very dry soil leaves roots unable to obtain enough water. Crop growth and harvests can suffer, with effects that vary between crops and seasons.

Dry air removes moisture from living plants and dead vegetation. Fires can start and spread more easily when dry material, wind and a source of ignition come together. Larger or longer fire seasons can expose people to more smoke and fine particles. Breathing this pollution can harm the lungs and heart and increase illness and death risks.

human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

incoming: Hot, sunny weather can speed reactions that form harmful ozone near the ground. Still air can let pollution build up, but suitable starting gases must also be present.

consequences: Persistent wind patterns can keep hot conditions in place through both day and night. This is one possible contributor, not the cause of every heat event. When nights remain hot after very hot days, people have less time to cool down and recover. Observed studies find that this continuous exposure can create greater health burdens than heat limited to the day.

Slow or strongly bent patterns in high-altitude winds can help weather systems remain in place. The outcome depends on the shape of the waves and surrounding winds. A long-lasting high-pressure pattern can divert storms and keep rain away from the same region. Dry conditions can then continue for longer.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Sulfur pollution can form particles that reflect sunlight and briefly cool the climate. Reducing that pollution improves air quality but also removes some of the cooling that had partly hidden warming from other gases.

Some powerful fire clouds carry smoke high into the atmosphere, where particles can remain longer. This adds to the particle layer rather than removing its cooling influence, although different smoke components can have different effects.

Sulfur particles formed after coal burning reflect some sunlight and temporarily mask part of greenhouse warming. They also cause serious air pollution. Reducing them removes some cooling while improving air quality.
outgoing: Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.
Changes in airborne particles can change cloud droplets, brightness and lifetime. This affects reflected sunlight where the particle-cloud connection is established.
Changes in particle-related heating and cooling can alter winds and seasonal rain. The effects on rainy seasons are uncertain and differ substantially by region.

incoming: Hot, humid weather can cause many people to use cooling equipment at once. The resulting jump in electricity demand can strain a power system that has little spare capacity.
Large computing facilities use substantial electricity in one place. Added demand can strain local or regional power systems, particularly at busy times.

Buildings designed to stay cooler need less powered cooling during hot hours. This can ease pressure on electricity supplies.

Expanding powered cooling can increase electricity use during the hottest hours. Efficient equipment, cooler buildings and careful demand management help limit that increase.

When electricity demand approaches available supply, moving some use to another time becomes more valuable. Only demand that can safely change should be shifted.
An electricity failure during high demand can interrupt water supplies, transport and communications. Emergency services may also lose equipment or access they depend on.
Carrying more electricity creates more heat inside a transformer. High demand combined with hot weather can shorten insulation life and increase the chance of failure.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current pollution and climate health or function loss from retained peak generation and current climate and local habitat condition deficit from peak-generation operation; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.

incoming: Making the binding ingredient in concrete releases carbon dioxide when limestone is chemically changed. This process release is separate from the fuel burned to heat the kiln.

Making concrete's binding material needs both high-temperature heat and a chemical change in limestone. Cleaner heat can reduce fuel emissions, but separate measures are needed for the carbon released by the limestone itself.

Using less cement and replacing part of its most emissions-intensive ingredient can reduce production emissions. Capturing carbon dioxide released during manufacture can address another part of the problem.

incoming: Conventional metal production can rely on large amounts of coal and energy. Replacing that equipment and its supply systems takes investment and suitable lower-emission alternatives.

Recycling, cleaner electricity, hydrogen and other production changes can reduce reliance on coal in steelmaking. The right combination depends on the plant and the steel required.
outgoing: Keeping coal- and gas-intensive metal-making methods in use continues to release carbon dioxide. Reductions depend on replacing or changing those processes effectively.
Steel plants that still depend on coal show where cleaner production is needed. Replacing or upgrading these plants requires a workable plan for equipment, energy and supply.

battery supply chain pressure.name: Battery Supply Chain Pressure
battery supply chain pressure.description: Growing demand for materials used to store power in phones, cars and other equipment. These materials must be mined, processed and moved to factories. Fast growth can strain supplies and add damage near mines and factories. Recycling and the way workers are treated also matter.

photo.caption: Evaporation ponds beside Gas Hure Lake, Qinghai, photographed from the ISS in September 2024. Its mineral-rich brines include lithium; the image illustrates extraction infrastructure rather than a supply shortage.
photo.credit: Astronaut photograph ISS071-E-715148 was acquired on September 22, 2024, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Johnson Space Center. The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 71 crew. The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed. The International Space Station Program supports the laboratory as part of the ISS National Lab to help astronauts take pictures of Earth that will be of the greatest value to scientists and the public, and to make those images freely available on the Internet. methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for present worker and water-function loss from adverse battery-material supply practices and current mine, processing and waste condition deficit attributable to battery materials; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Battery-specific share; not all mining nor the environmental benefits of displaced fossil fuel

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

components.label: Human impact
components.explanation: Worker and water-function loss from adverse battery-material supply practices.

components.label: Nature impact
components.explanation: Mine, processing and waste damage linked to battery materials.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Making more batteries requires reliable supplies of mined and processed materials. Constraints and environmental pressures at those stages carry through to battery production.
Building large battery stores increases demand for minerals, processing and manufacturing. The pressure depends on the type of storage, its lifespan and the use of recycled materials.
Making more electric vehicles increases demand for battery minerals, processing and factories. Battery size, reuse and recycling affect how much new material is needed.
outgoing: Growing battery production can concentrate extraction, water use and waste in mining regions. This can add to local pressure on land and water supplies.
Limited battery supplies can restrict one way of saving surplus wind or solar electricity. Other options, such as stronger grids or shifting demand, can also help use that power.
Expensive batteries or shortages of cells and minerals can delay electric-truck purchases. Diesel vehicles may remain in service for longer.

human.summary: Delays or higher costs in obtaining battery materials can slow access to storage and electric vehicles. Mining communities and workers can also face local pressures as supply expands.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

planet.summary: Growing battery production can concentrate extraction, water use and waste in mining regions. This can add to local pressure on land and water supplies.
consequences: Limited battery supplies can restrict one way of saving surplus wind or solar electricity. Other options, such as stronger grids or shifting demand, can also help use that power. If available clean power cannot reach users or be stored, fuel-burning generation may still be needed. The emissions effect depends on which power sources actually run instead.

Expensive batteries or shortages of cells and minerals can delay electric-truck purchases. Diesel vehicles may remain in service for longer. When electric freight options and their supporting systems are unavailable, diesel vehicles remain in use. Their continued fuel burning releases carbon dioxide.
planet.physicalLimit: Announced factories are not operating supply, and capacity is not actual production. Future projections are not current readings, and global market shares do not show impacts at an individual mine.

response.defaultDriver: Making more batteries requires reliable supplies of mined and processed materials. Constraints and environmental pressures at those stages carry through to battery production.
levers: Building large battery stores increases demand for minerals, processing and manufacturing. The pressure depends on the type of storage, its lifespan and the use of recycled materials.
Making more electric vehicles increases demand for battery minerals, processing and factories. Battery size, reuse and recycling affect how much new material is needed.

measurement.metric: Global battery demand growth and supply-chain concentration
measurement.unit: terawatt-hours, annual percent change, and global production share
measurement.geography: global battery and battery-material supply chain by production stage and chemistry
measurement.cadence: annual IEA assessment release
measurement.method: Keep battery demand, factory capacity, actual production, mineral needs and battery chemistry separate. Compare market shares only within the same supply-chain stage and year.
measurement.uncertainty: Battery-size estimates, vehicle sales, storage uses, private market data and stockpiling affect demand estimates. Ownership, trade, changing chemistry and revisions also matter.
measurement.boundary: Announced factories are not operating supply, and capacity is not actual production. Future projections are not current readings, and global market shares do not show impacts at an individual mine.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Chip factories use electricity, water, chemicals and process gases and create waste. Together these flows describe the resources used and pollution associated with the factories covered.
More computing equipment increases demand for advanced chips. Making those chips uses energy, water, chemicals and other materials.
outgoing: Chip production and cooling can use a significant share of local water supplies. Other users may face more competition where those supplies are limited.

Chip manufacturing can release heat-trapping gases through energy use and specialized process gases. These are not all carbon dioxide, so any combined climate total must retain the source's gas accounting.

human.summary: Chip production and cooling can use a significant share of local water supplies. Other users may face more competition where those supplies are limited. Facilities that need water for cooling may struggle when other users need the same limited supply. Essential services can be affected if reliable cooling water is unavailable.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
consequences: Chip manufacturing can release heat-trapping gases through energy use and specialized process gases. These are not all carbon dioxide, so any combined climate total must retain the source's gas accounting. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

planet.summary: Chip manufacturing can release heat-trapping gases through energy use and specialized process gases. These are not all carbon dioxide, so any combined climate total must retain the source's gas accounting.
planet.physicalLimit: A national average does not show how one factory performs. Total production, total environmental impact and impact per unit are different measures and must remain separate.

levers: Plan electricity supply, networks and demand together so cleaner options remain dependable.
Improve efficiency and maintain equipment, with backup arrangements suited to essential services and local hazards.

incoming: Chip factories need very clean water for production and cooling. In places with limited supplies, that use can compete with households, other businesses and nature.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current pollution health and function loss attributable to routine fossil backup operation and current local pollution and climate condition deficit from backup generation; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Only operation-related environmental costs; reliable backup supply can also have benefits

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: A strained power system may need expensive extra generation or face price spikes. These costs can add to household energy bills, depending on how prices are set.
Expensive electricity production during busy periods can add to customer costs. How much reaches household bills depends on pricing and market rules.
Electricity systems that rely on gas are exposed to changes in fuel prices. Those changes can affect customer bills, depending on market arrangements and protections.
Leaving available low-cost wind or solar power unused can add costs to the electricity system. The effect on household bills depends on how the market and tariffs work.
Removing salt from water uses electricity. Heavy reliance on this process can add energy costs, with household effects depending on prices and support.
outgoing: When households cannot afford energy bills, unpaid balances can put them at risk of losing service. Consumer protections and support affect whether disconnection occurs.
People who cannot afford to run cooling may face unsafe indoor temperatures. This can increase heat illness, especially where housing offers little natural protection.
High energy costs can stop households from buying or running enough cooling. Having an electricity connection or an air conditioner does not ensure that using it is affordable.

human.summary: When energy is too expensive, people may be unable to keep homes at safe temperatures or reach essential places. Bills can compete with other basic needs.
consequences: Households may use too little heating or cooling during dangerous weather.
Payment pressure can increase the risk of losing service or cutting spending on food, rent and medicine.
Businesses and public services can also face higher running costs.
human.hiddenCost: High energy costs can force households to cut other essentials or use less heating and cooling than they need.
human.whoPays: People with low incomes, inefficient homes or limited transport options may spend a larger share of their money on energy.

planet.summary: When households cannot afford energy bills, unpaid balances can put them at risk of losing service. Consumer protections and support affect whether disconnection occurs. Essential services may turn to temporary generators when normal power is unavailable. Many households lack that option, so a lost connection does not imply access to backup power.
planet.physicalLimit: Affordable service depends on supply costs, infrastructure, household income and support. There is no single physical threshold for an affordability crisis.

response.defaultDriver: Fuel-price changes, inefficient equipment and poorly targeted support can increase bills and exposure.
levers: Target bill support and efficient equipment toward households with the greatest need.
Plan dependable cleaner supplies and make changes in taxes or subsidies fair for low-income users.

measurement.method: Keep the policy or event, people included, money involved and eligibility rules clear. Explain the total used in each percentage. Exposure, access, affordability, available capacity and actual outcomes must remain separate.
measurement.uncertainty: Missing reports, changing eligibility, informal activity, financial valuations and survey error affect estimates. Assigning an outcome to a cause adds further uncertainty.
measurement.boundary: A physical hazard does not prove a social outcome occurred. Missing administrative records do not mean no cases.

incoming: When households cannot afford energy bills, unpaid balances can put them at risk of losing service. Consumer protections and support affect whether disconnection occurs.
Fair payments for changing electricity use can help participating households afford their bills. The benefit depends on programme design and whether households can participate safely.
Lower energy use can make household bills more affordable. This may reduce the risk of losing service, depending on prices and how upgrade costs are paid.
Upgrades that reduce household energy use can lower bills. More affordable bills can reduce the risk of electricity or heating being cut off.
outgoing: Losing electricity can stop cooling and essential equipment during hot weather. People may face greater illness and difficulty staying safe at home.

Power disconnection can remove cooling or interrupt essential home medical equipment during extreme heat. This can increase the risk of death, especially for people with limited alternatives or existing illness.
Essential services may turn to temporary generators when normal power is unavailable. Many households lack that option, so a lost connection does not imply access to backup power.
Losing electricity can stop fans and air conditioning during dangerous heat. Households unable to afford continued service may lose access to safe temperatures.
An electricity shutoff stops powered cooling when people may need it most. Households with health conditions can be especially vulnerable during dangerous heat.

human.summary: Losing utility service can turn financial stress into an immediate health and safety problem. Electricity may be needed for cooling, food storage, communication or medical equipment.
consequences: Households can lose essential protection during extreme heat or cold.

Emergency services may face more demand when routine payment problems lead to shutoffs.
human.hiddenCost: A household can have a connection but lose service when it cannot pay. Food spoilage, health risks and reconnection fees can add to the hardship.
human.whoPays: Low-income households, people using medical equipment and small businesses can be especially affected.

incoming: More ships using Arctic routes means more journeys exposed to changing ice conditions. Remote locations and limited rescue or repair services can make disruptions harder to manage.
A rapidly strengthening cyclone gives ships and ports less time to prepare. Closures, changed routes and delays may increase.
Coastal floods can close ports, damage access roads and stop cargo handling. Sea routes can be disrupted even when the open water remains navigable.
Moving sea ice can enter planned ship routes and narrow safe passages. Ships may need to wait, change course or seek icebreaker support even when total ice cover is low.
outgoing: Blocked or unsafe sea routes can force ships to change course. Delayed ships may arrive together at alternative ports, creating queues and slowing deliveries.
Disrupted sea routes can delay food deliveries or make them more expensive. Places that rely heavily on food brought in by ship are more exposed.
A blocked sea passage can interrupt many deliveries at once. This reveals how dependent a transport system is on a small number of routes.
Disrupted sea routes can delay food and farming supplies or make delivery more expensive. These changes can increase swings in market prices.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Keeping diesel trucks and their supporting systems in use delays their replacement. Electric freight needs suitable vehicles, charging and power supplies to overcome that dependence.
Continuing to use diesel trucks keeps releasing carbon dioxide from fuel burning. Long-lived vehicles and the services built around them can delay a switch to cleaner transport.
Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced.
Diesel freight releases gases that can form ground-level ozone in sunlight. Pollution may develop along transport routes or farther downwind.

Heavy road use wears tyres and can release tiny fragments containing synthetic materials. Not every dark roadside particle comes from tyres, and freight-specific claims need evidence about vehicle types.
Diesel freight releases fine particles and other harmful gases. People near busy freight routes can face greater exposure and related heart or lung risks.

human.summary: Diesel freight releases fine particles and other harmful gases. People near busy freight routes can face greater exposure and related heart or lung risks.
consequences: Continuing to use diesel trucks keeps releasing carbon dioxide from fuel burning. Long-lived vehicles and the services built around them can delay a switch to cleaner transport. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.

Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced. Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Severe damage to rivers, lakes or wetlands can remove species and reduce the abundance of those remaining. Their living communities become less like the earlier reference condition.
Removing water from wetlands changes or removes habitat for species adapted to wet conditions. Some populations may decline or disappear locally.
Species with less suitable, connected living space can become less abundant or disappear locally. This changes the area's original mix of life.
Small, separated populations can lose access to mates and resources. This can reduce abundance and increase local extinction risk for species that cannot cross the gaps.
Repairing damaged habitats can help native plants and animals recover. Recovery depends on removing the original pressures and maintaining a diverse, connected habitat.
Projects can help wildlife when they restore native habitats and connect them to other suitable areas. A project designed only for protection may not provide the same benefit.

Losing suitable cold habitat on isolated rocky peaks leaves specialised plants and animals with fewer places to survive. Small, separated populations may face a greater chance of disappearing locally.
Warming shifts the conditions that plants and animals can tolerate and the places where they can survive. These pressures add to habitat loss, harvesting and other human activities.

Replacing tropical forest with oil palms removes and separates habitats used by forest species. Keeping forest patches and improving plantation management can help, but does not recreate the original forest community.

Harmful introduced species can displace native wildlife and change habitats or food webs. Being non-native alone does not establish harm. The effects need evidence for the species and place concerned.
Removing older trees can reduce nesting holes, dead wood and layered habitats used by specialised wildlife. Effects differ between forests, and some managed areas retain or regain important features.

A lasting shift to more open vegetation removes conditions needed by many forest species. The new landscape may support other wildlife, so the loss concerns the original forest community rather than all biodiversity.
Persistent Pesticide Residues in Sediment and Biota

Chemicals stored in animal tissues can affect survival, reproduction or development if the dose is harmful. Finding a residue alone does not prove population damage, and effects differ between chemicals and food webs.
Less movement between habitats can isolate populations and limit access to food or cooler places. Connections are not always the main constraint, and they can also spread disease or invasive species.
Migratory Bird Timing, Route, and Stopover Disruption

Repeated difficulty finding food or suitable habitat during migration can reduce survival and breeding success. A changed route or date can also be a useful adjustment, so population effects need evidence across the birds' full yearly cycle.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction

Lasting changes in mountain forests alter shelter, food and connections used by wildlife. Some species lose habitat while others benefit from openings or forest expansion, so population changes need separate evidence.
Amphibian Chytrid Infection Prevalence and Mortality

Severe fungal infection can damage amphibian skin function and cause death. Many infections do not cause visible disease, and some populations recover despite continued exposure. Deaths need a confirmed cause.
Particles from seabed mining can settle over habitats or interfere with feeding. Effects depend on the organisms and the area reached by the plume.
Less inherited variety and more breeding between close relatives can reduce a population's ability to adjust to change. Some affected populations may become less likely to persist.
Lasting loss of savanna trees removes shade, food, nesting sites and shelter. Species that depend on that woody layer may decline.
Enough metal building up in tissues can harm survival, reproduction or behaviour. Effects depend on the metal, dose and species exposed.
Simpler habitats, pesticide exposure, nutrient losses and land clearing can harm plants and animals around farms. The effect depends on local practices and documented exposure.
Clearing and splitting forests removes habitats used by native species. Some plants and animals may become less common or disappear from the affected landscape.
Repeated acidic pollution can remove sensitive species from waters and nearby land. Effects are greater where soils and water have little ability to neutralise the acid.
Oil contamination can harm many species and damage habitats from deep water to shore. The extent of biodiversity loss depends on the spill's reach and the organisms exposed.
Salty or toxic wastewater reaching surface water can injure organisms and damage habitat. Effects depend on its contents, concentration, movement and the ability of the ecosystem to recover.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current smoke, displacement and essential-function loss from adverse changes in fire regime and residual habitat condition deficit from ecologically damaging changes in fire; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.

incoming: Warming can create hotter, drier conditions and longer periods suitable for burning. Actual fires still depend on fuel, ignition and local management.
Changing air-pressure patterns over the Pacific and North America can shift heat, rain and drought. Fire danger may then change in particular regions, sometimes days or weeks later.
Dry air removes moisture from living plants and dead vegetation. Fires can start and spread more easily when dry material, wind and a source of ignition come together.
Long dry periods can dry vegetation across seasons. This increases the amount that can burn and can extend the time of year with high fire danger.
Warming can increase heat and drying, changing when and how intensely fires burn. Fires still need burnable material and a source of ignition.
Damaged or cleared forests can interact with drying and human ignitions to change fire patterns. The result also depends on available vegetation and land management.
Heat and drought can dry vegetation before a fire starts, creating a sequence of connected hazards. Fire still needs burnable material and an ignition source.
outgoing: Very intense fires can create towering storm clouds. These can carry smoke much higher than ordinary fire plumes, allowing it to travel farther or remain aloft longer.
Repeated severe fires can leave surviving forest in separate patches. Connectivity depends on the pattern of burning and later regrowth.
Larger or longer-lasting fires can produce more persistent smoke. Health exposure increases where winds carry that smoke to people.
Larger or longer fire seasons can expose people to more smoke and fine particles. Breathing this pollution can harm the lungs and heart and increase illness and death risks.
More destructive fires can increase losses beyond what insurers planned for. Prices may rise, renewals may be restricted and some insurers may leave exposed areas.
Repeated severe fires can kill trees faster than forests regrow. A river catchment may then be left with less tree cover or a different type of vegetation.
Intense fire close to a railway can deform rails and damage track components. Smoke or a nearby line closure alone does not show that rails have bent.
Large or severe fires can release soot that travels downwind. Some may settle on snow and ice, depending on transport and weather conditions.
Wildfires produce carbon monoxide as material burns incompletely. The amount varies with the fuel and burning conditions.
Severe or repeated fires can burn peat, kill plants and change how water moves through the land. Recovery can become more difficult after repeated damage.
Longer or more severe fire seasons increase the chance that fire reaches dry peat. Repeated burning can occur before the wetland has recovered.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction
Severe fires can remove mountain trees and seed sources. Lasting forest loss occurs when trees cannot regrow. Many forests normally recover from fire, and some lower-intensity fires support renewal.
Frequent or severe fire can kill young woody plants before they grow large enough to withstand burning. This can reduce tree cover over time.
Severe fires can kill tall canopy trees by burning crowns or damaging bark and roots. Some injured trees die later, including after insect attack.
Trees injured but not killed by fire may become suitable hosts for some beetles. Fire can also kill the insects or their hosts, so a burned area does not automatically predict an outbreak.
Tundra fires change vegetation, soil warmth and frozen-ground conditions. This can alter whether shrubs establish successfully after the disturbance.
More severe or frequent fires can expose nearby or downwind populations to more smoke. Hospital use may rise where that exposure worsens illness.
More smoke-producing fires create more opportunities for people to breathe fine particles. Winds, where people live and how they reduce exposure determine the actual amount inhaled.
Longer fire seasons or repeated fires can keep smoke over communities for longer. Exposure lasts only where the plumes reach people at the stated levels.
Severe northern fires can remove moss, plants and organic soil that insulate frozen ground. Where the ground contains much ice, later thaw can make it sink and form new hollows or ponds.
Severe northern fires remove insulating vegetation and soil and can darken the surface. Frozen ground beneath the burned area may then thaw faster than comparable unburned ground.
Incomplete burning in wildfires releases soot and other dark fine particles. Larger or more frequent smoke events increase opportunities for elevated soot downwind, depending on transport.

incoming: Clearing sections of a forest can split continuous habitat into smaller pieces. More exposed edges and larger gaps can make those pieces harder for wildlife to use.
Repeated severe fires can leave surviving forest in separate patches. Connectivity depends on the pattern of burning and later regrowth.
Logging and access roads can create gaps and edges in older forests. The amount of separation depends on how harvesting is done and must be assessed across the wider landscape.
outgoing: Breaking up a forest leaves smaller or more isolated places for wildlife. Their value depends on size, quality and whether animals can move between them.
Gaps between forest patches can stop species reaching suitable cooler habitat. Their occupied area may shrink when movement cannot keep pace with changing conditions.
Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats.

Splitting forests into separate patches can make it harder for some species to move, breed or recolonise an area. Other species can cross the gaps, so a map alone does not prove that movement has stopped.
Splitting habitat into smaller pieces can leave fewer animals or plants breeding in each area. With less movement between groups, inherited variety may decline over generations.

human.summary: Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats. If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.

human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current coastal protection, food and livelihood function loss after mangrove damage and current mangrove condition deficit and unrecovered lost habitat; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Current remnant damage stock; no future storm exposure or automatic irreversible-loss premium

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

incoming: Rising seas can overwhelm mangroves if soil does not build up fast enough. They are especially exposed where buildings or steep ground prevent them from moving inland.
Erosion can remove the soil and stable shoreline that support mangrove roots. Losing these trees also weakens the natural barrier they form against storms.
outgoing: Losing coastal trees and roots removes some resistance to waves and moving water. Nearby people and buildings can become more exposed during storms.
Without mangrove roots to hold sediment and slow water, a shoreline can lose material more easily. Local wave conditions and sediment supply affect the rate.
Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage.

human.summary: Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage. Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

response.defaultDriver: Rising seas can overwhelm mangroves if soil does not build up fast enough. They are especially exposed where buildings or steep ground prevent them from moving inland.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

incoming: Severe or repeated warm-water episodes can kill corals after stress and bleaching. If recovery is too slow, the reef's hard framework can lose complexity and break down.
Changing seawater chemistry can slow the building and repair of coral skeletons. If losses outpace replacement, the reef framework can weaken.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef.
Repeated breakage can remove the connected, three-dimensional structure of a reef. If growth and repair cannot keep up, habitat complexity and resistance to waves decline.
outgoing: Losing reef structure removes shelter, feeding areas and places for young fish to grow. Fisheries depending on those habitats can become less able to sustain catches.
Repeated damage can weaken the solid structure built by corals. As that structure breaks down, reef habitat can become smaller, separated and less stable.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Heat and other stresses can reduce the survival of young corals and their ability to settle on a reef. This makes recovery harder where the reef is already damaged.

incoming: Losing trees around rivers can increase erosion and change water flow and habitat. Severe or repeated damage can reduce the ability of freshwater communities to survive and recover.
Releasing water without normal treatment can add germs, nutrients and harmful chemicals to rivers or lakes. Severe or repeated contamination can damage their living communities and functions.
Barriers can isolate aquatic populations and prevent access to breeding sites or refuge. Repeated or widespread isolation can weaken the river's living community.
Draining wetland areas changes water storage, natural filtering and habitat. Severe changes can undermine nearby freshwater communities and their functions.
Barriers at stream crossings can stop animals reaching shelter or breeding areas. Repeated isolation can reduce populations and make recovery after damage harder.
Removing side channels and floodplain connections reduces the variety of river habitats. Fish and other wildlife may lose places to feed, breed or shelter.
Warming changes water temperatures, river flow and flood or drought extremes. These changes can put freshwater plants and animals under pressure.

Some farm chemicals can harm aquatic plants and animals when exposure is high enough or repeated. Detection alone does not prove harm, and crossing a screening threshold does not establish that a whole ecosystem has failed.
Continued river-bank loss can add fine sediment, bury habitat and remove shade. River plants and animals may lose suitable places to live.
Large, lasting mussel losses remove animals that filter water and help stabilise riverbeds. Nutrient movement and habitats supported by dense mussel groups may also change.
Forest loss can change river flows, water quality and stream habitats. Freshwater wildlife may be harmed where these catchment changes reach the water.
Acid entering poorly protected waters can harm sensitive species and release harmful aluminium from surrounding materials. Food webs can change where the water and soil cannot neutralise the acid.
Spills or poorly contained wastewater can carry salts, metals and other contaminants into streams or groundwater. Aquatic life can be harmed within the area reached by the release.
Farm pumping can intercept groundwater that would otherwise feed springs, streams or wetlands. Connected habitats may lose water during dry periods.
Industrial pumping can reduce groundwater flowing into connected streams and wetlands. Less flow can shrink habitats and worsen water conditions.
Heavy pumping for towns and cities can lower the water supporting connected springs and wetlands. Habitats that depend on that flow may be put at risk.
Coastal pumping can reduce fresh groundwater reaching connected streams and wetlands. These habitats may lose an important water source.
Water lost from storage can reduce the flow available for rivers and aquatic habitats. Effects depend on whether enough water is still released for the environment.
Heavy withdrawals can reduce river flows and separate aquatic habitats. Effects are greater when the amount taken is large compared with the natural flow.
Changes in exchange between groundwater and surface water can alter stream flow and temperature. Connected wetlands and aquatic habitats may lose support or experience different conditions.
outgoing: Severe damage to rivers, lakes or wetlands can remove species and reduce the abundance of those remaining. Their living communities become less like the earlier reference condition.

human.summary: Damaged rivers and lakes can become less useful for fishing, recreation and dependable water supplies. The current measurements describe particular ecological conditions, not a global count of people affected.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current pollination and food-web service function loss from adverse insect decline and present composition and food-web condition deficit in affected landscapes; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Regional biomass studies are context, not a measured global percentage applied to all land

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

scoreBreakdown.summary: Human and nature impacts count equally. Each is scored out of 10.

components.label: Human impact
components.explanation: Pollination and food-web service function loss from adverse insect decline.

components.label: Nature impact

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Extreme heat and changes to habitats can put insects under pressure. Some populations may shrink, although the effects differ between species and places.
Removing varied habitats and exposing insects to farm chemicals can reduce their numbers. The effect depends on farming practices and the species involved.
Clearing forests removes food, shelter and stable local conditions for insects. Populations can decline where the remaining habitat cannot support them.
Breaking a forest into smaller patches can leave insect populations isolated. Smaller populations may struggle when they cannot move between suitable habitats.
outgoing: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.

human.summary: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work. Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

planet.summary: If declining insect numbers include pollinating species, fewer animals may be available to transfer pollen. Effects depend on which insects are lost and whether others can replace their work.
planet.physicalLimit: An unsurveyed habitat is unknown, not empty or healthy. Finding a species, counting its numbers, assessing habitat condition and establishing extinction require different evidence.

response.defaultDriver: Extreme heat and changes to habitats can put insects under pressure. Some populations may shrink, although the effects differ between species and places.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.
