methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.
Strong drying conditions increase plants' water demand. Plants may close tiny leaf openings to conserve water, which can reduce growth and make harvests less reliable.
Ozone entering leaves can damage plant tissues and reduce growth. Harvest effects depend on the crop, exposure and region. An estimate for one crop cannot be assumed to apply to all others.
Hail can physically damage crops. Changes in where and when hail occurs alter harvest risk, with different outcomes for crops at different growth stages.
Very dry soil leaves roots unable to obtain enough water. Crop growth and harvests can suffer, with effects that vary between crops and seasons.
Crops that need animals to transfer pollen may set less fruit or seed when that help declines. Harvests can become smaller or less reliable.
With less organic material, soil can hold less water and nutrients. Crops may then be more sensitive to dry periods and other growing conditions.
Excessive heat can damage flowering, seed formation and the way plants use sunlight to grow. Harvests can become smaller or less dependable.
When plant nutrients become much more expensive, farmers may use less or apply them at the wrong time. This can make harvests smaller or less dependable.
Livestock farms that depend on crops for animal feed are exposed when those harvests change sharply. A poor crop harvest can mean less feed or higher feed prices.
Dangerous working conditions can reduce the time available for planting, tending or harvesting crops. Missing these time-sensitive jobs can make harvests less dependable.
Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.
A mix of crops, healthier soils, better water management and useful forecasts can make harvests more dependable. These measures reduce some risks but cannot prevent every loss.

Heat can change crop development, water needs and success in producing seeds or fruit. Harvests may become more variable, but outcomes differ where warmer weather eases cold limits or irrigation protects crops.
Heat, drought and heavy rain can affect flowering, seed growth and harvest timing. Different exposure between seasons and regions can make crop harvests less dependable.
Heat, drought and heavy rain can damage crops at different stages of growth. Their combined effect on harvests depends on the crop, timing and farm management.
Ground-level ozone can damage the way sensitive crops use sunlight and grow. Enough exposure can reduce harvests or make them less dependable.
Restricted roots and poor air or water movement make crops less able to cope with very wet or dry conditions. Harvests can become less dependable.
outgoing: Unreliable harvests increase the need for farming methods that handle heat, water shortages and other shocks. The most useful changes depend on local crops and conditions.
Unreliable harvests can reduce local food supplies and increase prices. Households may then find it harder to obtain enough nutritious food.
Poor harvests of major food crops can tighten supplies and make prices less stable. Stored reserves and substitute foods can soften the effect.

human.summary: Unreliable harvests can affect farm income, debt and the cost of basic foods. Widespread losses can also increase the need for imports or aid.
consequences: Farmers may struggle to repay costs when harvests vary sharply between seasons.
Higher food prices put particular pressure on households already spending much of their income on staples.
Governments and aid agencies may need to buy emergency supplies after major failures.
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

levers: A mix of crops, healthier soils, better water management and useful forecasts can make harvests more dependable. These measures reduce some risks but cannot prevent every loss.

incoming: Where people rely heavily on local fish, falling supplies may require more food from elsewhere. That can expose households to overseas prices and transport interruptions.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Frequent ploughing, removing crop remains and leaving fields bare can expose soil. Wind and heavy rain can then carry away the fertile upper layer more easily.
Plant cover and roots help hold soil in place. Restoring them can reduce the amount of fertile ground carried away by wind and water.
Keeping soil covered, maintaining roots and disturbing it less can reduce erosion. Better water management can also slow the washing away of fertile ground.
Removing trees leaves soil with less protection from rain and fewer roots holding it. Erosion can increase on vulnerable slopes during heavy rain.
Ground tightly packed by cattle absorbs water less easily and may support fewer plants. Rain can then create more runoff and erosion where slopes and soil are vulnerable.
Tightly packed soil lets less water soak in and restricts roots. More runoff can carry away topsoil where rainfall and slopes create enough force.
outgoing: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains.
Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.

human.summary: Losing the upper layer of soil removes nutrients and reduces the ground's ability to hold water. Crops may then produce smaller or less dependable harvests.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains. With less organic material, soil can hold less water and nutrients. Crops may then be more sensitive to dry periods and other growing conditions.
human.hiddenCost: Losing the upper soil layer removes nutrients and water-holding capacity. Farmers may need more inputs while waterways receive extra sediment.
human.whoPays: Farmers, downstream water users and public land managers can bear the costs.

planet.summary: Erosion carries away the carbon-rich upper soil. If that loss is faster than new organic material builds up, less well-decayed plant matter remains.
planet.physicalLimit: Soil can be removed much faster than it forms. The rate depends on slope, cover, soil and rainfall.

response.defaultDriver: Bare ground and unsuitable farming practices can leave soil exposed to wind and runoff.
levers: Use locally suitable cover, crop rotations and reduced soil disturbance.
Reward measured soil protection and control runoff on erosion-prone land.

measurement.method: Keep the habitat, species or group, survey method and survey effort clear. State the reference condition and area used for percentages. Habitat area, habitat health, numbers of organisms and benefits they provide are separate measures.
measurement.uncertainty: Some species are harder to detect and some places are surveyed more often. Map detail, season, reference condition and how causes are identified affect estimates.
measurement.boundary: An unsurveyed habitat is unknown, not empty or healthy. Finding a species, counting its numbers, assessing habitat condition and establishing extinction require different evidence.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current secure-housing and recovery-function loss linked to environment-related mortgage distress and no independent ecological endpoint within mortgage exposure; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

incoming: Losing electricity can stop cooling and essential equipment during hot weather. People may face greater illness and difficulty staying safe at home.
Working cooling systems can help prevent hot conditions from becoming a health emergency. Their protection depends on access, affordability and reliable power.
Humid heat limits cooling through sweat. This can increase heat illness and strain the heart, lungs and kidneys, especially during prolonged exposure.

When nights remain hot after very hot days, people have less time to cool down and recover. Observed studies find that this continuous exposure can create greater health burdens than heat limited to the day.
Hot nights can prevent the body and the home from cooling down. Health risks can therefore be greater than an average daily temperature alone would suggest.
If a strained electricity system fails during extreme heat, cooling and medical equipment can stop. The interruption can increase illness and demand for care.
People who cannot afford to run cooling may face unsafe indoor temperatures. This can increase heat illness, especially where housing offers little natural protection.

Replacing coal power with lower-emissions electricity reduces a source of future warming. This can ease future heat-related health risks, alongside the more immediate benefit of less combustion pollution.
Well-designed building upgrades can slow indoor overheating. This can keep temperatures safer for longer, including when cooling is limited.
Heat pumps that provide cooling as well as heating can help keep indoor temperatures safe. Protection depends on access, affordability and reliable electricity.
Shade, suitable ventilation and reflective surfaces can reduce the heat entering or staying inside buildings. This can lower people's exposure to dangerous indoor temperatures.
Coordinating cooling spaces, health services and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. The plan needs staff, funding and follow-through.
Efficient cooling, affordable energy and contact with vulnerable residents can reduce illness during hot weather. These measures work best together.
Hot, humid air makes sweat evaporate less effectively, so the body has more difficulty losing heat. Illness risk varies with age, activity, housing, previous exposure to heat and access to cooling.
Hotter air makes it harder for the body to release heat and can strain the heart and other organs. Health effects depend on humidity, age, housing, existing illness and access to cooling.
Extra daytime and nighttime heat in cities increases people's exposure to high temperatures. This can add to illness risks, especially where cooling is limited.

Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.
More frequent or severe heat increases exposure to conditions that can cause illness. Health services and people without reliable cooling can face greater pressure.
People unable to keep indoor temperatures safe face greater heat illness risks. Older people, those with existing illness and households with limited resources may be especially exposed.
outgoing: Heat-related illness and demand for care can slow recovery after a disaster. Households and health services with fewer resources may struggle for longer.
Growing illness during hot weather shows where cities need stronger preparation. Plans can connect forecasts with cooling, health services and support for people at greatest risk.
Repeated severe heat illness can increase pressure to consider moving people or services. That becomes more likely where safe housing, cooling and health care cannot be maintained locally.

human.summary: Heat-related illness and demand for care can slow recovery after a disaster. Households and health services with fewer resources may struggle for longer.
human.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

incoming: Temperature changes can affect where disease-carrying insects survive and how quickly germs develop inside them. Some places may become more suitable for transmission, while excessive heat can make others less suitable.
Flooding can leave standing water, damage drains and change how people store water. In some places, this creates more breeding sites for mosquitoes and increases contact with people.

Clearing forests changes shade, standing water, wildlife and contact between people and insects. In some tropical settings, these changes favour mosquitoes that carry disease, but the effect is not universal.
Rapid city growth without adequate drains, waste services or water supplies can create breeding places for some disease-carrying insects. Dense populations and travel can increase contact and spread.
Changes in temperature and rain can make some places suitable for disease-carrying insects for longer. Effects vary by disease and can reverse where conditions become too hot or dry.
outgoing: Illness carried by insects can slow recovery after a disaster. People with less access to prevention and treatment may face a larger burden.

human.summary: Changing temperatures and rain can make some places or seasons more suitable for disease-carrying insects. People may face infections where preparation is limited.
consequences: Mosquito- or tick-borne diseases can create new demands on local prevention systems.
Health services may need longer periods of monitoring and treatment.
Illness can interrupt work, schooling and household income.
human.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

incoming: Court cases can expose disagreements about who should pay for protection and recovery. They may draw attention to funding gaps without necessarily closing them.
Households and governments struggling to replace disaster losses may have little money left for future protection. Unequal recovery can therefore deepen gaps in preparation for the next hazard.
When insurance is unavailable or unaffordable, households and governments pay more disaster costs themselves. This can leave less money to reduce future risks.
outgoing: Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse.
Too little funding can limit the planning, housing, compensation and services needed for a fair move. Good decision-making still matters even when money is available.
Funding shortages can leave gaps in hazard monitoring, useful alerts and preparation. People may receive less warning or have fewer ways to act on it.
Too little investment can delay cooler housing, shaded spaces and public cooling facilities. Communities already receiving fewer services may remain less protected.

human.summary: Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse.
human.hiddenCost: Delaying protection can leave people exposed to preventable damage and make later recovery more expensive.
human.whoPays: Communities with little funding or borrowing power may struggle to obtain protection, even where need is high.

planet.summary: Too little investment can leave refrigerated food and medicine storage poorly protected from heat and power cuts. Transport problems can make the losses worse. incoming: Damage to roads, power lines or utilities in remote polar areas can interrupt essential services. Difficult access and limited alternatives can make recovery harder.
A shortage of voltage-changing equipment can delay repairs and power-network upgrades. Essential services may remain exposed to outages for longer.
Heat can interrupt a port's work when equipment or workers cannot operate safely. The disruption is harder to contain where backup equipment and alternative routes are limited.
When an airport stops operating, a region may lose an important route for people, supplies and emergency help. The effects are greater where few alternative routes are available.
Fast-moving water can wash material away from around bridge foundations. A weakened or closed bridge can cut an important transport link.
A blocked sea passage can interrupt many deliveries at once. This reveals how dependent a transport system is on a small number of routes.
Designing essential services for future floods can make failures less likely. Backup routes, spare capacity and maintenance help services continue when one part is damaged.
An electricity failure during high demand can interrupt water supplies, transport and communications. Emergency services may also lose equipment or access they depend on.
Facilities that need water for cooling may struggle when other users need the same limited supply. Essential services can be affected if reliable cooling water is unavailable.
Frequent reliance on backup generators can reveal weaknesses in normal electricity supply. Services may remain vulnerable if backup fuel, equipment or delivery also fails.
Storms, tides and rising sea levels can bring seawater onto low-lying buildings and services. Whether they fail depends on flood depth, protection, equipment design and available backups.
Warming and related changes in moisture and salt exposure can speed damage to concrete and steel. Some structures may need earlier repair or have a shorter useful life.
Avalanches can bury or damage roads, railways, power lines and communications equipment. Repeated closures are especially disruptive where few alternative mountain routes exist.
Heat, floods, fires and coastal hazards can damage power, water, transport and communications equipment. Repeated damage can shorten its useful life and interrupt connected services.
Damage to an undersea cable can interrupt services that depend on it. The disruption is greater where there are few alternative routes, landing points or spare connections.
A failed transformer can interrupt electricity to essential services. Replacements can take a long time, leaving connected facilities more vulnerable until supply is restored.
Submarine Cable Landing-Site Concentration and Exposure

Losing shared cable landing or power facilities can remove several communication paths at once. Essential services are less affected where traffic can switch to independent routes with enough spare capacity.
Heat, floods, fires and storms can strain power, transport and other services. Damage is more likely where design and maintenance do not match the hazards faced.
A large network exchange can become a shared failure point if power, cooling or route options are limited. Several dependent services may be interrupted together.
Failure of major data routes or switching equipment can interrupt communications used by power, water, transport and emergency services. Alternative paths determine how much service continues.
Losing mobile masts, connecting cables or backup power can interrupt public warnings and emergency communication. Distributed equipment still needs reliable supporting services.
Insufficient drinking-water treatment can affect homes, hospitals and emergency services together. It becomes a shared weak point for services that need safe water.

Hot rails can expand and bend sideways when the track cannot contain the force. Inspections, speed limits or closures can interrupt passenger and freight services, while severe failures can cause derailments.
outgoing: Failures in transport, water or health services can prevent people from getting protection during extreme heat. Several failures together can increase the risk of death.
Failures of essential services can lead to legal disputes about foreseeable climate risks. These disputes may concern whether operators disclosed risks or took reasonable steps to protect people.
Weak power and communication systems can interrupt warnings. Alerts may fail to reach the people who need them, especially in the final step to homes and communities.

Broken roads, ports, storage or power supplies can delay food and increase transport or spoilage costs. Food reserves and alternative routes can prevent those disruptions from turning into price rises.
Damaged roads, power, water or communications can prevent aid from reaching people. Funding, security and coordination can also block help even when physical systems still work.

Unreliable power and poorly protected buildings can leave people without safe indoor temperatures. Those unable to afford better housing or backup options face greater exposure, although cost barriers can exist even with reliable power.
Failure of a fuel tank, pipe, hose or protective barrier can allow fuel to reach nearby water. The risk depends on the damaged equipment and its connection to the waterway.

methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. incoming: Imported food becoming scarce or expensive affects households unevenly. People with fewer savings and supply alternatives can find it harder to recover after a disaster.
Heat-related illness and demand for care can slow recovery after a disaster. Households and health services with fewer resources may struggle for longer.
Illness carried by insects can slow recovery after a disaster. People with less access to prevention and treatment may face a larger burden.
People who receive no useful warning have less chance to prepare or reach safety. The resulting losses can make recovery harder for groups already facing disadvantages.
Warnings can reduce unequal disaster losses when they reach vulnerable groups and come with real options for protection. Access to transport, shelter and support matters.
A planned move can reduce unequal disaster losses when people receive suitable housing, services, compensation and ways to earn a living. These protections need to be delivered, not just promised.
People forced to move have unequal access to savings, housing, documents and aid. These differences can widen the gap between households able to recover and those left behind.
outgoing: Communities unable to rebuild may face pressure to move. Unequal access to recovery funds then becomes a challenge for decisions about land, housing and public support.
Households and governments struggling to replace disaster losses may have little money left for future protection. Unequal recovery can therefore deepen gaps in preparation for the next hazard.

human.summary: Households and governments struggling to replace disaster losses may have little money left for future protection. Unequal recovery can therefore deepen gaps in preparation for the next hazard.
human.hiddenCost: Financial losses can spread through bills, borrowing, insurance and public spending. The size of the burden depends on contracts, available support and how the risk is shared.
human.whoPays: Households, businesses and public budgets may carry different parts of the cost. Limited savings or access to credit can make the same disruption harder to absorb.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Pesticides and a lack of varied flowers or habitat can contribute to losses of pollinating insects or colonies. Parasites, disease, nutrition and weather also matter, so the affected species and exposure need to be identified.
Heat and changing seasonal timing can stress some pollinating insects. Population or colony losses usually involve several pressures, including food, habitat, chemicals and disease.

Losing forests and other natural habitat removes flowers, nesting sites and shelter used by pollinating insects. This can add to pressures from chemicals, disease and climate rather than acting as the only cause of colony loss.

Farm chemicals drifting beyond their target can reach bees directly or through contaminated food brought back to a colony. Colony harm depends on the chemical, dose and exposure, alongside other stresses.

incoming: Sunlight allows certain polluting gases to react and form ozone near the ground. It is formed in the air rather than released directly, and the outcome depends on the mix of gases and local conditions.
Some carbon-containing gases react with other pollutants in sunlight to form ozone near the ground. How much forms depends on the mix of gases and the local air conditions.
Hot, sunny weather with little air movement can help ground-level ozone build up. The gases that form it, clouds and air mixing also matter, so temperature alone does not determine pollution.
outgoing: Ozone entering leaves can damage plant tissues and reduce growth. Harvest effects depend on the crop, exposure and region. An estimate for one crop cannot be assumed to apply to all others.

Breathing ground-level ozone irritates and damages airways, especially in exposed or vulnerable people. Studies reviewed for World Health Organization guidelines also link short-term outdoor increases with a small rise in daily deaths from all causes.

incoming: Longer-term North Pacific temperature patterns can change where unusually warm ocean episodes are more likely or intense. Individual events still depend on additional conditions.
Multi-decade Atlantic temperature changes can make regional seas warmer or cooler as a starting point. Unusually warm episodes still depend on several immediate causes.

Under the very high-emissions scenario SSP5-8.5, marine heatwaves are projected to occur eight times as often globally in 2081–2100 as in 1995–2014. The assessed likely range is three to fifteen times. This is a scenario estimate, not a guaranteed outcome.
outgoing: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species.
Unusually warm seawater can favour some harmful algae when nutrients and other suitable conditions are present. Warmth alone does not guarantee a harmful outbreak.
Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter.
Severe or repeated warm-water episodes can kill corals after stress and bleaching. If recovery is too slow, the reef's hard framework can lose complexity and break down.
Unusually warm surface and upper-ocean water can supply energy to a tropical cyclone and limit cooling beneath it. Rapid strengthening still depends on winds, humidity, storm structure and its path.
Long periods of unusually warm seawater affect marine species differently. Changes in survival, feeding and energy transfer can disrupt food chains, and larger predators may recover more slowly.
Unusually hot seawater can damage seagrass and kill plants. Severe or repeated events can reduce the area and condition of these underwater meadows.
Unusually hot seawater can make it harder for young shellfish to grow and form shells. This may add to stress from changing water chemistry, with different limits for each species.
Prolonged unusually warm seawater can disrupt the partnership between corals and the tiny algae living inside them. Corals may turn pale, with responses differing between species and reefs.
Coral Larval Survival and Recruitment Failure
Seawater above the temperatures young corals can tolerate can reduce survival and successful settlement. Effects vary by species and stage of growth.

Long periods of unusually warm sea water can harm kelp and reduce supplies of cool, nutrient-rich water. Brief events do not always cause lasting loss, and some forests recover when other pressures are limited.
Unusually hot seawater can move suitable habitat farther away, deeper or toward the poles. Some fish move, while others stay, adjust or return after the event.
Marine heatwaves can occur with wind and current changes that bring fewer nutrients to the surface. This can reduce the amount of drifting plant life or change which sizes are most common.

human.summary: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can kill sensitive animals, damage habitat or move fish away. These changes can undermine fisheries, with effects that vary between places and species. Severely depleted fish stocks leave fewer fish available to catch. Ports and markets may then receive smaller or less reliable supplies.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Unusually warm seawater can favour some harmful algae when nutrients and other suitable conditions are present. Warmth alone does not guarantee a harmful outbreak. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.

Prolonged warm seawater can help some disease-causing germs grow in new places or seasons. Salt content, human or animal contact and other local conditions also matter. Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Microbes can turn some nitrogen added to farm soil into nitrous oxide, a heat-trapping gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's basic method estimates 0.010 kilograms of nitrogen released in this gas per kilogram of qualifying nitrogen added, with a default uncertainty range of 0.002–0.018.
Nitrogen washed from fields can be changed by microbes in downstream soils and water. Some is released as nitrous oxide, adding an indirect source of emissions.

Manure, crop remains and other nitrogen inputs can release nitrous oxide through soil processes. Emissions depend on the practices and conditions. The basic Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimate for qualifying managed-soil inputs is 1% of added nitrogen, with a default range of 0.2–1.8%.
Making nitric acid for some fertilisers produces nitrous oxide as a by-product. This link applies to that manufacturing process, not to every type of fertiliser production.
outgoing: Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.

Nitrous oxide lasts long enough to spread through the atmosphere and add to heat trapping. Its effect is assessed from global abundance with other gases accounted for, so a sector's emissions cannot directly replace that measurement.

incoming: When less deep water reaches the surface, fewer nutrients may be available to tiny sunlit-water organisms. Their growth can decline, reducing food at the base of marine food chains.
Stronger separation between surface and deep ocean water can keep nutrients below the sunlit layer. Tiny drifting plants may grow less where they already lack nutrients.
Marine heatwaves can occur with wind and current changes that bring fewer nutrients to the surface. This can reduce the amount of drifting plant life or change which sizes are most common.
outgoing: Less growth by tiny drifting organisms can leave less food for the animals above them in the food chain. Fisheries that depend on this production may receive less reliable catches.
Changes in the tiny organisms that grow using sunlight alter the food available to other sea life. Different species and feeding relationships may then become dominant.

consequences: Changes in the tiny organisms that grow using sunlight alter the food available to other sea life. Different species and feeding relationships may then become dominant. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for limited current ecosystem-service function loss from degraded or isolated habitat patches and present patch connectivity and community condition deficit; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

incoming: Heavy pumping can draw salty groundwater into wells. If that water is repeatedly used on fields, evaporation can leave salt around roots. This does not happen everywhere, especially where water stays fresh and drainage removes salts.
Poorly managed irrigation and drainage can leave dissolved salts around plant roots. Salty groundwater rising toward the surface can add to the build-up.
Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect.
Seawater entering fields or freshwater supplies brings dissolved salts with it. Salt left around crop roots can make farming more difficult on low-lying land.
outgoing: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

human.summary: Too much salt around roots makes it harder for crops to take in water. Harvests can fall or become less reliable, depending on the crop and how the land is managed.

methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. incoming: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust.

outgoing: Sulfur pollution can form particles that reflect sunlight and briefly cool the climate. Reducing that pollution improves air quality but also removes some of the cooling that had partly hidden warming from other gases.
Sulfur dioxide reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid. It can then reach the ground in rain, snow or dry particles, sometimes far from its source.
Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.

incoming: Ships can carry organisms in stored water, on their hulls or with cargo. An introduced species becomes invasive only if it establishes, spreads and causes harm. Transport or detection alone does not prove that.
Aircraft and cargo can move living organisms to places they would not normally reach. Most do not establish harmful populations, so flight numbers cannot be treated as a count of invasions.
Warming can make new places suitable for some introduced species or help them survive longer seasons. It can also make conditions worse for other invaders, so effects differ by species and region.
outgoing: Harmful introduced species can displace native wildlife and change habitats or food webs. Being non-native alone does not establish harm. The effects need evidence for the species and place concerned.

Introduced animals carrying the fungus can expose native amphibians as they move between waters. Finding both together does not prove transmission. Timing, movement or genetic evidence is needed.

incoming: Seawater expands as it warms. As the ocean stores more heat, this expansion directly contributes to the rise in average sea level.

Warming makes seawater expand, contributing to the rise in average sea level. Melting land ice and changes in water storage add separate contributions, while local land movement affects what a coastline experiences.
When more coastal ice loses contact with the ground, there may be less resistance to glacier movement. Faster movement of land ice into the ocean raises sea level.
Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level.
Floating shelves help hold back ice on land. When they weaken, inland ice can flow into the ocean faster and add to sea-level rise.
Warming makes seawater expand and melts ice stored on land. Both processes raise average sea level.
Ice moving from land into the ocean adds water mass and raises sea level. The loss of already-floating ice matters mainly when it lets ice on land flow faster.

Ice lost from land adds water to the ocean and raises average sea level. Greenland's measured loss during 1992–2020 was equivalent to 13.5 millimetres globally, with an assessed range of 11.4–15.6 millimetres.
outgoing: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.
Rising seas can overwhelm mangroves if soil does not build up fast enough. They are especially exposed where buildings or steep ground prevent them from moving inland.
Higher coastal sea levels can push salty water toward underground freshwater. Pumping, replenishment, geology and connected canals or rivers determine the local response.

Higher sea levels make previously rare coastal water levels easier to reach. Across the assessed tide-gauge locations, relative sea-level rise is projected to make recent extreme still-water levels occur roughly 20–30 times as often by 2050. Local tides, storms and land movement affect the result.

human.summary: Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions. A thinner freshwater reserve beneath an island can leave wells with less water or more salt. Making that supply safe to drink may become harder.
consequences: Higher sea levels make previously rare coastal water levels easier to reach. Across the assessed tide-gauge locations, relative sea-level rise is projected to make recent extreme still-water levels occur roughly 20–30 times as often by 2050. Local tides, storms and land movement affect the result. Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.
human.hiddenCost: Higher water levels can repeatedly disrupt drains, pipes and roads before a major coastal disaster occurs.
human.whoPays: Residents, utilities, insurers and local public budgets can face growing maintenance and protection costs.

incoming: Warmer air and ground can lengthen the thaw season and speed decay in northern soils. Wet areas with little oxygen may release more methane.
Thawing ground exposes previously frozen plant material to decay. Where the soil stays waterlogged, this can produce methane that escapes into the air.
Sinking thawed ground can form ponds and wet hollows. Plant material decaying there with little oxygen can become a local source of methane.
outgoing: Methane made in thawing northern soils and lakes can escape into the air if it is not broken down first. The amount varies greatly with temperature, wetness and the route the gas takes.

human.summary: Methane made in thawing northern soils and lakes can escape into the air if it is not broken down first. methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. incoming: When water use is already close to available supply, seasonal or drought-related changes can leave lakes and reservoirs short. Imports, lower demand and careful operation can sometimes keep storage stable.
Less rain, runoff or river inflow means less water entering lakes, wetlands and reservoirs. Storage can fall if other inflows do not make up the loss.
Evaporation removes water from lakes and reservoirs. Their levels can fall when incoming water does not replace it.
Some lakes and wetlands exchange water with underground reserves. Changes in that exchange can raise or lower the amount stored at the surface.
Taking or diverting water can reduce lake and reservoir storage. The effect depends on how withdrawals compare with incoming water and operating rules.
Long periods of little rain reduce water entering lakes and reservoirs. Storage can fall or become less dependable if withdrawals continue.
Warming can increase evaporation and change when snowmelt and river water arrive. This can alter how much surface water remains stored through the year.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Changing amounts of water in lakes and reservoirs can make household, farm and industrial supplies harder to plan. Effects depend on timing, local demand and backup sources.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

levers: Limit water withdrawals to what the connected water system can support, while protecting essential human and environmental needs.
Reduce pollution and improve storage, drainage or treatment where local evidence shows these are the relevant problems.

incoming: Some farm chemicals remain in soil and sediment long after use and can enter living things. Current farming alone does not prove where an older chemical came from, and not all pesticides persist or enter food chains.

Some chemicals in water bind to sediment and enter animals through water or food. Many break down quickly or do not build up appreciably, while older contaminated sediment can remain a source after water levels fall.
outgoing: Chemicals stored in animal tissues can affect survival, reproduction or development if the dose is harmful. Finding a residue alone does not prove population damage, and effects differ between chemicals and food webs.

human.summary: Some chemicals can remain in organisms and pass through food chains, potentially exposing people through food or work. Risk depends on the chemical, dose and route of exposure.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.

planet.summary: Chemicals stored in animal tissues can affect survival, reproduction or development if the dose is harmful. Finding a residue alone does not prove population damage, and effects differ between chemicals and food webs.

response.defaultDriver: Some farm chemicals remain in soil and sediment long after use and can enter living things. Current farming alone does not prove where an older chemical came from, and not all pesticides persist or enter food chains.
levers: Use farming practices suited to the local soil, water and climate, with protection for workers and livestock.
Keep soils covered where appropriate, limit avoidable nutrient and chemical losses, and manage total water use rather than efficiency alone.

ice albedo feedback loops.name: Ice Albedo Feedback Loops

incoming: Melting snow and sea ice expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight. This adds heat and can encourage further melting, with the strength of the effect varying by place and season.

incoming: Clearing and splitting forests can make the remaining trees less able to withstand heat, drought, pests and fire. Trees may die where several of these pressures occur together.
When many dominant trees die across adjoining areas, the losses form a wider episode of forest die-off. Mapping the pattern helps distinguish it from isolated tree deaths.

Large beetle populations can overwhelm susceptible trees and disrupt their water and nutrient supply. Wide areas may die, but other stresses often contribute and delayed surveys can make the cause difficult to separate.
Warming can add heat and drying stress to forests. Large-scale tree loss depends on other pressures and uncertain local limits, so it cannot be inferred from temperature alone.
Long water shortages can stop trees moving enough water to survive. Heat, pests, fire injury and the condition of the forest can add to the stress.

Acidic pollution can wash useful nutrients from soil and make aluminium more available. This can weaken some trees against cold, pests and other stresses, rather than acting as a universal sole cause of forest loss.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Widespread tree deaths can reduce forest products, shade and cultural benefits and change local fire conditions. Human effects depend on the forest and what nearby communities rely on it for.

human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

planet.summary: Tree deaths change canopy cover, stored carbon and living space for other species. Regrowth, decay, fire and remaining vegetation shape the longer-term result.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established

response.defaultDriver: Clearing and splitting forests can make the remaining trees less able to withstand heat, drought, pests and fire. Trees may die where several of these pressures occur together.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

incoming: Where rainwater and sewage share a pipe system, too much incoming water can escape through an overflow outlet. This connection applies only to systems built to carry both together.
Heavy rain can send more runoff into pipes that carry both rainwater and sewage. Overflow occurs only where such a combined system exists and the incoming water exceeds its capacity.

incoming: An interruption in imported food or a sharp price rise can increase the need for aid. Shortfalls are more likely where local reserves, household income and aid capacity are limited.
Damaged roads, power, water or communications can prevent aid from reaching people. Funding, security and coordination can also block help even when physical systems still work.
Insufficient funding can force aid organisations to delay, reduce or close programmes. The effect depends on each operation's needs, access and freedom to use the funds.
Conflict, restrictions and attacks can stop aid workers reaching people. Supplies and funding cannot meet needs if access remains blocked.
Several disasters or conflicts occurring together can create more needs than aid services can meet. The shortfall depends on the capacity and circumstances of each response.
An expanding animal-to-human disease outbreak can increase needs for testing, care and containment at the same time. A resource gap occurs only if these needs exceed available response capacity.
More people facing acute hunger increases demand for food assistance. Funding and access limits can leave part of that need unmet.

carbon monoxide.description: A poisonous, colourless gas produced when fuels do not burn completely. Breathing it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. The danger depends on the concentration, time exposed and the person's health and activity.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current poisoning-related health and function loss from harmful carbon-monoxide exposure and small indirect current habitat condition deficit through adverse atmospheric chemistry; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Concentration and incomplete combustion are context; fatal and nonfatal health consequences are consolidated

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

incoming: Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced.
Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates.
Wildfires produce carbon monoxide as material burns incompletely. The amount varies with the fuel and burning conditions.
outgoing: Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.

Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.

human.summary: Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.
human.hiddenCost: Illness can bring treatment costs, time away from work or school and extra demand on carers and health services. The amount depends on who is exposed and what protection is available.
human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

planet.summary: Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.
planet.physicalLimit: Do not assign a reading to one source without an assessment that defines and supports that connection.

response.defaultDriver: Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

gulf stream transport and position.name: Gulf Stream Transport and Position
gulf stream transport and position.description: Changes in the strength and route of the powerful current carrying warm water through the western North Atlantic. incoming: Part of the strong northward Atlantic surface current belongs to the ocean's wider overturning circulation. Changes in that wider system can affect it, but winds also drive the current, so the two are not interchangeable.

Long-lasting North Atlantic pressure and wind changes can influence the position of the current farther downstream. Relationships vary by place and time, and matching patterns alone do not prove one direct cause.
outgoing: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.

human.summary: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current. Flooding from the sea can add salt and other contamination to drinking-water sources or disrupt intakes. Water plants may then have difficulty providing safe supplies.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

planet.summary: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.
domains: ocean water, currents and marine life
planet.physicalLimit: One section does not represent the whole current or Atlantic circulation. Do not infer collapse from short-term variation or use coastal sea level alone as proof of changing currents.

response.defaultDriver: Part of the strong northward Atlantic surface current belongs to the ocean's wider overturning circulation. Changes in that wider system can affect it, but winds also drive the current, so the two are not interchangeable.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: Gulf Stream section transport and path position
measurement.unit: Sverdrups of volume transport, kilometres or degrees latitude of a declared path contour, metres per second of velocity, and centimetres of cross-current dynamic sea-level difference reported separately
measurement.geography: named current segment and cross-stream section such as the Florida Straits at 27 degrees north, Cape Hatteras separation region, or downstream longitude band with depth and contour definitions
measurement.cadence: daily transport and altimetry observation with monthly, annual, and multi-decadal method-consistent assessment
measurement.method: Identify the exact section of current, depths, period and measuring instruments. Keep calibration and tidal corrections, gaps and uncertainty. Distinguish current position from water volume carried, and the Florida Current from the wider Gulf Stream and Atlantic overturning circulation.
measurement.uncertainty: The current carries more water farther downstream, and different depths can change differently. Wind-driven circulation and overturning are not the same, while instrument corrections affect trends.
measurement.boundary: One section does not represent the whole current or Atlantic circulation. Do not infer collapse from short-term variation or use coastal sea level alone as proof of changing currents.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current annual-equivalent health and service-function loss where floodplain exposure results in damage and present floodplain condition deficits after damaging flood episodes; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

incoming: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time.

If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.

Carbon dioxide accumulating in the air reduces the heat Earth can release to space. Yearly emissions alone do not determine the change because oceans and land absorb a varying share. The assessment uses global concentration relative to a stated baseline.

More methane across the atmosphere traps additional heat and also affects ozone and water vapour high above Earth. A local leak or brief concentration spike is not equivalent to a change in the global annual heat balance.

Nitrous oxide lasts long enough to spread through the atmosphere and add to heat trapping. Its effect is assessed from global abundance with other gases accounted for, so a sector's emissions cannot directly replace that measurement.

Using less powerful heat-trapping cooling gases and preventing leaks reduces their contribution to warming. The benefit is measured against what would happen if those releases continued without controls.
outgoing: When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.

human.summary: When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts.
