incoming: Too little oxygen makes sheltered coastal water less suitable for young fish and shellfish. Fewer may survive to join the adult populations caught nearby.
Separated layers in warm river-mouth waters can make oxygen shortages worse. Young fish and shellfish may then have less suitable sheltered habitat.

Changes in seawater chemistry can harm the growth or survival of some young fish and shell-forming animals. Effects differ between species. Evidence of exposure alone does not show that an entire estuary has lost its nursery role.
outgoing: Losing sheltered habitat for young fish can mean fewer survive to adulthood. Where this stage limits population recovery, the chance of a serious decline in catches increases.
Damage to places where young fish grow can reduce future adult populations. Coastal fishing communities may then receive smaller or less predictable catches.

human.summary: Damage to places where young fish grow can affect catches later, after those fish would have reached harvestable size. Coastal food and income effects may therefore be delayed.
consequences: A fishery can decline without an obvious sudden die-off of adults.
Less successful breeding and survival of young fish can make future catches less dependable.
Households relying on seafood may face reduced income and food availability.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to places where young fish grow may reduce later catches, so fishing losses can appear well after the initial damage.
human.whoPays: Fishing communities and small seafood businesses can lose future income and supplies.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current smoke-health, displacement and livelihood function loss from damaging peat fires and present peat-soil and wetland condition deficit from deep burning; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Current burned and impaired stock; do not multiply carbon depth, area and recovery time into separate damage premiums

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

incoming: Draining peat lowers its moisture and makes it easier to ignite. Once burning, dry peat can smoulder for a long time below the surface.
Longer or more severe fire seasons increase the chance that fire reaches dry peat. Repeated burning can occur before the wetland has recovered.
Damage to wetland plants and water flow can leave peat dry and exposed. Fires may start more easily, burn deeper and become harder to put out.
outgoing: Burning peat releases carbon stored over long periods as carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The amount depends partly on the area burned and how deep the fire reaches.

human.summary: Burning peat releases carbon stored over long periods as carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The amount depends partly on the area burned and how deep the fire reaches. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

planet.summary: Burning peat releases carbon stored over long periods as carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The amount depends partly on the area burned and how deep the fire reaches.
planet.physicalLimit: A wetland fire is not necessarily burning peat. Confirm the peatland location, and do not turn missing burned-area records into zero.

response.defaultDriver: Draining peat lowers its moisture and makes it easier to ignite. Once burning, dry peat can smoulder for a long time below the surface.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

measurement.metric: Peat-fire burned area and carbon emission
measurement.unit: hectares burned and tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent with peat depth, combustion factor, and reporting interval stated
measurement.geography: mapped peatland fire perimeter, province, basin, or country
measurement.cadence: event-based with seasonal and annual summaries
measurement.method: Match checked fire detections or boundaries with confirmed peatland maps. Keep burn depth, duration, moisture and the assumptions used to estimate emissions, including limits from clouds and smoke.
measurement.uncertainty: Underground smouldering is hard to observe. Burn depth, peat density, repeat fires and uncertain emission rates can produce large differences in estimates.
measurement.boundary: A wetland fire is not necessarily burning peat. Confirm the peatland location, and do not turn missing burned-area records into zero.

incoming: Warm, moist air near the ground can rise more strongly if the air above allows it. Warming higher up, dryness or a layer that blocks rising air can prevent this potential from becoming a storm.
outgoing: More strongly rising air can support heavier rain, but moisture, storm movement and organisation also matter. High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it.
Lightning Flash Density and Seasonality Anomaly
Strong rising air can move water and ice through clouds in ways that help generate lightning. Other cloud conditions matter, so one measure of atmospheric energy is not a lightning forecast.

human.summary: More strongly rising air can support heavier rain, but moisture, storm movement and organisation also matter. High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it. Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
human.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
human.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.

planet.summary: More strongly rising air can support heavier rain, but moisture, storm movement and organisation also matter. High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it.
consequences: Strong rising air can move water and ice through clouds in ways that help generate lightning. Other cloud conditions matter, so one measure of atmospheric energy is not a lightning forecast.
planet.physicalLimit: CAPE, a measure of potential rising-air energy, alone cannot predict a storm, hail, tornadoes, lightning or heavy rain. Other conditions and observed outcomes are needed.

response.defaultDriver: Warm, moist air near the ground can rise more strongly if the air above allows it. Warming higher up, dryness or a layer that blocks rising air can prevent this potential from becoming a storm.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.metric: Convective available potential energy and inhibition anomaly
measurement.unit: joules per kilogram for parcel-specific CAPE and CIN, with lifted index, humidity, shear, and vertical motion reported separately
measurement.geography: named sounding station, satellite pixel, reanalysis grid, forecast domain, or climatological region
measurement.cadence: hourly to six-hourly environmental analysis with seasonal and annual climatology review
measurement.method: Keep the full vertical temperature and moisture profile and the method used to estimate rising-air energy. Also record layers that block rising air, winds changing with height and the trigger that could lift the air.
measurement.uncertainty: Results change with the air parcel chosen and the accuracy of moisture readings. Models and satellites can smooth important layers, while simple calculations may overstate the energy a real updraft uses.
measurement.boundary: CAPE, a measure of potential rising-air energy, alone cannot predict a storm, hail, tornadoes, lightning or heavy rain. Other conditions and observed outcomes are needed.

incoming: Sustained warming can raise the height at which snow lasts through summer above an ice cap's summit. The cap then loses its remaining area where snow can build up over the long term.
Repeated winters with too little snow leave small ice caps with less new ice to replace melting. Their summits and connecting ice can thin until a once-continuous cap breaks apart.
Soot makes snow and ice absorb more sunlight. Persistent extra melting can help thin and break up an already vulnerable small ice cap.
outgoing: Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level.

human.summary: Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level. Higher seawater levels can push salt into the shallow freshwater reserve beneath a small island. The usable layer may become thinner or saltier, depending on local conditions.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

planet.summary: Losing an ice cap's summit removes stored land ice and may expose darker ground that speeds further melting. Water from the shrinking ice cap contributes to rising sea level.

response.defaultDriver: Sustained warming can raise the height at which snow lasts through summer above an ice cap's summit. The cap then loses its remaining area where snow can build up over the long term.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

incoming: Heavy rain and flood peaks can increase water force against river banks. Saturated or undercut banks may collapse where they are vulnerable.
A rapid rise in runoff can increase river depth and speed. Banks erode when the force of moving water exceeds the ground's resistance.
Losing trees can increase runoff and sediment reaching rivers. Where bank vegetation is also lost, fewer roots hold the bank in place.
outgoing: Continued river-bank loss can add fine sediment, bury habitat and remove shade. River plants and animals may lose suitable places to live.

human.summary: Eroding riverbanks can remove land and damage nearby routes or property. Extra sediment can also complicate water use downstream, depending on where it travels.

response.defaultDriver: Heavy rain and flood peaks can increase water force against river banks. Saturated or undercut banks may collapse where they are vulnerable.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.
Address the documented local pressures, such as clearing, pollution or harmful harvesting, and track whether wildlife and habitat actually recover.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.

incoming: Warming may expose more bare mountain ground while reducing the cold, snowy conditions some species need. Suitable habitat can shrink even where the total ice-free area grows.
Thawing frozen ground on exposed rocky peaks changes moisture, stability and cold local conditions. Specialised species can lose suitable habitat even as the total area of bare rock grows.
Earlier snow loss reduces the time that cool, moist patches remain on exposed mountain peaks. Specialised plants and animals may face a longer period of heat and drying.
outgoing: Losing suitable cold habitat on isolated rocky peaks leaves specialised plants and animals with fewer places to survive. Small, separated populations may face a greater chance of disappearing locally.

human.summary: Changes to isolated mountain habitats can threaten specialised wildlife and valued natural places. The available evidence does not establish a direct, measured health or income burden on people.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

incoming: Splitting forests into separate patches can make it harder for some species to move, breed or recolonise an area. Other species can cross the gaps, so a map alone does not prove that movement has stopped.
Development can remove habitat and add roads, noise or light that interfere with wildlife movement. Parks, gardens and safe crossings can preserve useful links for some species.
outgoing: Less movement between habitats can isolate populations and limit access to food or cooler places. Connections are not always the main constraint, and they can also spread disease or invasive species.
Migratory Bird Timing, Route, and Stopover Disruption

Losing resting or seasonal habitats can force migrating birds to travel farther or leave them with less food. Some use alternative sites, so fewer birds at one stop does not by itself prove a failing route.
Losing usable routes between habitats can reduce breeding between separated groups. Small, isolated populations can then lose genetic variety more easily.

human.summary: Breaking connections between habitats can make wildlife populations harder to sustain. Human effects depend on local uses and values. They cannot be calculated from a broken route alone.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.

incoming: Warmer central and eastern Pacific water shifts rising air and tropical storms eastward. This can weaken or move the usual east-to-west circulation, but one event does not establish a long-term trend.

Cooler central and eastern Pacific water can strengthen the usual pattern of rising air in the west and sinking air in the east. The response differs between events and does not by itself explain a decades-long trend.
outgoing: Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence.

human.summary: Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence. Unreliable seasonal rains can disrupt planting, watering and harvesting. Farms that depend heavily on these rains may produce less food.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current local safe-water and fishery-function loss during harmful sediment pulses and present fjord benthic and water-clarity condition deficit from adverse pulses; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

incoming: Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.
Meltwater carries fine rock and soil into the water below glaciers. How much arrives, and at what depth, depends on the amount of water and how it enters the basin.
Heavy rain can wash loose material from glacier-fed rivers and deltas. Short bursts of flow may carry fine particles and larger sediment into nearby coastal waters.
Breaking ice and falling icebergs can disturb sediment near a glacier front. Underwater slides and cloudy currents may move material that had already settled.
outgoing: No outgoing relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.

human.summary: Large amounts of sediment entering a narrow coastal inlet can change water conditions and seabed habitats. Consequences for fishing or other uses depend on the event and location.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

planet.summary: A sudden sediment supply can cloud water or cover seabed habitats. The effect depends on grain size, amount and where currents deposit the material.
domains: No separate direct ecosystem effect established
planet.physicalLimit: Glacier retreat rate alone does not measure sediment delivery.

response.defaultDriver: Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.
levers: Reduce heat-trapping emissions to limit further warming of ice and frozen ground.
Use local monitoring and hazard maps to plan water supplies, transport and development around changing ice and ground conditions.

incoming: Hot air makes it harder for an electrical transformer to release the heat it produces. Its hottest parts can become hotter still, ageing insulation faster and increasing failure risk.

outgoing: A failed transformer can interrupt electricity to essential services. Replacements can take a long time, leaving connected facilities more vulnerable until supply is restored.

freeze-thaw rock fracturing.name: Freeze-Thaw Rock Fracturing

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Heat and dry soil together can make it harder for trees to move enough water and keep growing. Earlier damage and pests can add to this pressure and contribute to tree death.

In western North American pine forests, warming can help some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter. During severe drought, weakened trees may be less able to resist the increased beetle pressure.
Long water shortages can disrupt a tree's water transport and weaken its defences. The air's demand for moisture also matters, so temperature alone is not enough to describe the exposure.
Severe fires can kill tall canopy trees by burning crowns or damaging bark and roots. Some injured trees die later, including after insect attack.
Large bark-beetle populations can attack and kill host trees. The trees selected are not always simply the ones that were already most stressed.
outgoing: When many dominant trees die across adjoining areas, the losses form a wider episode of forest die-off. Mapping the pattern helps distinguish it from isolated tree deaths.

human.summary: Losing large upper-layer trees can remove shade, forest products and valued habitat. Effects on people vary with the forest and the resources they depend on.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

response.defaultDriver: Heat and dry soil together can make it harder for trees to move enough water and keep growing. Earlier damage and pests can add to this pressure and contribute to tree death.
levers: Protect remaining suitable habitat and restore damaged areas where recovery is possible.

incoming: North Atlantic pressure patterns change winds and heat exchange over the ocean. These can strengthen, weaken or shift its northern circular flow, but no atmospheric phase gives one fixed response everywhere.

Changes in salt content alter seawater density and can change northern Atlantic circulation. Fresher water does not automatically mean weaker flow because temperature, winds and the water carried by currents also matter.

Warmer or less strongly cooled surface water may sink less and change northern Atlantic flow. Temperature alone cannot determine the response because salt content and transported heat also affect density and circulation.

human.summary: Changes in the broad North Atlantic circulation can alter the movement of heat and nutrients. Local effects on people need separate evidence. One circulation index does not directly measure fishing or coastal losses.

human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

planet.summary: Changes in this broad circulation alter the transport of heat, salt and nutrients in the North Atlantic. Different regions can change differently, and this is not the same as the ocean's deep overturning circulation.

levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

measurement.metric: North Atlantic subpolar-gyre circulation strength
measurement.unit: square metres per second squared of wind-stress curl, centimetres of sea-surface-height anomaly or gradient, metres per second of geostrophic velocity, and Sverdrups of named boundary or gyre transport reported separately
measurement.geography: declared Labrador, Irminger, Iceland, Rockall, eastern or full North Atlantic subpolar-gyre domain with contour, depth, section, and basin boundary stated
measurement.cadence: daily to monthly reanalysis and altimetry with seasonal hydrography and multi-year method-consistent trend review
measurement.method: Define the northern Atlantic circulation area, depth and period. Keep sea height, winds, temperature, salt, density and current readings with their methods. Distinguish flow strength, area, position and water properties.
measurement.uncertainty: There is no single universal index. Sea height reflects both water mass and expansion, while winds and density changes can act in opposite directions. Horizontal circulation is different from Atlantic overturning.
measurement.boundary: Regional cooling or one sea-height reading does not prove weaker circulation. Do not combine incompatible indices or treat one decade-long phase as a steady climate trend.

incoming: Strongly separated water layers mix less easily, slowing the oxygen supply to the bottom. Oxygen can run low as organisms continue to use it, especially where much organic material is decaying.
Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed.
Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life.
outgoing: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

human.summary: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web. Changes in feeding relationships can alter which fish are available and when. Fishing businesses may receive a less predictable mix or quantity of seafood.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

planet.summary: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.

response.defaultDriver: Strongly separated water layers mix less easily, slowing the oxygen supply to the bottom. Oxygen can run low as organisms continue to use it, especially where much organic material is decaying.
levers: Reduce the heat-trapping emissions and local pollution that add pressure to marine habitats.
Protect and restore suitable coastal habitats, and manage fishing and coastal development around observed local conditions.

incoming: Excess nutrients can change oxygen, algae and ammonia levels in freshwater. Sensitive young mussels may be harmed where exposure becomes high enough.
Dams and other barriers can change flow and prevent movement of fish that carry young mussels during part of their life cycle. This can limit mussel spread and recovery.
Long periods of low water can expose mussel beds, increase heat and concentrate pollution. Fish needed for the mussels' life cycle may also lose access.
outgoing: Large, lasting mussel losses remove animals that filter water and help stabilise riverbeds. Nutrient movement and habitats supported by dense mussel groups may also change.

human.summary: Losing mussels can change river ecosystems and species valued by local communities. Population counts alone do not establish a direct drinking-water or financial loss.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

incoming: Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly
Strong rising air can move water and ice through clouds in ways that help generate lightning. Other cloud conditions matter, so one measure of atmospheric energy is not a lightning forecast.

Warming changes moisture, rising air and the ice processes involved in lightning. Models disagree on how these effects combine, so the direction of future lightning change remains uncertain in many regions.
outgoing: Lightning Ignition under Fire Weather Conditions

Lightning reaching the ground can ignite vegetation when it is dry enough and rain does not put the fire out. Most flashes do not start a recorded fire, and later spread depends on weather and response.

human.summary: Changes in where and when lightning occurs can affect people outdoors and exposed equipment. Risk also depends on protection, activity and whether strikes reach vulnerable places.

levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.

incoming: Heat and other stresses can reduce the survival of young corals and their ability to settle on a reef. This makes recovery harder where the reef is already damaged.
Seawater above the temperatures young corals can tolerate can reduce survival and successful settlement. Effects vary by species and stage of growth.
Stressed adult corals may have less energy to reproduce and support their young. Fewer larvae may be produced, or fewer may survive and settle successfully.
Changing seawater chemistry can interfere with early coral growth and the signals young corals use to find a place to settle. Sensitive species may have lower survival.
outgoing: If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef.

human.summary: If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef. incoming: Forest loss can increase erosion, change river channels and remove streamside habitat. Some stretches may become unsuitable, separating populations along the river.
Dams and water diversions can block movement and separate river habitats. Their effects need evidence about the actual barriers and the species trying to pass them.
Poorly designed pipes, crossings and gates can stop aquatic animals moving along streams. Whether a crossing acts as a barrier depends on its design and the species involved.
Embankments and straightened channels can cut rivers off from nearby floodplains and side habitats. Documented barriers are needed to assess how much wildlife movement is restricted.
outgoing: Barriers can isolate aquatic populations and prevent access to breeding sites or refuge. Repeated or widespread isolation can weaken the river's living community.

incoming: Warming can dry lower forest margins and prevent young trees from establishing, while allowing trees to grow higher where cold once limited them. Both boundaries and local moisture need to be checked before claiming the forest is shrinking overall.
Long dry periods can weaken mountain trees and prevent regrowth after damage. Some forests recover when moisture returns, so a short decline in greenness is not proof of permanent loss.
Severe fires can remove mountain trees and seed sources. Lasting forest loss occurs when trees cannot regrow. Many forests normally recover from fire, and some lower-intensity fires support renewal.
outgoing: Lasting changes in mountain forests alter shelter, food and connections used by wildlife. Some species lose habitat while others benefit from openings or forest expansion, so population changes need separate evidence.

human.summary: Changes in mountain forests can affect local resources, recreation and valued habitats. Human effects depend on which forest areas are lost and what communities rely on them for.
human.hiddenCost: Damage to land or water can reduce the benefits people receive from healthy ecosystems and create restoration costs. The source does not provide a measured monetary total for all of those effects.
human.whoPays: Land managers, local communities, resource users and public budgets may face costs. Who pays depends on land rights, responsibility for damage and available support.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Warmer air can carry more water vapour, allowing long bands of moist air to transport more water. This does not guarantee more events or stronger winds in every place, and historical trends depend on the available record.
outgoing: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event.

Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment.

human.summary: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event. Very heavy rain can overwhelm airport drains and reduce visibility. Flights and ground operations may be delayed or cancelled.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
consequences: Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment. Changed incoming river flows may no longer fit a dam's release plans. Operators can struggle to meet water, flood-control or electricity commitments.
human.hiddenCost: Making water safe, finding replacement supplies and repairing damaged systems can be costly. Effects depend on the local source, users and available alternatives.
human.whoPays: Households, farmers, water utilities and public services can face costs when dependable water is lost. The burden depends on prices, support and access to another supply.

incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific.

Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions.
Changes in east-to-west tropical Pacific winds affect how surface water moves and how cold water rises from below. The direction of the wind change determines the response.

human.summary: Weaker east-to-west winds over the equatorial Pacific allow warm surface water to move east. This can reinforce warming in the central and eastern Pacific. Changes in Pacific ocean temperatures can bring heat, drought or flooding to farming regions. These conditions can damage harvests and interrupt food supplies.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Stronger, rather than weaker, east-to-west Pacific winds push warm water west and bring colder water up in the east. That opposite phase of the wind measure supports cooler tropical Pacific conditions. Changes linked to unusually cool Pacific waters can bring destructive rain to some regions and drought to others. Harvests and fisheries may be affected in different ways across regions.
human.hiddenCost: Unreliable food supplies can mean lost farm or fishing income, wasted products and higher delivery or purchase costs. Stocks, trade and public support can soften those effects.
human.whoPays: Producers, workers, food businesses and consumers can all be affected. Households spending much of their income on food have less room to absorb price rises.

incoming: Losing seagrass removes plants that take up carbon and can expose carbon-rich seabed to erosion and decay. Stored carbon may then be lost.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. incoming: Removing methane from air uses highly reactive chemicals called hydroxyl radicals. More methane can use some of that capacity and stay longer, but other chemical and weather changes can increase removal instead.

Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.
outgoing: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.

human.summary: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere. When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
human.hiddenCost: Service interruptions can bring repair costs, lost working time and spending on backup supplies. Wider losses depend on how long the interruption lasts and which activities rely on it.
human.whoPays: Service operators, customers, workers and public budgets can share the costs. People without alternative services are more exposed to disruption.

planet.summary: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.
planet.physicalLimit: Methane growth alone does not show a global decline in removal capacity. Compare matching lifetime definitions, and do not assign changes to one gas without checking the wider chemistry.

response.defaultDriver: Removing methane from air uses highly reactive chemicals called hydroxyl radicals. More methane can use some of that capacity and stay longer, but other chemical and weather changes can increase removal instead.
levers: Reducing heat-trapping emissions limits further warming. Local health and environmental protection is still needed for changes already under way.
Track local conditions and use warning systems suited to the people and services exposed.

measurement.cadence: annual multi-year inversion and chemistry-model assessment
measurement.method: State how the air's methane-removal capacity is defined and averaged. Keep methane, other reactive gases, moisture, ozone, fires and lightning in the chemical model, along with the observations used to check it.
measurement.uncertainty: Hydroxyl radicals last too briefly for a dense global monitoring network. Models disagree about trends and are sensitive to emissions, chemistry, air movement and how places are weighted.
measurement.boundary: Methane growth alone does not show a global decline in removal capacity. Compare matching lifetime definitions, and do not assign changes to one gas without checking the wider chemistry.

consequences: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

incoming: Heavy pumping near the sea lowers freshwater levels. This can draw salty water toward wells and reduce the usable supply.
Repeated flooding by the sea can add salt to connected underground freshwater stores. Shallow or exposed stores may become less suitable for drinking or farming.
Salt moving through river mouths can also reach connected underground water. This can make coastal wells and reserves saltier.
outgoing: Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.
As coastal wells become saltier, ordinary supplies may be less usable. Utilities or households may turn increasingly to equipment that removes salt from water.

human.summary: Salt or other contamination in coastal groundwater can make wells less dependable. The amount of water underground may hide a decline in its usefulness.
consequences: Wells may still contain water that has become too salty for normal use.
Farms and utilities lose flexibility when a formerly reliable freshwater source deteriorates.
Communities may become more dependent on imported water or costly salt removal.
human.hiddenCost: Underground water can remain present but become too salty to use without extra treatment or a replacement supply.
human.whoPays: Well users, farmers and coastal utilities can face higher costs or lost access.

planet.summary: Saltier underground water gives utilities fewer easy-to-treat supplies. Extra treatment or replacement sources may be needed.
planet.physicalLimit: Recovery from salt contamination can be slow and depends on the underground geology and water flows.

response.defaultDriver: Heavy pumping and seawater movement can worsen quality where management tracks only the quantity withdrawn.
levers: Monitor salt levels as well as water levels and limit damaging withdrawals.

incoming: Unreliable harvests can reduce local food supplies and increase prices. Households may then find it harder to obtain enough nutritious food.
Reliance on imported food exposes households to supply and price changes elsewhere. Disruptions can make enough nutritious food harder to afford or obtain.
Sharp or unpredictable changes in basic food prices make household budgets harder to manage. Families with little income or stored food can struggle to buy enough.
Warming-related heat, drought and floods can damage harvests and food transport. Higher prices or reduced supplies make adequate food harder to obtain for households with little money or reserves.

Long-lasting damage to soil, vegetation and water supplies can make food production less reliable. Income, imports, technology and public support can protect households from some of the resulting losses.
Farms dependent on costly inputs or facing damaged soil and limited water can become less reliable. Food access is affected when these pressures change harvests, prices or household income.
Several hazards can disrupt food production, income and access at the same time. Conflict, inequality and market conditions can make the resulting hardship better or worse.
Blocked routes, conflict or restrictions can stop food aid reaching people in crisis. Households may go without adequate food even when supplies exist elsewhere.
Funding cuts can mean food aid reaches fewer people or provides smaller rations. Hunger can worsen among households depending on that support.
outgoing: Long-lasting difficulty obtaining enough food can push people to leave their homes. Jobs, conflict and other economic conditions also influence whether people move.
More people facing acute hunger increases demand for food assistance. Funding and access limits can leave part of that need unmet.
More people facing severe hunger increases the need for urgent food, nutrition and delivery support. Response services must expand quickly enough to meet it.

scoreBreakdown.note: Estimated current impact. Higher means more harm. Values are rounded.

incoming: Making and using fertilisers increases the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus available in the environment. Some can escape into rivers and coastal waters if losses are not controlled.
Nitrogen that crops do not absorb can wash or drain into waterways. It can encourage excessive algae growth and the oxygen loss that follows.
Sewage released without adequate treatment carries nitrogen and phosphorus into water. These nutrients can worsen pollution in rivers, lakes and coastal areas.
Producing large amounts of short-lived clothing creates more wastewater and waste to manage. Pollution reaching rivers or coasts depends on what that waste contains and how effectively it is treated.
Nitrogen applied to fields but not absorbed by crops can wash away or move through soil. It may then pollute rivers, lakes or groundwater.
Leaking or overflowing manure stores can send nitrogen and phosphorus into water. Applying the manure to fields at unsuitable times can create another route for losses.
outgoing: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.
Excess nutrients and organic matter can add stress to coastal reefs. This may make heat-related bleaching and recovery worse, depending on local conditions.
Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed.
Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions.
Excess nutrients can change oxygen, algae and ammonia levels in freshwater. Sensitive young mussels may be harmed where exposure becomes high enough.
Extra nitrogen and phosphorus can fuel algae growth. As the algae decay, they may use up enough oxygen to create persistent low-oxygen areas in vulnerable waters.

human.summary: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops. Toxic algae or low oxygen can kill fish or make seafood unsafe. Harvest closures and damaged stocks can then interrupt supplies arriving at ports and markets.
domains: food supplies and ways of earning a living
consequences: Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions. Dense jellyfish groups can clog fishing nets, harm catches or affect fish-farm enclosures. Local fishing operations may be interrupted while the event lasts.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current coastal protection and food-function loss from adverse seagrass decline and present seagrass community, sediment and habitat-function condition deficit; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current unmet shelter, food, care and essential-function loss attributable to aid funding shortfalls and no independent ecological endpoint within unmet humanitarian services; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: Budget gaps do not directly equal harm; actually unmet needs estimated with health and service overlap consolidated

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

outgoing: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust.
Coal-burning releases sulfur dioxide, which can turn into acid and settle downwind. Emissions at a power station do not by themselves show how much reaches a particular place.
Sulfur dioxide from coal burning can form fine particles downwind. Exposure to these pollutants can harm the lungs and heart, with controls affecting how much is released.

consequences: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust. Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.

Sulfur particles formed after coal burning reflect some sunlight and temporarily mask part of greenhouse warming. They also cause serious air pollution. Reducing them removes some cooling while improving air quality. Some airborne particles have partly offset warming by reflecting sunlight. Removing that cooling influence can add near-term warming unless the warming influence of other gases also falls enough.

human.whoPays: People who become ill, their families, employers and public health services can share these costs. People with little income or access to care may have fewer ways to cope.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. outgoing: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity adds to the total released into the air. This record covers only the activities, places and years specified in its source, so it should not be counted again in an overlapping total. The cited assessment gives a median direct climate impact of 760 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for the assessed coal technology, with a range of 670–870. CO₂-equivalent combines gases by their warming effect. It is not a measurement of carbon dioxide alone.

Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity joins emissions from other sources and builds up in the atmosphere. Its contribution to warming accumulates over time, rather than staying near the place where it was released.

Some carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity is eventually absorbed by the ocean. It changes seawater chemistry as part of the combined global total. A particular local change cannot be assigned to this source alone.

human.summary: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity adds to the total released into the air. This record covers only the activities, places and years specified in its source, so it should not be counted again in an overlapping total. The cited assessment gives a median direct climate impact of 760 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for the assessed coal technology, with a range of 670–870. CO₂-equivalent combines gases by their warming effect. It is not a measurement of carbon dioxide alone. Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
domains: power, water, transport and other essential services
consequences: Carbon dioxide from burning coal to make electricity joins emissions from other sources and builds up in the atmosphere. Its contribution to warming accumulates over time, rather than staying near the place where it was released. Hotter air can make aircraft takeoff more difficult and put extra strain on runways and ground operations. The effects depend on the aircraft, airport and conditions.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

methodCopy.title: How the TULIP Score works
methodCopy.summary: TULIP Score gives a one-decimal view of estimated current impact on a 1–10 scale. This release uses labelled internal estimates at the 28 September 2026 cut-off. Older source evidence informs some estimates; this is not a measured 2026 global total or a ten-year forecast.
methodCopy.components: People and nature each receive 50% weight in every issue score. People covers attributable health and essential-function loss. Nature covers affected habitat area and its present condition deficit. A zero component needs an explicit scoped absence estimate; missing evidence is never silently treated as zero or given to the other component.
methodCopy.formula: TULIP maps each consequence amount separately against fixed benchmarks, using a logarithmic curve between them, then averages the two scores and rounds once. Benchmarks, health/function equivalence and weights are TULIP choices. They do not change when unrelated topics are added. A documented rare, irreversible ecological loss can add up to 1 point to nature before averaging, at most 0.5 overall, with a ceiling of 10.
methodCopy.missing: Every published issue in this release has an Internal estimate. Its harmed-population, loss-per-person, affected-area and condition assumptions are documented separately from source measurements. These are provisional judgments, not independently calibrated facts. New issues need their own reviewed assessment before publication.
methodCopy.evidence: Historical records and WMO standard normals provide context. Unusualness, exposure, citations and graph connections are not harm amounts. The human estimate represents annual-equivalent health/function loss; nature represents a present condition stock. Their comparison is an explicit TULIP convention. Source years and transfer assumptions remain in the assessment record.
methodCopy.limits: An aggregate score is not the worst local impact or an event probability. Scores for overlapping pathways must not be added. This release has no calibrated confidence interval. Sensitivity tests are hypothetical changes to assumptions, not uncertainty bounds. Response topics receive no danger score. Future scenario outlooks are separate from the current rating.

required: Compatible current global outcome aggregation and counterfactual attribution for current climate-related health and function loss allocated to civil-aviation fossil co2 and current climate-related habitat condition deficit allocated to civil-aviation fossil co2; independently supported consequence conversion and uncertainty.
evidenceAudit.reuse: Bibliographic and physical context only, except explicitly identified source endpoints. Citations do not validate authored magnitude assumptions.
evidenceAudit.boundaryReview: CO2-only source history; persistent contrails, airport hazards and noise are excluded

sensitivity.note: Halving/doubling amounts and changing weights are hypothetical stress tests, not confidence bounds, probability distributions or validated model alternatives.

outlook.basis: No future scenario number or historic trend multiplier enters this current estimate.
